World.title: Nakonde election preps advance
World.content:
Electoral stakeholders in Nakonde district in Muchinga Province have commended the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) for promoting transparency and ensuring peace during the preparations for Thursday’s general elections.

Nakonde Forum for Persons with Disabilities Chairperson, Martin Gondwe, thanked ECZ for exhibiting transparency and hoped this would be maintained throughout the electoral process.

Speaking in an interview with the Zambia News and Information Services (ZANIS), Mr Gondwe called on all political parties to preach peace in communities ahead of the polls.

Mr Gondwe further appealed for inclusion of persons with disabilities in the voting process and asked if braille tactile jackets will also be available during the verification exercise.

“Make sure you preach peace wherever you are going, in our camps. Persons with disabilities and women inclusive, we want to participate in a violence-free election this year,” he said.

And United Party for National Development (UPND) Chairperson for Nakonde District, Derick Banda, said the process had been peaceful.

He expressed optimism that the same peaceful mood will prevail as poll staff are deployed and dispatched to polling stations tomorrow.

He also expressed gratitude to other stakeholders who have been available from inception, to ensure transparency.

“So far so good, the process has been peaceful for us. The most important thing we always preach is peace. Even from the time we received the ballot papers it has been peaceful,” he said.

And National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) Mwenzo Constituency Chairperson, Frederick Siame, called for continued transparency during the dispatch of poll staff and verification of election material.

Mr Siame also expressed satisfaction with how the election preparations have been conducted in the district.

“So far so good. As we do the verification exercise when dispatching poll staff, we need to verify what the contents are. What we are asking for is the same transparency that has prevailed to continue,” Mr Siame said.

World.title: ZAF, NAPSA, LWSC seal deal
World.content:
Ministry of Defense Permanent Secretary Maambo Hamaundu has described the signing of a contract for the design and construction of a bulk water pipeline system for several housing developments in Lusaka as a significant step towards improving access to reliable water supply.

The pipeline will serve Kingsland Housing Estate, Zambia Air Force Twin Palm Base, Datong and River View Park, respectively.

Speaking during the signing ceremony, Mr Hamaundu said the project underscores the beginning of a transformative development initiative, aimed at providing sustainable infrastructure and improving the quality of life for citizens.

He said the initiative demonstrates what can be achieved when government institutions and strategic partners work together towards a common national purpose.

Mr Hamaundu said the government remains committed to improving the lives of Zambians through deliberate investment in infrastructure, housing, water supply and sanitation.

He said access to clean and reliable water is a fundamental human necessity and an important driver of national development, as it supports public health, education, economic productivity, environmental sustainability and social well-being.

Mr Hamaundu said the project aligns with the government’s broader development agenda of ensuring that citizens have access to essential services that promote dignity, good health and economic opportunity.

He noted that improved access to safe water and sanitation can reduce disease outbreaks, improve productivity and make housing developments more attractive to investors.

Mr Hamaundu commended the multi-sectoral partnership involving the Zambia Air Force, the National Pension Scheme Authority (NAPSA) and the Lusaka Water Supply and Sanitation Company Limited.

Lusaka Water Supply and Sanitation Company Managing Director Jilly Chiyombwe said the project represents an investment of approximately 150 million kwacha by NAPSA through Sable Projects, will include the construction of about 12 kilometres of a 450-millimetre diameter water pipeline, a 1,000-cubic-metre ground reservoir and associated project infrastructure.

And NAPSA Acting Director General Joshua Malipenga described the project as an important milestone in efforts to provide sustainable infrastructure to support residential and commercial development in the rapidly growing area.

World.title: We will expand student loans-HH
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema says his administration plans to expand student loans, bursaries and meal allowances, to accommodate more students beyond just public universities.

President Hichilema has assured that his administration will continue to invest in the education sector as this will not only contribute to job creation, economic growth, but also increase national revenue.

The President said that once re-elected for a second term, he intends to introduce a student internship programme for students to be attached to various institutions, in order to help them secure jobs once they graduate.

The Head of State said this during an engagement with students from over 50 higher institutions of learning in the country, at State House, in Lusaka.

“It does not matter whether you are from a private university or public university because a student from a private university is no different from a student in a public university. Why? They are all citizens of Zambia”, he stressed.

The President also indicated that his administration has transformed education into an economic sector, in order to generate more income for the nation and support delivery of various services such as health and infrastructure, among others.

He noted various reforms scored by his administration in the education sector, such as the signing of free education into law, re-introduction of meal allowances, infrastructure development as well as distribution of desks.

Earlier, students’ representatives commended the government for various achievements scored in the education sector over the last four years, plus.

Nelson Nyirenda, a fifth year student at Levy Mwanawasa Medical University thanked President Hichilema for signing free education into law, increasing the Constituency Development Fund (CDF) and student loans.

And a representative from the National Council of Student Unions (NACOSU), Vincent Sakala noted that students and the health sector in the country are the biggest beneficiaries of CDF.

“Students are the biggest community in the country, sponsored by CDF. Come August 13th, we have resolved to give 5.8 million votes to President Hichilema”, he pledged.

Another Student of Levy Mwanawasa University, Brian Malambo expressed confidence that if given another term, President Hichilema would drive the country towards economic stability through his strategies aimed at boosting production.

World.title: IBA cautions broadcasters to adhere to election guidelines ahead of Thursday elections
World.content:
The Independent Broadcasting Authority (IBA), has cautioned broadcasters to adhere to outlined guidelines and not publish unverified information ahead of this year’s General Election.

Speaking during a press briefing in Lusaka today, IBA Director General, Webster Malido, who urged broadcasters to exercise caution when handling information, noted that elections results should only be broadcasted once they have been announced by the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ).

Mr Malido states that this is to ensure that the public receives accurate, reliable and verified information concerning the elections.

“Broadcasters are urged to avoid content that promotes hurt speech, violence or the dissemination of unverified information,” he stated.

He emphasised that all election related content should be accurate, verified and in a manner that represents public interests in order to avoid the spread of misinformation.

The Authority further encouraged members of the public as well as political parties and other stakeholders to make use of the complaint’s procedure established under the election guidelines.

“Complaints relating to the coverage of political parties, candidates or electoral issues should first be submitted to the broadcasting station concerned which is required to respond within two days’ o during the election period,” he stated.

Mr Malido highlighted that where no response is received during that period, only then can the matter be escalated to the Authority in accordance with the law.

The authority has since assured the public and electoral stakeholders of continued monitoring of election throughout the election period aimed at support compliance with the law, address complaints and ensure that all election coverage serves public interests among others.

World.title: Liberia: Boakai Names Retired Army General to Head Anti-Drug Agency
World.content:
The Executive Mansion says Ziankahn's appointment reflects the President's confidence in his "leadership, integrity, and operational experience."

President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has made perhaps his most consequential national security appointment since assuming office, naming former Defense Minister, retired Major General Daniel Dee Ziankahn, as Director General of the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency (LDEA) in a move that signals a fundamental shift in the government's strategy against transnational narcotics trafficking.

The appointment comes at a defining moment for Liberia's anti-drug campaign -- one marked by record cocaine seizures, allegations of institutional infiltration by organized crime, dismissals of senior security officials, and mounting international scrutiny over whether Liberia has become an emerging transit and storage hub for global narcotics syndicates.

Rather than selecting another career drug enforcement officer, President Boakai has entrusted the agency to one of the country's most experienced military minds, suggesting that the administration increasingly views narcotics trafficking not merely as a law enforcement problem but as a national security emergency.

Ziankahn's appointment follows months of extraordinary anti-narcotics operations that have transformed Liberia's security landscape.



The crisis reached international prominence after authorities intercepted approximately 237.6 kilograms of cocaine valued at about US$19 million at Roberts International Airport earlier this year. That operation exposed what investigators described as sophisticated trafficking methods involving airport operations and triggered an extensive criminal investigation.

Only weeks later, authorities executed an even more dramatic operation in Duazon, Margibi County, where investigators seized nearly 3.97 metric tons of suspected cocaine with an estimated international street value exceeding US$370 million -- one of the largest narcotics seizures ever recorded in Liberia and among the most significant in West Africa.

The scale of both seizures fundamentally altered perceptions of Liberia's role in international narcotics trafficking.

For years, security analysts had warned that West Africa was increasingly serving as a bridge between cocaine-producing regions in Latin America and lucrative consumer markets in Europe.

The Liberian seizures appeared to reinforce those concerns, suggesting that international trafficking organizations may have established increasingly sophisticated logistical networks within the country.

The investigations that followed produced consequences extending far beyond the drug seizures themselves.

As investigators traced the alleged trafficking operations, allegations emerged suggesting that elements within the security architecture may have been compromised.

President Boakai responded with an unprecedented series of administrative actions, dismissing, suspending and ordering investigations into officials from several security institutions, including the Liberia National Police (LNP), National Security Agency (NSA), Roberts International Airport (RIA), and the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency itself.

Those measures reflected the administration's determination to demonstrate that no institution would be insulated from accountability if credible evidence of misconduct emerged.

The actions also exposed what many analysts consider the greatest institutional threat confronting the country's anti-drug campaign: the possibility that sophisticated international criminal organizations may seek to infiltrate state institutions responsible for combating them.

Such concerns are not unique to Liberia.

Across the world, transnational narcotics organizations have historically relied not only on logistical sophistication but also on corruption, insider facilitation and institutional compromise.

Why Ziankahn?

Against that backdrop, President Boakai's choice of Daniel Dee Ziankahn appears highly strategic.

Unlike many previous leaders of the LDEA, Ziankahn arrives with decades of experience in military command, institutional reform and national security planning.

During his tenure as Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces of Liberia (AFL), he became widely associated with efforts to professionalize Liberia's post-war military following years of civil conflict.

Working alongside international partners, including the United States, he helped oversee reforms aimed at transforming the AFL into a disciplined, professional institution operating under democratic civilian control.

His subsequent service as Minister of National Defense further expanded his experience managing complex security institutions and coordinating with regional and international partners.

More recently, Ziankahn has served as Military Adviser to President Boakai, providing strategic advice on national and regional security matters.

His appointment therefore brings together operational military leadership, institutional reform experience and direct presidential confidence.

Unlike a conventional law enforcement appointment, it places a seasoned strategic commander at the helm of the country's principal anti-narcotics agency.

The Executive Mansion emphasized that Ziankahn's appointment reflects the President's confidence in his "leadership, integrity, and operational experience," while assigning him direct responsibility for intensifying Liberia's campaign against illicit drugs and organized crime.

The President has also appointed to the LDEA Precious Rue as Deputy Director General for Operations and Prince Mulbah as Deputy Director General for Administration, pending Senate confirmation.

All three officials have been instructed to assume their responsibilities immediately in acting capacities.

The restructuring also returns Ernest Tarpeh to the National Security Agency, while former Officer-in-Charge Fitzgerald Biago has been indefinitely suspended from the Liberia National Police over ethical concerns pending further investigation.

Although the Ministry of Justice reportedly found no evidence directly linking Biago to narcotics trafficking, President Boakai concluded that ethical issues identified in the investigation warranted additional scrutiny.

That distinction reflects the administration's emerging message: legal innocence does not necessarily preclude administrative accountability where questions of institutional integrity arise.

Ziankahn's appointment inevitably raises broader questions about the evolving character of Liberia's anti-drug campaign.

Drug enforcement agencies traditionally operate as civilian law enforcement institutions emphasizing criminal investigations, prosecutions and intelligence gathering.

By selecting a retired four-star military officer to lead the LDEA, President Boakai appears to be elevating narcotics trafficking to the level of a national security threat.

That does not necessarily imply militarization of policing.

Rather, it suggests greater emphasis on intelligence coordination, operational discipline, inter-agency cooperation and strategic planning.

The President has directed the new leadership to work closely with the Ministry of Justice, Joint Security and international partners to dismantle trafficking networks, strengthen border controls and improve intelligence capabilities.

Such coordination will likely become increasingly important as investigations continue across multiple jurisdictions.

Liberia's response carries significance beyond its borders.

International partners -- including the United States, the European Union, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), ECOWAS and INTERPOL -- closely monitor countries serving as potential transit points for narcotics trafficking.

Major cocaine seizures often become tests of institutional credibility.

Foreign governments generally assess not only whether drugs are intercepted but also whether investigations reach the criminal networks responsible and whether compromised public officials are held accountable.

Close 

Boakai's successive dismissals, suspensions and institutional reforms therefore appear designed partly to reassure international partners that Liberia remains committed to confronting organized crime despite the scale of recent challenges.

Yet appointments alone cannot dismantle sophisticated international trafficking networks.

Experts note that sustainable success will depend on broader institutional reforms, including stronger financial investigations, improved border surveillance, enhanced intelligence-sharing, witness protection mechanisms, prosecutorial capacity and judicial efficiency.

Liberia must also continue strengthening airport security, maritime surveillance and anti-money laundering systems if it hopes to disrupt the financial infrastructure sustaining organized criminal enterprises.

Equally important will be restoring public confidence in institutions that recent investigations have exposed to allegations of misconduct.

Announcing the appointments, President Boakai reaffirmed that narcotics trafficking represents one of Liberia's gravest threats to national security, public health and national development.

"Our fight against drugs is a fight for the future of Liberia," the President declared. "We will continue to strengthen our institutions, hold public officials to the highest ethical standards, and pursue those who seek to poison our communities. There will be no safe haven for drug traffickers or those who aid and abet them."

Those remarks reinforce an earlier pledge made after the first major cocaine seizure that his administration would dismantle the criminal networks operating within Liberia rather than merely seize narcotics shipments.

The assignment, for Ziankahn, may become the most demanding chapter of a career spanning military leadership, defense policy and national security.

It also represents, for the President, a high-stakes bet that disciplined leadership, institutional credibility and strategic coordination can restore confidence in an agency whose reputation has been shaken by allegations of internal compromise.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - August 11, 2026
World.content:
Zambia Election Set for Closely Fought Opposition Battle

Zambia's 13 August election has become a closely contested battle between the ruling United Party for National Development and the Tonse-Pamodzi opposition alliance, led by newcomer Brian Mundubile and backed by former Patriotic Front structures. The election is expected to test the opposition's strength and serve as a referendum on President Hakainde Hichilema's record. The government has made progress on debt restructuring, economic growth and inflation. But the high cost of living remains a big concern for voters. The poll is also taking place amid concerns over alleged state interference, restrictions on opposition activity and controversial legislative changes, making it a key test for Zambia's democracy.

WHO Warns DR Congo Ebola Response Falling Behind

More than 1,900 people have died in the Democratic Republic of Congo's Ebola outbreak. 60-70% of deaths occur in communities before patients reach treatment centres. The WHO said that the concentration of healthcare services in Bunia, Ituri province, is forcing patients to travel long distances and seek care too late. Poor transport systems may also increase transmission. The agency plans to expand treatment facilities closer to communities, add 400 Ebola beds and strengthen public awareness and early referrals. WHO is also looking to the town of Aru, where no new cases have been reported for two weeks after authorities expanded surveillance and response beyond individual patients to surrounding communities.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Nigeria Lassa Fever Cases Reach 1,000 in 2026

Nigeria has reported 1,000 confirmed cases of Lassa fever and 237 deaths in 2026, with cases reported in 23 states and 116 local government areas. Five states, Ondo, Bauchi, Taraba, Edo and Benue, account for 86% of confirmed cases. At least 53 healthcare workers have also been infected, prompting the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention to introduce a 30-day protection plan for frontline staff. The agency has said that late presentation, high treatment costs, poor sanitation and limited awareness are contributing to the outbreak and high fatality rate. Lassa fever is a viral haemorrhagic disease transmitted primarily through contact with food or household items contaminated by the urine or faeces of infected rodents.

Malawi Land Audit Flags Irregular Plot Allocations

Malawi's Ministry of Lands is set to release findings from a pilot land ownership audit in Lilongwe that reportedly uncovered irregularities in the allocation of plots in the affluent Area 3 and Area 10. The audit was launched in February 2026 to improve transparency and accountability in land administration. It is said to have identified politically exposed individuals, including current and former ministers, judges and MPs, among those allegedly linked to irregular land acquisitions. The findings could trigger political controversy, with questions remaining over whether those implicated will be publicly named or face legal or disciplinary action.

UN Somalia Auction Raises Security Concerns

The UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) has opened a tender to auction vehicles, generators, IT equipment, medical supplies, construction machinery and other assets. This comes as Washington moves to end funding for the mission's logistical support by the end of 2026. UNSOS provides critical transport, fuel, food and other supplies to about 12,000 African troops and police serving under AUSSOM in the fight against al-Shabab. The auction has raised concerns among civil society groups over transparency and oversight. Regional leaders have warned that any premature reduction in international support could create a security vacuum as al-Shabab continues to operate in parts of Somalia.

Close 

Climate Change Shifts Africa's Malaria Risk

Climate change is reshaping malaria risk across Africa, with rising temperatures making parts of southern Africa and high-elevation areas of East Africa increasingly suitable for transmission, according to a new Nature study. Some parts of West and Central Africa may have become too hot for optimal malaria transmission. The region still bears about 95% of the global malaria burden. But experts warn that climate change is only part of the equation, with funding gaps, drug and insecticide resistance, and weak health systems still major threats. They are urging countries in emerging risk areas to step up malaria prevention and surveillance while maintaining elimination efforts in high-burden areas.

World.title: South Africa: Immigrant Traders See Their Livelihoods Destroyed By March and March
World.content:
Traders with documents and permits chased away, leaving Bellville bus terminus market almost empty

Dozens of immigrant traders who usually traded at the Golden Arrow terminus in Bellville are staying away because of anti-immigrant protests.

When we visited the once bustling site last week, it was quiet with only a handful of traders. Many stalls were deserted.

Some traders we spoke to said they had tried to set up shop in other areas but were stopped. They have not traded at the bus site since the March and March 30 June "deadline" demanding "illegal immigrants" leave South Africa.



"I need to pay rent, put food on the table, and pay the bills," a Zimbabwean man who asked to remain anonymous told GroundUp.

He said he has been selling clothes in Bellville for about five years. He left Zimbabwe in 2008 when its economy collapsed.

While he has not been directly threatened, he has witnessed others being harassed.

"They will take your stuff and throw it on the ground," he said.

"It hurts, but as much as it hurts, it's their country, and they're also marginalised people."

Another trader, who introduced herself as Meye, said she has had a permit to trade since 2010. She fled the DRC in 2003.

"We are legal; everything is correct. But they say we are foreigners and we need to go back to our country."

A single mother of three, she says she is now struggling to feed and school her children.

Another single mother, Safia, says she has been unable to trade despite having refugee status and a trading permit. She came from Somalia in 2010.

She said law enforcement needs to protect the traders better.

"I can't sleep at night because of what is happening. I can't even pay my rent. I can't support my children," she said.

Abdulhakim Husein, Western Cape director of the Somalia Association of South Africa, told GroundUp that he had been assisting traders since the start of July.

He said many asylum seekers and refugees are traders as they have to rely on being self-employed. They came from Somalia, DRC, Zimbabwe, Angola and Burundi.

He said that at a meeting on 13 July (which the City confirmed), it was agreed that traders with valid permits should be allowed to trade. But on 14 July, they received a message warning them about a March and March protest in the area.

Husein said they have approached a legal NGO for assistance.

City spokesperson Luthando Tyhalibongo said foreign nationals whose immigration status has been verified by Home Affairs are permitted to trade with a valid permit. These cost R78 per month.

Close 

"It is a concern whenever permitted traders, whether South African citizens or foreign nationals lawfully permitted to trade, are prevented from engaging in legal economic activity," he said.

He said intimidation and threats should be reported to SAPS.

World.title: South Africa: Gauteng Gets 500,000 Grade 1 and 8 Applications - South African News Briefs - August 11, 2026
World.content:
Gauteng Records Nearly 500,000 Grade 1 and 8 Applications

Almost half a million applications have been submitted for Grade 1 and Grade 8 places in Gauteng for the 2027 academic year since the online application system opened, reports EWN. The Gauteng Department of Education has said that improvements have been made to streamline the process. Education MEC Lebogang Maile has urged parents to apply early. The department also says learners awaiting specialised placement should receive interim support rather than remain on waiting lists, with officials focusing on successful placements and resolving outstanding cases.

Strong Winds Damage Homes in Free State

The South African Red Cross Society is assessing damage caused by strong winds and heavy rainfall in Koppies and other parts of the Free State, reports SABC News. Several homes have reportedly been damaged, including roofs blown off, as severe weather persists. Red Cross volunteers are working with disaster management authorities and municipalities. Assessments continue, with humanitarian assistance being provided to affected households.

Fadiel Adams Unlikely to Testify at Madlanga Commission

National Coloured Congress leader Fadiel Adams is unlikely to testify before the Madlanga Commission, reports EWN. This comes after the commission received his affidavit and supporting documents late. Adams was expected to testify about his involvement in an Investigating Directorate Against Corruption probe into alleged corruption within Crime Intelligence. In 2024, he asked IDAC to investigate claims that the Political Killings Task Team had misused secret service funds for luxury accommodation and vehicles.

World.title: Somalia: UN Puts Somalia Mission Assets Up for Sale As U.S. Funding Cutoff Looms
World.content:
Mogadishu, Somalia — The United Nations Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) has opened a tender seeking licensed auctioneers to sell off a wide range of its vehicles, generators and other equipment in Somalia, a notice published on the UN Global Marketplace shows.

The call for expressions of interest, issued August 6, comes as Washington moves to cut off funding for the UN's logistical support mission by the end of 2026, deepening uncertainty over the future of international backing for Somalia's fight against al-Shabab.

The tender matters now because it lands at the center of a widening rift between the United States and the United Nations over how and whether, to keep supporting Somalia's security transition. UNSOS underpins the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), supplying transport, fuel, food and other non-lethal supplies to roughly 12,000 African troops and police fighting a resilient insurgency. Any wind-down of that support network would strike at the core of the mission's ability to operate.

Under the terms of the tender, UNSOS is looking to establish a local contract for the "commercial sale" of UN-owned property. The initial deal would run three months, with up to three additional three-month extensions depending on performance and operational need.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The list of items up for sale is extensive: vehicles, generators, computers and IT equipment, office equipment, shipping containers, security watchtowers, wastewater treatment plants, prefabricated accommodation materials, medical and laboratory equipment, electrical appliances and heavy construction machinery. UNSOS said the list is indicative and may grow.

Interested firms have a narrow window to respond, with registration required by August 11 -- just five days after the notice was published.

Civil society analysts in Mogadishu have indicated that the auction notice does not lay out a clear mechanism for independent oversight, warning that disposing of mission assets without transparency could weaken public trust and open the door to diversion of state property.

The auction notice does not link the sale to the funding dispute. But it follows a July 1 letter in which the United States cited concerns over Somalia's performance against al-Shabab and its handling of security and governance issues, and comes as Washington has pushed back against extending UN logistical support for AUSSOM beyond current arrangements.

Somalia has fought al-Shabab for nearly two decades, and the group still holds sway over parts of the country. Leaders of AUSSOM troop-contributing nations have warned that a premature drawdown in support could open a security vacuum.

World.title: Malawi: Bombshell Land Audit to Name Ministers, Judges and MPs Over Illegal Plot Grabs
World.content:
Malawi's Ministry of Lands, Housing and Urban Development is set to hold a highly anticipated press briefing this Wednesday to unveil the findings of a pilot land ownership audit conducted in Lilongwe - findings that are set to implicate some of the country's most powerful figures.

According to an invitation letter seen by this publication, Minister of Lands Chimwemwe Chipungu will personally preside over the briefing, which is expected to shed light on widespread irregularities uncovered during the audit process.

'The Ministry embarked on the Land Ownership Audit exercise in February 2026 as part of efforts to strengthen land administration systems, promote accountability in land ownership and enhance transparency and efficiency in the management of land resources,' the invitation reads.



The audit is understood to have uncovered significant irregularities in the allocation of plots specifically within Lilongwe's Area 3 and Area 10, two of the capital's most sought-after and valuable residential districts.

Most explosively, the audit has reportedly named a string of politically exposed individuals - including ministers serving in both the current and former administrations, sitting judges, and members of parliament - among those alleged to have acquired plots in the affected areas without following proper procedure.

The revelations, if confirmed at Wednesday's briefing, threaten to ignite a fresh political storm in Malawi, given the seniority of those reportedly implicated and the sensitivity surrounding land allocation in a country where access to prime urban plots has long been a source of controversy and allegations of favouritism.

The findings also land amid a period of intense scrutiny over transparency and accountability in public institutions more broadly, following separate controversies including the stalled parliamentary probe into the K128 billion Amaryllis Hotel purchase and mounting pressure over undisclosed presidential travel costs.

It remains to be seen whether Wednesday's briefing will name the individuals implicated publicly, or whether further legal or disciplinary action is being considered against those found to have benefited from irregular land allocations.

Ministry officials have not yet responded to requests for further comment ahead of the scheduled press briefing.

World.title: Uganda: Govt Orders Bus Drivers to Switch After Long Journeys to Curb Fatigue
World.content:
The government has introduced new measures requiring bus operators to change drivers after long-distance journeys, as authorities intensify efforts to curb driver fatigue following a series of fatal road crashes in recent weeks.

Works and Transport Minister Fred Byamukama announced the measures after meeting bus operators, Traffic Police and other transport stakeholders at the Ministry headquarters on Monday evening.

Under the new directive, buses travelling more than 300 kilometres will be required to have a different driver for the return journey.

A driver who completes the outbound journey on a route exceeding 300 kilometres will not be allowed to drive the same bus back along that route.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Traffic Police has been directed to apprehend operators and drivers who disregard the requirement.

For journeys of less than 300 kilometres, a driver will be allowed to travel to the destination and return once. After completing the return journey, the driver must stop work for the day and cannot undertake a third leg on the same day.

The measures are intended to reduce driver fatigue, which authorities and transport sector stakeholders have identified as one of the factors contributing to road crashes.

The directive comes after a series of deadly crashes involving buses and other passenger vehicles in July and early August.

On July 7, at least 14 people were killed and 28 injured when an Opit Travellers bus collided with a trailer at Bobi Trading Centre along the Kampala-Gulu Highway in Omoro District. Preliminary police findings linked the crash to reckless driving.

A week later, a bus carrying more than 70 students of Mwebaza High School to Jinja for a study trip collided with a passenger train at the Namumira railway crossing in Mukono. One teacher was killed and several students were injured.

The same week, another school bus carrying students from St Paul Secondary School, Katakwi, was involved in a crash along the Mbale-Iganga Highway after it rammed into a stationary trailer. The driver was killed and 15 people, most of them students, were injured.

The most serious incident occurred on July 16 when a King David Junior School bus carrying pupils from an educational trip to Sipi Falls crashed at Chekwatit along the Kapchorwa-Mbale Road.

Police subsequently confirmed that 24 people, including the bus driver, had died. Investigations into the cause of the crash remain ongoing.

The tragedy prompted the Ministry of Education and Sports to suspend all school trips and excursions. Police later clarified that the suspension applied to vehicles transporting learners on school trips and did not affect ordinary public transport buses.

The concentration of crashes involving buses and other passenger vehicles has also triggered calls for tougher enforcement of driver and vehicle safety requirements.

Transport leaders in Northern Uganda recently attributed the rising crashes to factors including driver fatigue, speeding, dangerous overtaking and indiscipline. They also urged bus companies to strengthen driver recruitment, check drivers' accident histories and ensure they receive adequate rest.

The Ministry of Works and Transport has separately proposed an electronic clocking-in system for public-service vehicle drivers to monitor their driving hours, rest periods and speeding.

The proposal was presented to Parliament's Committee on Physical Infrastructure in July after ministry officials reviewed a series of crashes.

The ministry said investigations into the July crashes had revealed non-compliance with transport regulations, including unlicensed buses, unaccredited drivers, mechanical defects and weak enforcement.

Under the proposed electronic monitoring system, drivers would record their journeys at designated points, allowing authorities to establish how long they had been driving and how much rest they had received.

The government has also said it plans to strengthen digital verification systems for detecting unlicensed vehicles and unauthorised drivers, while reviewing the National Road Safety Action Plan.

The recent measures build on earlier action against bus operators.

In May, the Ministry of Works and Transport suspended Nile Star bus operations for 30 days following a fatal crash in Nwoya in which seven passengers were killed and 16 others seriously injured.

The ministry said Nile Star buses had been involved in 11 crashes over the preceding year, resulting in 91 deaths and 56 injuries. The minister at the time cited possible driver fatigue and poor management of driver schedules among the concerns.

The government has also intensified scrutiny of heavy commercial vehicles. Earlier this month, authorities ordered all Sino trucks to undergo mandatory mechanical inspections within a two-month period, warning that vehicles failing to meet safety requirements could be taken off the road.

Close 

The renewed focus on bus operations comes as road crashes continue to claim lives.

On August 4, at least 14 people were killed when a passenger van collided with a sand-carrying truck in Kalungu District, according to police. Four others were injured, while the truck driver reportedly fled the scene.

Byamukama has urged bus operators to comply with the latest driver-management requirements, saying the measures are aimed at protecting passengers and other road users.

The government says Traffic Police will be expected to enforce the new rules, particularly on long-distance routes where driver fatigue can become a major safety risk.

The latest directive therefore adds another layer to the government's emerging road-safety strategy, which now includes tighter driver monitoring, scrutiny of vehicle condition, enforcement against unlicensed operators, restrictions on school transport activities and measures aimed at ensuring drivers get adequate rest.

World.title: Nigeria: Lassa Fever - 53 Health Workers Infected As Cases Hit 1,000 in 2026
World.content:
The NCDC said 23 states have now reported at least one confirmed case across 116 local government areas (LGAs)

Nigeria has recorded 1,000 confirmed cases of Lassa fever, with 237 deaths in 2026, according to the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC).

The figure includes 53 healthcare workers who have been infected with the disease, highlighting the continued risk faced by frontline health workers responding to the outbreak.

The agency released its situation reports for epidemiological weeks 29 and 30 on Monday, covering 13 to 19 July and 20 to 26 July, respectively.



According to the Week 30 report, Nigeria recorded 17 new confirmed cases and six deaths during the week, bringing the cumulative figures to 1,000 confirmed cases and 237 deaths.

More details

According to the NCDC, the case fatality rate increased slightly from 23.5 per cent in Week 29 to 23.7 per cent in Week 30.

The NCDC said 23 states have now reported at least one confirmed case across 116 local government areas (LGAs).

Ondo, Bauchi, Taraba, Edo and Benue accounted for 86 per cent of all confirmed cases, with Ondo recording the highest proportion at 32 per cent, followed by Bauchi with 25 per cent. Taraba accounted for 13 per cent; Edo, 10 per cent and Benue, six per cent.

Health workers remain at risk

The NCDC reported one new healthcare worker infection in Week 30, bringing the number of healthcare workers infected with Lassa fever in 2026 to 53.

The agency said infections among healthcare workers remain one of the challenges in controlling the outbreak.

It said it had developed a 30-day Healthcare Worker Protection Plan to reduce infections among frontline health workers in high-burden states, with support from the World Health Organisation (WHO) and the US Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

The agency also reported training frontline healthcare workers, strengthening infection prevention and control programmes, pre-positioning personal protective equipment and providing technical support to investigate and mitigate healthcare worker infections.

Challenges

The NCDC identified late presentation of patients as one of the challenges contributing to the high case fatality rate.

It also cited poor health-seeking behaviour linked to the high cost of Lassa fever treatment and clinical management.

Other challenges identified by the agency include poor environmental sanitation, limited awareness in high-burden communities and infections among healthcare workers.

Close 

The NCDC recommended year-round community engagement on Lassa fever prevention and urged healthcare workers to maintain a high level of suspicion for the disease, ensure timely referral and treatment, and adhere to standard infection prevention and control procedures.

About Lassa Fever

Lassa fever is a viral haemorrhagic disease transmitted primarily through contact with food or household items contaminated by the urine or faeces of infected rodents.

Human-to-human transmission can also occur through contact with bodily fluids.

Symptoms typically begin with fever, weakness and headache but can progress to severe complications, including bleeding, respiratory distress and organ failure if not treated early.

MADISON, Wis. – Supporters of Democratic candidate for Wisconsin governor Francesca Hong expressed confidence ahead of Tuesday that the far-left progressive and member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) can win the Democratic gubernatorial primary on a platform centered on economic relief.

"She's speaking to working-class issues. Everybody's struggling right now. The price of gas is insane. Trying to pay for your groceries is insane, trying to pay your rent is insane," campaign canvasser Josiah Wampfler told Fox News Digital at Hong’s campaign headquarters in Madison. "We're all struggling, and she's presenting solutions to bring down prices and to have improved government programs."

The affordability crisis has plagued many Americans amid rising costs of groceries, housing and healthcare. The House passed legislation — showing a rare display of bipartisanship earlier this year with a 390-9 vote — to deliver policies aimed at growing the supply of affordable housing in the U.S.

‘COMMON SENSE AGAINST CRAZY’: TRUMP-BACKED CANDIDATE SOUNDS ALARM ON SOCIALIST HONG IN WISCONSIN RACE

Hong enters primary night as a polling frontrunner in a Democratic showdown that was upended this summer after several high-profile contenders — including former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes and current Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez — exited the race, while Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley briefly suspended his campaign before re-entering.

A member of the DSA, the 37-year-old former chef and single mother has drawn backing from prominent national progressives, including Reps. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., and Ro Khanna, D-Calif.

Hong’s platform includes state-guaranteed paid leave, raising Wisconsin’s minimum wage from $7.25 to $20 per hour, and placing a one-year moratorium on new AI data center construction. Her tax proposal would raise state income taxes by 1% on couples earning over $431,000 and individuals earning over $323,000.

Supporters and volunteers poured into the Madison headquarters on Election Day, preparing for final voter outreach pushes.

WISCONSIN DEM SOCIALIST GUBERNATORIAL HOPEFUL DODGES WHETHER SHE STILL WANTS TO ‘ABOLISH POLICE’

"I think what I've seen inside of Madison and throughout the state is that people are looking for change — dare I say radical change — because we have been subjected to a lot of very moderate views for a long time, and people are suffering," she said.

Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and the national DSA organization declined to endorse her in the Wisconsin gubernatorial contest. "I have so much respect for the senator and the congresswoman, and they are working tirelessly to make sure that we can that we can flip Congress and the Senate," she said to a crowd of reporters and her supporters standing behind her.

Hong's supporters, however, dismissed the lack of national backing as standard procedure for state-level executive races.

"They haven't really endorsed in gubernatorial races. They're focused on the federal level," Dana added. "And I think it's actually really, really impressive that Fran has been able to do this without many national endorsements."

World.title: WNBA silence on DiJonai Carrington's 'White privilege' post exposes Sandy Brondello double standard
World.content:
Three weeks ago, the WNBA needed less than 24 hours to suspend Toronto Tempo head coach Sandy Brondello for making a comment that wasn't explicitly racial.

More than two days after Chicago Sky guard DiJonai Carrington explicitly invoked race by posting "WHITE PRIVILEGE @indianafever" on Threads moments after being ejected from a game against the Fever, the league apparently had nothing to say.

Carrington then suited up and played for the Sky against the Seattle Storm on Monday night.

FLORIDA ATTORNEY GENERAL OFFERS HIS RESPONSE TO BRUTAL FOUL ON SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM

Seems like a pretty clear double standard.

Let's start with Brondello.

During a July 17 game against the Atlanta Dream, Brondello became upset after officials called a foul on Nyara Sabally while she battled Angel Reese for a rebound. Sabally went down in pain, and Brondello complained that Reese was a "protected species."

Brondello is Australian, where "protected species" is a common sports expression used to describe an athlete perceived to receive favorable treatment from officials. The context made her meaning pretty clear, too. She was complaining about a foul call.

Still, because Reese is Black, the comment was quickly given a racial interpretation. Reese also leaned into the racial narrative by posting "ARE WE SURPRISED" shortly after the game.

Brondello apologized the following morning, saying her frustration was with the officiating and acknowledging that her words had an impact beyond what she intended, "particularly for Black women in our league."

Apparently, that wasn't enough.

On July 18, less than a day after Brondello made the comment, the WNBA suspended her without pay for one game. The league called it an "inappropriate comment" and said coaches and team personnel are expected to uphold the "highest standards of professionalism and respect."

Reese later thanked the WNBA for taking action and said there is "no place for discrimination or hate" in the league.

ANGEL REESE THANKS WNBA FOR SUSPENDING SANDY BRONDELLO, FRAMES 'PROTECTED SPECIES' COMMENT AS DISCRIMINATION

Keep that standard in mind.

DiJonai Carrington explicitly invoked race after WNBA ejection

On Saturday afternoon, Carrington struck Fever guard Sophie Cunningham across the head while Cunningham attempted a layup. Officials reviewed the play, upgraded the foul to a Flagrant 2 and ejected Carrington late in the first quarter.

Minutes later, while the game was still being played, a post appeared on Carrington's Threads account.

"WHITE PRIVILEGE @indianafever."

Not "protected species," which is an Australian sports phrase that someone else interpreted through a racial lens.

"WHITE PRIVILEGE."

Carrington made an explicitly race-based comment and tagged another WNBA franchise almost immediately after being ejected from a WNBA game.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

OutKick and Fox News Digital contacted the league shortly after Carrington's post Saturday and asked whether the WNBA viewed it as an allegation that race or racial bias played a role in her ejection, whether the league had spoken with Carrington and whether it was reviewing the matter for potential discipline.

No response.

OutKick followed up with the WNBA again Monday morning and Monday night, giving the league another opportunity to explain its position before publication.

Again, no response.

The Chicago Sun-Times also reported Monday that the WNBA didn't respond to its request for comment.

Meanwhile, Carrington wasn't backing away from her use of the phrase.

Responding Monday to Emmanuel Acho, who criticized the idea that her ejection represented white privilege, Carrington insisted people were misunderstanding her.

"I've never once claimed that the assessment of the foul was white privilege (that was your assumption)," Carrington wrote.

OK.

Then what was?

Carrington didn't say.

Instead, she defended her qualifications to discuss white privilege, saying she attended "one of the top universities" to educate herself on the subject and would never use the term as a "rhetorical weapon" without "the proper evidence to substantiate it."

Evidence of what?

Carrington posted "WHITE PRIVILEGE," tagged the Fever and did so almost immediately after an ejection. She now says she wasn't referring to the assessment of the foul and insists she has evidence to substantiate whatever accusation she was making.

Yet neither Carrington nor the WNBA has explained what that accusation actually is.

The WNBA needs to explain its standard

Maybe the league believes the situations involving Brondello and Carrington are completely different.

It’s hard to identify a material distinction that explains the dramatically different responses, and the WNBA hasn’t offered one. The league could argue that Brondello’s comment was made by a head coach during live game action, while Carrington’s came from her own social media account after she was ejected.

WNBA MEDIA DEFENDS DIJONAI CARRINGTON AFTER DANGEROUS SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM HIT REVEALS GLARING BIAS

Still, is the league OK with one of its players posting on social media about an incident moments after being ejected, while the game is still being played, especially when the post makes a race-based allegation whose target remains unclear?

Maybe the league is perfectly fine with it.

Then it should say that.

The league didn't offer Brondello days of silence while it figured out how to handle an ambiguous phrase. It acted the next day, even though Brondello publicly apologized and explained that her comment had nothing to do with race.

Carrington, meanwhile, used an unmistakably racial term, tagged an opposing franchise, later said she had evidence to support using that term and still hasn't explained exactly whom she was accusing of white privilege.

More than two days later, she took the floor for another WNBA game without the league publicly acknowledging the situation at all.

That's particularly notable given what WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert recently told Congress when lawmakers questioned whether the league fairly protects and disciplines all of its players.

"In all instances, the League seeks to apply the WNBA rulebook and applicable disciplinary processes consistently across all games and for all players," Engelbert wrote.

Well, this would be a good time to demonstrate that consistency.

This isn't an argument that Carrington automatically deserved the exact same one-game suspension Brondello received. Perhaps the WNBA reviewed the situation and concluded Carrington violated no league rule.

If so, say that.

But the league can't aggressively police one comment because of its perceived racial implications, then simply look the other way when a player explicitly invokes race during a game and pretend nobody is going to notice the difference.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Brondello was suspended for words that weren't explicitly racial but were interpreted that way.

Carrington explicitly wrote "WHITE PRIVILEGE."

So far, only one of them has faced consequences from the WNBA.

And until the league explains why, its supposed commitment to consistent standards falls completely flat.

The only thing consistent about the WNBA is its uncanny ability to get in its own way.

World.title: Cruise fee doubles at vacation hot spot as passengers brace for even steeper hikes
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Cruise passengers heading to Mexico are now paying a higher fee to visit some of the country's most popular destinations as the latest increase in a phased tax plan takes effect.

As of Aug. 1, the fee for foreign cruise passengers visiting Mexican ports increased from $5 to $10 per person, with additional increases scheduled over the next two years, according to Mexico's phased plan.

The charge applies to foreign cruise passengers visiting popular cruise destinations, including Cabo San Lucas, Puerto Vallarta, Cozumel and Costa Maya. It can be collected by cruise lines or their shipping agents.

BELOVED CRUISE SPOT WILL BE OFF LIMITS THROUGH 2027 AS SAFETY CONCERNS LINGER

Clint Henderson, a managing editor of the travel site The Points Guy and based in New York, told Fox News Digital the increase likely won't be enough to deter most travelers, but said it adds to the growing expenses consumers face when traveling.

"While it's not horrible and likely won't be a deal-breaker for most tourists, it's another example of prices going up for travel across the board, and it's frustrating as a consumer rights advocate," Henderson said.

"Consumers keep getting hit with more and more taxes and fees for everything related to travel," he added.

The $10 charge is only one step in Mexico's plan, with the fee scheduled to increase again over the next two years.

CRUISE LINE'S TOUGHER BOOKING RULES IGNITE BACKLASH OVER HIGHER DEPOSITS AND PAYMENTS

"The messed-up thing about this new fee is [that it's] just one of several increases to come over the next few years," Henderson said. "It will eventually go up to $21 over the next few years."

"Consumers keep getting hit with more and more taxes and fees."

"We'll have to see if this ends up denting cruise demand for Mexico," he added.

Henderson noted that cruise passengers had previously been exempt from the immigration fee imposed on certain foreign travelers entering Mexico.

ANGRY CRUISE PASSENGERS BLAST MAJOR LINE OVER SURPRISE DAILY GRATUITY HIKE

"That's no longer the case," he said, "and it's going to raise costs for tourists."

The $10 charge, however, is still significantly lower than the fee Mexico originally planned to impose on cruise passengers.

Fox News Digital previously reported that Mexico's Congress approved an immigration levy of 860.56 pesos, roughly $42 at the time, on foreign cruise passengers in December 2024 — prompting pushback from the cruise industry.

The law took effect Jan. 1, 2025, but Mexico granted cruise passengers a 100% fiscal credit through the end of June, effectively postponing collection of the fee.

Following negotiations between the Mexican government and the Florida-Caribbean Cruise Association (FCCA), the two sides reached an agreement that set the initial fee at $5 per passenger beginning July 1, 2025.

CLICK HERE TO 

"On behalf of the FCCA and our member cruise lines — representing over 95% of cruise capacity in the Caribbean and Latin America — we thank the Federal Government of Mexico for working with us to reach an ‘in transit fee’ agreement," the FCCA told Fox News Digital at the time.

The association said the agreement was intended to protect cruise tourism while supporting Mexican communities that rely on visitors.

Under the phased plan, foreign cruise passengers paid $5 beginning in July 2025 before the fee doubled to $10 on Aug. 1 of this year.

The next increase is scheduled for July 1, 2027, when the charge will rise to $15 per passenger.

Then, beginning Aug. 1, 2028, travelers will pay $21 through Sept. 30, 2030, under the current plan.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

The impact of additional taxes and fees can become more noticeable when travelers are paying for an entire family, Henderson said.

"It's definitely making Mexico more expensive as all these taxes and fees start to add up," he said.

The increase arrives as travelers are seeing jumps in costs throughout the industry.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Unfortunately, cruising, like everything else, is getting more expensive," Henderson said in a previous interview.

He pointed to higher expenses for staffing, entertainment, food, beverages and fuel as some of the costs facing cruise operators.

"There's a lot of demand. There's a lot [of] people [who] want to cruise," Henderson said. "It's become very popular and things have gotten much more expensive."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Still, Henderson said cruising can offer good value when travelers consider the transportation, accommodations and entertainment included in the price.

"Cruising is still a relative bargain," he said.

Fox News Digital’s Ashley DiMella contributed reporting.

An Oklahoma teenager accused of sexually assaulting and strangling two high school girls walked free without serving a day in prison, spurring public outrage as a victim’s family prepares to fight back.

"We’re moving on to the next phase, which is civil litigation," Rachel Bussett, an attorney representing the family of one girl in the case, told Fox News Digital.

OKLAHOMA TEEN ACCUSED OF RAPING TWO GIRLS WALKS FREE; DA FURIOUSLY CALLS IN FEDS: ‘MADE MY BLOOD BOIL’

"They were sad and upset, obviously, because they didn't want the deal to go through this way, but they weren't surprised," Bussett said. "They knew that it was going to happen from the beginning."

World.title: Cut off by your adult child? Psychology researcher reveals what parents should do next
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Family estrangement has become increasingly common in the U.S. — but experts stress that reconciliation may still be possible after relatives have cut ties.

A 2025 YouGov poll found that 38% of U.S. adults were estranged from at least one close family member, including 16% who were estranged from a parent and 10% from a child. Among parents estranged from their children, 70% said they would consider reconciling.

Research also suggests that many parent-child estrangements eventually experience a period of renewed contact. In one nationally representative study published in the Journal of Marriage and Family, 81% of adult children who experienced estrangement from their mothers later became unestranged, as did 69% of those estranged from their fathers.

5 REASONS MORE AMERICANS ARE CUTTING OFF THEIR OWN PARENTS, ACCORDING TO PSYCHOLOGIST

While every relationship is different and there are no guarantees, Texas-based psychology researcher Dr. Richard Blake stated that the majority of estrangements do come to an end – but willingness to change and find common ground is key.

In many cases, parent-child estrangements are a cycle — "they'll re-engage, then they'll fall out again," Blake said. "One of the key things from the research is that adult children will reach out and if they see nothing has changed, they'll estrange again."

In an interview with Fox News Digital, the psychology researcher shared the following steps that may increase the likelihood of repairing a fractured relationship.

No. 1: Aim for stability first

Estrangement from an adult child can be seen as a form of "ambiguous loss" — a situation in which someone is gone, but there is still hope they could return, according to Blake.

He compared the situation to having a child missing in action: "You don't know if he's dead or alive and you kind of have to grieve, but you don't really know if you should be grieving, because there's hope."

SECOND LADY USHA VANCE GETS CANDID ABOUT NEW BABY, JUGGLING FOUR CHILDREN AND MOTHERHOOD

Research supports the significant emotional toll of estrangement. In a 2025 study of older parents, being cut off from an adult child was associated with poorer well-being and a reduced sense of purpose, as well as greater depressive symptoms.

Before attempting a reconciliation with an estranged parent or adult child, Blake said the first priority should be stabilizing oneself.

"What I tend to recommend first is to get that person stable, have healthy habits and build a community," he advised. "Good mental health practices are really important."

No. 2: Listen and validate

When communication with an estranged family member is possible, Blake recommends repeating back what the other person has said and acknowledging how they experienced the conflict before offering a different perspective.

"Listen to the other person and then actually repeat back what they said as you understood it, and validate that – like, ‘Oh, I can see why you felt like that. I see why you interpreted it in that way,’" Blake said.

It’s important to resist the impulse to immediately correct, contradict or defend, and to acknowledge the other person's experience without necessarily agreeing with every aspect of their account, according to the expert.

After listening, parents should be open-minded about making some changes as needed, Blake said.

"I really tell our parents … if you're 100% perfect, great … but most parents have done something wrong, something that they want to change. And if they want a relationship with their child, they are going to have to change some things."

No. 3: Pause before reacting to accusations or labels

Certain labels used during family disputes can make compromise more difficult, Blake noted, an issue he refers to as "moralized language."

"I talk about these therapy words that get thrown at parents … abuse, toxic boundaries, narcissists, gaslighting, all those things," he said. "In the research, when you use moralized language like that, compromise becomes far more difficult."

"I don't think anyone can promise, ‘I can get your kids back.’"

To parents on the receiving end of this type of terminology, Blake’s first recommendation is not to immediately react.

"I tell adult parents to pause before they really react, because it's understandably going to make them very angry."

Taking time before responding can help keep the conversation from escalating and allow both sides to focus on the underlying conflict rather than reacting in the moment.

No. 4: Focus on specific behaviors and events

After pausing, Blake recommends asking the other person to explain specifically what they mean, going beyond broad labels to the behaviors underlying the complaint.

"Okay, you've used the word toxic – can you describe the behavior or behaviors that you consider to be toxic?" he asked as an example.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Blake distinguished between describing a person’s behavior and its impact on you, and assigning that person a sweeping label.

"If someone says, ‘When you criticize my weight, I left dinner feeling really, really upset,’ that's a fact. That's the person's interpretation," he said.

"But if you say, ‘You're toxic because you always criticize me,’ it’s very difficult to come back from that. So it sort of inflames the situation."

That approach shifts the conversation away from judgments about character and toward concrete actions and events that can actually be discussed.

No. 5: Use ‘I’ statements; avoid ‘always’ and ‘never’

When continued communication is appropriate, Blake suggested using language that focuses on a person’s own experience of a conflict rather than beginning with an accusation.

CLICK HERE TO 

"First, I would start by using ‘I’ statements, rather than ‘you,’" he advised. "It'd be like, ‘When you said this, I felt like this. When this happened, I did this.’"

This allows the person to discuss their own reaction to a specific interaction rather than beginning with an accusation.

Blake also recommends avoiding absolutes, such as "you always..." or "you never..." when trying to resolve a conflict.

In cases involving abuse, threats or other safety concerns, however, reconciliation or continued communication may not always be appropriate, he noted.

No guarantees

Although Blake maintains there is always hope for a reconciliation, he acknowledged that there is no single guaranteed formula for restoring a fractured relationship.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

While there are many people who are "selling" reconciliation services, Blake cautioned, "I don't think anyone can promise, ‘I can get your kids back.’"

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The goal is to create better conditions for reconciliation, not to promise that specific actions can achieve it, he noted.

Ultimately, Blake’s advice is for the person to focus on things within their control, such as embracing healthy habits, aiming for stability and building a community.

World.title: Cam Newton backs Aaron Rodgers, claiming NFL 'players, coaches and executives' used fake COVID vaccine cards
World.content:
It escaped vast attention last week when Aaron Rodgers suggested during his appearance on "The Pat McAfee Show" that NFL people got past league COVID-19 protocols by obtaining "fake" vaccination cards. And now, former quarterback Cam Newton is joining that chorus.

Newton, appearing on his "4th & 1" podcast on Monday, addressed the 2021 NFL protocols that required all team employees – players, coaches, staff, everyone – to get Covid-19 shots so as to avoid stringent frequent testing in order to enter team facilities.

All coaches were forced to take the shots or not work. Players who did not have their shots indeed had to submit to daily testing and had to wear a mask within the team facility and practice distancing guidelines during meals, meetings and workouts.

AARON RODGERS EVISCERATES ANTHONY FAUCI AFTER PLEADING THE FIFTH AT SENATE HEARING: 'ABSOLUTE CRIMINAL'

"If we're being honest," Newton said on his podcast, "Going back to 2020, there were multiple players, coaches, and executives that fraudulently got their COVID shot. Yes, I said it."

That allegation supports what Rodgers said last week in the middle of what was mostly a viral criticism of Anthony Fauci's testimony in front of the United States Senate.

Fauci, one of the leading members of the White House Coronavirus Task Force in 2020 under President Donald Trump, was a strong proponent of the vaccines when they were rolled out during President Joe Biden's administration. He testified before the Senate and invoked the Fifth Amendment so as to not incriminate himself under questioning from Senators.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Rodgers took Fauci to task for pleading the Fifth a total of 111 times but added this:

"A lot of people had probably fake vax cards back in the day," he said during the latter portion of his McAfee interview. "I remember seeing some of the vax cards. It was like written in crayon.

"I'm like, alright, so we're going to pass that off [as legitimate], but we [unvaccinated] are going to be second-rate citizens over here. I got to wear a yellow armband, train in the back, can't be around more than three people."

Rodgers called it a "crazy time" and it indeed was because wearing masks into restaurants but taking them off during the meal wasn't science derived from the virus being unable to affect people sitting down as opposed to standing up.

It was all performative.

"What a crock of (expletive)," Rodgers said, describing the madness.

Newton apparently agrees because he says people simply got around the NFL's protocols by buying their freedom.

"You're like, Cam, what do you know? It's like, man, I knew multiple people in that locker room didn't get the Covid shot," Newton said. "But they got a card that they paid for.

"Boy, nurses was making big bank. But that card and that little [stamp] .... Man, folks was trying to get in that club. 'Hey, man, you got your vaccination card? Yeah, yeah, I got it...' "

SWITZERLAND FIRES HOCKEY COACH WHO ADMITTED TO FAKING VACCINATION STATUS FOR 2022 BEIJING OLYMPICS

It should be noted that while Newton recalled Cardgate as starting in 2020, it actually began in 2021. And he had his issues with the vaccine during that time.

He was unvaccinated and when he traveled away from the New England Patriots for a medical appointment, he had trouble with the protocols.

The Patriots, for which Newton was the presumptive starting quarterback, said in a statement that Newton went to the appointment and was away for three days, testing negative each day for COVID-19.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

But due to a "misunderstanding about tests conducted away from NFL facilities" Newton became subjected to a five-day, re-entry cadence before he could return to the team facility.

Newton, who had become an inconsistent passer, lost practice time, then lost his starting job to rookie Mac Jones, and eventually lost his job on the team when he was released.

He later said he felt "bamboozled" by the entire issue.

But if Rodgers and Newton are right about fake vaccination cards being a thing around the NFL at the time, there was apparently much bamboozling being done by a number of people.

World.title: Primaries test the Democratic Party and ‘red alert’ after Colombia earthquake: Morning Rundown
World.content:
Progressive Democrats fight for primary wins in Wisconsin and Minnesota. A military intelligence assessment finds Iran’s priorities have shifted away from nuclear weapons and onto the Strait of Hormuz. And the U.S. experiences its hottest month ever recorded.

Here’s what to know today.

Progressives and Trump face major tests in Tuesday’s primaries

Democratic Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong Nam Y. Huh / AP

A week after a big win for progressive Democrats in Michigan’s Senate primary, the party’s ideological and generational divides are on full display again in another set of primaries, particularly in Wisconsin and Minnesota.

This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox.

In Wisconsin, state Rep. Francesca Hong’s campaign for governor is a major swing-state opportunity for the democratic socialist — and potentially a huge general election test for her movement and the broader Democratic Party. Hong, who has established a substantial polling lead, faces Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, whose candidacy intended to unite the establishment wing of the Democratic Party.

In Minnesota, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan faces moderate Rep. Angie Craig in the Democratic primary for the Senate. Flanagan has stressed her support for progressive policies while Craig has touted her 2018 win, which flipped the GOP-held House seat, as evidence that she can keep the seat in Democratic hands.

Meanwhile in South Carolina, Republicans will vote for a new Senate nominee after Sen. Lindsey Graham’s death. President Donald Trump threw his support behind appointed Sen. Darline Graham, the late senator’s sister, but it’s possible the crowded race will head to a runoff if no candidate wins a majority.

Primary races are also set for Vermont and Connecticut. And in Alabama, voters in a handful of House districts will pick their nominees now that a new congressional map is in effect, presenting a test of Trump’s endorsements.

Read more about the races to watch.

NBC News’ chief data analyst Steve Kornacki dives deeper into the last-minute effort to thwart Francesca Hong in Wisconsin in The Data Dive, a new subscriber-exclusive newsletter on the numbers, trends and data shaping the biggest stories heading into the midterms. Read today’s edition here.

More politics news:

The son of Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., was arrested on charges of sexual exploitation of a child, authorities said. Tyler Boebert, 21, was taken into custody and later released on $10,000 bond, Garfield County Sheriff’s Office said. The charges are linked to a 2024 video Tyler Boebert allegedly recorded with a 17-year-old, according to an affidavit in support of an arrest warrant. He was 18 at the time.

Trump signed an executive order that aims to reduce the number of universally recommended vaccines for children from 18 shots to 11.

For subscribers: The Senate’s newest odd couple — Sens. John Fetterman and Dave McCormick — is raising Republican eyebrows and Democratic alarms.

Republican officials in North Carolina selected state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom to replace Rep. Chuck Edwards on the November ballot after Edwards dropped his re-election bid following sexual harassment allegations.

Iran’s priority shifts to the Strait of Hormuz, U.S. assesses

A U.S. military intelligence assessment says Iran’s strategic priority has shifted from its nuclear program to the Strait of Hormuz, according to two U.S. officials. Trump has also been told by military officials that the U.S. could try to take the strait by force but that it would be long, deadly and very costly campaign, with no certainty the U.S. would win.

Iran and Oman have been negotiating the terms of a potential deal on the strait, with the U.S. on the sidelines. Trump insists that the U.S. Navy controls the strait, but negotiations to open the crucial waterway appear at an impasse, with Iran making new demands in recent days that seem to put a deal out of reach. Those demands include that the U.S. permanently end the war and compensate Iran for war damages, according to Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council.

More on Iran’s shifting priorities.

More than 100 dead after Colombia earthquake

Search efforts are underway after a powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake shook western Colombia yesterday, killing at least 132 people, injuring at least 700 and leaving many trapped under the rubble. The worst-hit cities include Pereira, Cali, Quibdó, Manizales and Armenia, all of which remain under “red alert,” the nation’s highest-level disaster threat level. The quake’s epicenter was reported in the municipality of San José del Palmar.

Seven airports have suspended operations, and hospitals, roads, transportation, aqueducts, energy and telecommunications have been disrupted in the hardest-hit areas, Colombia’s nonprofit Association of Capital Cities said.

Here’s what else we know.

The U.S. just had its hottest month on record

July was a month chock-full of extreme weather events. Now, it has two more distinctions: the hottest July ever recorded and the hottest month in the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s 132 years of record-keeping, the agency said.

The average temperature in the contiguous U.S. was 76.9 degrees — 3.3 degrees above the 20th-century average — and almost every part of the country experienced heat waves. There was also widespread drought, wildfires and heavy rainfall in nearly every corner of the country.

A look back at July’s extreme weather.

Staff Pick: A ‘pattern’ that keeps repeating

NBC News; Getty Images

Many will be familiar with the story of Renee Good, the Minneapolis woman whose killing by an ICE agent elicited fierce protests and reverberated nationally. But many may not know the story of Ruben Martinez, a young man in Texas who was also a U.S. citizen — and who was also killed in his car by an immigration officer a year earlier. Since then, there have been other similar shootings by immigration agents in Chicago, Houston and Maine.

We spoke to Martinez’s mom and other families’ advocates and officials, who described a “pattern” or “playbook”: the way the victims were described by ICE, the way the investigations were conducted and more importantly, what they saw as a lack of accountability over the fatal shootings. — Suzanne Gamboa, NBC News national reporter

Read All About It

For subscribers: Jury selection began in the high-profile trial of former gang member Duane “Keffe D” Davis, who is accused of ordering the murder of rap icon Tupac Shakur in 1996.

A proposed rule by the Trump administration would fix a loophole that allows additives in food. But critics say it wouldn’t prevent new ingredients from being introduced.

Jackie, one half of the internet’s beloved bald eagle pair Jackie and Shadow, has died after weeks of intensive medical care.

Mark Zuckerberg’s mega-yacht didn’t respond to a call for help from a small boat in Alaska. Instead, a 42-year-old tour boat steamed to the rescue.
