I expected more from the president.” The head of the Partido Republicano, Arturo Squella, agreed with Kast that the debate should remain in Congress without executive involvement.

Similar measures have been in force in Hungary since 2022 and in Spain's Castilla y León region.

World.title: De la Espriella gives the first earthquake toll and entrusts Colombia to Jesus Christ
World.content:
De la Espriella gives the first earthquake toll and entrusts Colombia to Jesus Christ

10th Monday, August 2026 - 19:16 UTC Full article

The toll, as of 12:30 local time, is preliminary

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella reported 111 dead and 87 injured on Monday from the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck the west and center of the country, in an address containing extensive religious references. “I entrust our country to the Lord Jesus Christ,” he said after chairing a meeting of the unified command post set up at the National Disaster Risk Management Unit.

The toll, as of 12:30 local time, is preliminary. The president listed 1,575 homes damaged and 37 destroyed, 61 buildings collapsed, 18 health centers, 52 schools and 17 community centers damaged, 18 roads affected and six airports out of service. The priority, he said, is rescuing people trapped under rubble. The government agreed to declare a national disaster situation, to be signed during the day.

De la Espriella announced he would personally lead the response and issue updates every two or three hours. He will travel to Quibdó, capital of Chocó, with the health and defense ministers, while Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara Restrepo heads to the coffee-growing region and Transport Minister Elsa Noguera to Valle del Cauca. Command posts have been set up in Bogotá, Armenia and Quibdó. The foreign ministry will coordinate international cooperation, and the president said the country's allies had offered assistance.

“Today all Colombians, without ideological distinctions, have to unite behind a single cause: the victims of this natural disaster,” he said. He argued that those affected would recover “with the help of God,” of the government and of the international community, and asked God to “protect Colombia.” Unlike his earlier appearances, he did not close with his customary slogan, “Firm for the Homeland.”

Religious language has been a constant feature since before he took office. The president was sworn in on Friday using the constitutional formula “I swear to God,” closed a speech to troops in Cali with “Long live Christ the King,” and included an interfaith segment in the ceremony. Days earlier he had gathered his incoming cabinet at a spiritual retreat, after which he said that “God must be placed at the center of every decision.”

Those statements have opened a debate over the scope of state secularism. The 1991 constitution established a non-confessional state, and in 1994 the Constitutional Court struck down a provision requiring the president to renew annually the country's official consecration to the Sacred Heart of Jesus. Senator Jennifer Pedraza walked out of the inauguration session, saying the ceremony threatened the secular character of the state. Constitutional lawyer Juan Manuel Charry has argued, by contrast, that a public official retains personal convictions while exercising office.

World.title: US border wall expansion threatens memory of Porvenir massacre
World.content:
A border wall construction project in Big Bend National Park in West Texas began last week, with a separate, nearby access road threatening the archaeological landscape of Porvenir, the site of a 1918 massacre of ethnic Mexican villagers.

Contractors began work Thursday on 17 miles of low, noncontiguous barrier fences and patrol roads, with conservationists reporting bulldozers clearing native vegetation.

One new access road appears to cut directly through Porvenir, which was a small farming community along the Rio Grande over 100 years ago.

On Jan. 28, 1918, Texas Rangers, local ranchers and apparently U.S. Army soldiers removed 15 unarmed ethnic Mexican residents (13 men and two teenage boys) from their homes and executed them, according to a lengthy report in Texas Monthly last week.

The location remains a sacred place for descendants and an archaeological site. A 2015 excavation found military-issued cartridge casings, evidence that challenged the historical narrative that the killings were carried out solely by vigilantes and Texas Rangers. The Texas Historical Commission erected a marker in 2018 after descendants campaigned for recognition.

Archaeologist David Keller told Texas Monthly that a newly built access road about 16 feet wide crosses the eastern third of the archaeological area and has been traversed by heavy machinery.

He said contractors and local officials indicated the route could eventually be widened to 100 or 120 feet.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is managing the project through Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

The CBP said the barriers, though low and not connected, are intended to prevent off-road vehicles from traveling to and from the Rio Grande, adding that the Porvenir access route is not finalized and public feedback will be considered.

DHS awarded a US $1.7 billion contract in May for the work, which has drawn widespread bipartisan opposition.

Even supporters of President Donald Trump have opposed the project for using billions of taxpayer dollars to build low fencing in a rugged, remote part of Texas where few illegal crossings have been recorded.

Podcaster Joe Rogan, who endorsed Trump in 2024, called the plan “B.S.” on his podcast, the San Antonio Current reported.

“This is the most heinous attack on an American national park in generations,” Laiken Jordahl, national public lands advocate for the Center for Biological Diversity, said in a statement posted to Instagram.

The Current reported that it was the first time in U.S. history that the federal government waived such a broad set of environmental protections for construction inside a national park.

With reports from Texas Monthly, AZFamily, San Antonio Current and Texas Standard

World.title: Mexico sends over 300 firefighters to British Columbia
World.content:
Listen to this article

More than 300 Mexican firefighters and technical personnel specializing in forest fires have travelled to British Columbia (B.C.), Canada, to support emergency efforts during the intense wildfires that have led to the evacuation of more than 20,000 people in the areas of Summerland and Peachland.

The Mexican teams arrived in separate contingents during the first few days of August, with the first group, comprising more than 100 people, arriving in Abbotsford on Aug. 3, and more than 200 crew arriving subsequently. A fourth delegation left on Sunday.

We’re beyond grateful to our friends and partners in Mexico for sending hundreds of firefighters to B.C. They’re joining a team of roughly 2,000 wildfire service personnel who are working tirelessly to get these fires under control. pic.twitter.com/5i8vFQFStr — David Eby (@Dave_Eby) August 6, 2026

Groups are deployed primarily throughout Fraser Canyon and the Thompson/Okanagan region, where they are participating in firefighting and control operations.

The contingent also features an incident management team, marking the first from Mexico to be deployed to B.C. under the mutual aid agreement between the two countries.

The tasks that the Mexican crew carry out include direct fire attack and the extinguishing of hot spots using hand tools and pumps, as well as reconnaissance and monitoring of areas where heat persists. They also participate in felling trees deemed hazardous and installing equipment to ensure a water supply during suppression operations.

B.C. Premier David Eby recognized the crew’s work and gave a welcoming speech as one of the contingents arrived at the airport.

“Mexico heard the call and, as you can see, has stepped up in a significant way,” Eby said.

Okanagan Falls park acting as base camp for over 300 wildfire firefighters from B.C. and Mexico

Watch this video on YouTube

Meanwhile, Minister of Forests Ravi Parmar said that he felt proud of the firefighters’ joint work.

“I’m proud of the wildland firefighters from Canada and Mexico who are not thinking about borders but are answering the call, as we do when our neighbours need us,” Parmar said.

Mexico’s envoys are made up of experienced personnel from the National Forestry Commission (Conafor), the National Commission of Protected Natural Areas (Conanp), state and municipal environmental agencies, Civil Protection, rural fire management brigades and civil society organizations.

The arrival of the firefighting crews comes as B.C. faces more than 100 active wildfires spanning 156 square kilometers. In addition to Mexico, British Columbia has received support from Australia, New Zealand and other Canadian provinces and territories.

With reports from Now Toronto, Publimetro, CBN Noticias and the CBC

World.title: Navy ramps up security presence in Mazatlán after high July homicide count
World.content:
After Mazatlán in July recorded its highest monthly homicide total of the year, the Mexican Navy on Saturday announced the deployment of more than 1,700 of its personnel to the Sinaloa port and resort city.

In a statement, the Navy Ministry (SEMAR) said that the deployment was occurring “within the framework of ‘Operation Sable’ Mazatlán” and was aimed at the “strengthening of security” in the city, the second largest in Sinaloa after state capital Culiacán.

The deployment comes after 36 homicides in Mazatlán in July, the city’s highest monthly total of murders in 2026, according to the newspaper El Sol de Mazatlán. It also follows the arrival of 900 Mexican Army troops in Mazatlán on July 23. The bolstering of the army’s presence in the city was part of a security reinforcement in response to a series of armed attacks.

In its statement, SEMAR said that the navy deployment reflects “the institution’s ongoing commitment to the well-being” of Mazatlán residents and tourists.

The ministry said that “operational actions will be focused on strategic areas … with the priority objective of reestablishing peace and public order and weakening illicit infrastructure that fuels schemes of violence and places the health of the population at risk.”

The term “illicit infrastructure” was a reference to clandestine drug laboratories and the cartel assets that support the distribution of narcotics, such as vehicles.

In its statement, SEMAR also issued what it called a “respectful call” for citizens and tourists to have “full confidence and certainty in the deployed forces.”

The ministry said that the central focus of the Mexican Navy’s operations is to “protect Mexican families while acting at all times with strict adherence to human rights, the proportional use of force and the current legal framework.”

“Its presence in the streets and on the coast has the sole aim of providing a safe and protected environment,” SEMAR said.

Violence in Mazatlán

Of the 36 people murdered in Mazatlán in July, 32 were men and four were women, El Sol de Mazatlán reported on Monday. The newspaper wrote that two cases were investigated as femicides, while two of the victims were minors.

Among the armed attacks in Mazatlán last month was one allegedly perpetrated by the “Los Chapitos” faction of the Sinaloa Cartel against marines, two of whom died from wounds they sustained. Marines returned fire and killed 10 criminals.

Much of the violence in Sinaloa is related to an ongoing battle between Los Chapitos, led by sons of convicted drug lord Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán, and “Los Mayos,” a Sinaloa Cartel faction formerly led by Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada. The battle intensified in 2024 after Zambada was kidnapped by Joaquín Guzmán López and forced onto a plane that flew him to New Mexico. Both Zambada and Guzmán López, a son of “El Chapo,” were arrested by U.S. authorities at the Doña Ana County International Jetport in the U.S. border state in July 2024.

While the majority of the fighting between Los Chapitos and Los Mayos has occurred in Culiacán and surrounding areas, the battle has spilled into other parts of Sinaloa, including Mazatlán.

As Mexico News Daily reported last month, on July 17 and 18, six armed attacks were reported in Mazatlán in less than 24 hours, leaving four people dead and three others wounded. Between July 22 and 23, five more people were murdered.

El Sol de Mazatlán reported that episodes of violence in Mazatlán in July, including attacks on homes with firearms and explosives, occurred in rural and urban areas of the municipality of Mazatlán, including parts of the city frequented by tourists. Among those areas, the newspaper reported, were San Marcos, Lomas de Monterrey, Santa Fe, Infonavit Alarcón, Hacienda del Seminario, Lomas del Ébano, Zona Dorada and Pradera Dorada.

With reports from Expansión and El Sol de Mazatlán

World.title: Most avocado exports to the US have resumed after last week’s suspension
World.content:
Approximately 75% of avocado packing facilities in Mexico’s Michoacán state have been cleared for export following a pause in the avocado trade with the United States over security concerns, Julio Berdegué, Mexico’s advisor for international agri-food affairs and strategic issues under the USMCA, announced on Saturday.

The re-approved facilities handle roughly 85% of Michoacán’s avocado exports and the rest will be restored soon, according to Berdegué.

Mexico exports over 1 million tonnes of avocados a year, according to data from the Mexican Agriculture Ministry. Meanwhile, Michoacán contributes the highest avocado production of any Mexican state, with an export market valued at US $3.65 billion.

U.S. avocado imports from Michoacán were temporarily suspended on Wednesday after the U.S. Embassy issued an alert regarding a “threat to U.S. interests.” It marked the third time in just over four years that the United States has suspended avocado trade with Mexico for security reasons.

The embassy statement announcing the suspension did not reveal the nature of the threat, but President Sheinbaum has since said that the suspension followed a meeting at the U.S. embassy related to threats against some of the inspectors hired by the United States to monitor sanitary quality.

A meeting scheduled for the following day with an organization of avocado producers revealed that there had been an increase in extortion cases in certain regions of Michoacán.

In response to the news, Mexico worked to “rapidly strengthen” security in the state for the “immediate and gradual” resumption of the export program, said U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson.

Following the suspension, Michoacán Governor Alfredo Ramírez Bedolla deployed an extra 300 security operatives to Michoacán’s avocado-growing region “as a preventive measure.” Then, on Thursday morning, the federal Defense Ministry announced it had sent more than 1,500 soldiers to the state to “protect avocado producers and packing plants in the region.”

Exports resumed from the municipalities of Tancítaro, Tacámbaro and Uruapan, as well as the area between Morelia and Pátzcuaro, on Saturday.

To prevent future security issues, the Mexican government has established a permanent working group to monitor security in the region and prevent extortion of producers.

With reports from ABC Noticias and La Jornada

World.title: Opinion: After growing up in Mexico, was I prepared for US high school?
World.content:
My parents took a big risk when they moved their newborn twins from Manhattan to a small town in central Mexico. Yet, I couldn’t be more grateful that they did.

My family came to San Miguel de Allende when I was six months old, and I lived there until I was 15. And although we love San Miguel, my parents thought it best to send me back to the United States for high school. Having mastered the arts of reading, writing and calculating in Mexican schools, I think it’s safe to say that I learned to be a student there.

I attended SMA-based Academia Internacional from preschool through third grade. Their school emphasizes diversity and individuality, with a multicultural student body comprising both Mexican and American students. At Academia, I met my best friends and made my favorite childhood memories. I began studying French in the third grade, took advanced English classes through the Cambridge program at school, performed dance shows at the local theater and, most importantly, became queen of the monkey bars.

In fourth grade, I transferred to Colegio Newland, another bilingual and diverse school that emphasizes leadership and hands-on learning. The school follows an innovative curriculum that integrates technology into the classroom, with much of our learning centered around a platform called Knotion. At Newland, I was the middle school student body president, competed in spelling bees, traveled to geography competitions in other cities and even created a haircare brand for my entrepreneurship class. I also played tennis and took piano lessons outside of school.

As I reflect on my schooling, I realize many people assume the Mexican education system is mediocre or easy. But in reality, it challenged me while providing a foundation I needed to comfortably transition to a U.S. high school. I recall my middle school teachers constantly assigning pop quizzes, and to make matters worse, they would hand back our tests from lowest grade to highest — yikes. I struggled a lot in the subject of history, and after failing an exam, I spent weeks studying to improve my grade, only to discover that the content was fascinating. Thanks to Newland, I found a passion for it.

My parents loved raising my brother and me in San Miguel and considered it the perfect place for young children. However, they believed it made sense for us to return to the United States for high school. And like many parents, mine worried about the transition and whether I was academically prepared for a more “rigorous” school. Nevertheless, they were confident my brother and I would be okay because of the values we grew up learning. In San Miguel, people respect each other, always offer help and love to joke around. My brother and I were raised with those same values. And because of them, we adapted and made friends quickly.

I started by studying for the SSAT, the entrance exam required by most private high schools in the U.S., and it was rough. In Mexico, standardized tests barely exist, so I was unfamiliar with the idea of them. Additionally, I had never taken an exam in English, making it difficult to understand academic vocabulary. However, being fluent in Spanish often helped me identify the meaning of words with Latin roots. And ironically, my Mexican upbringing was the strongest part of my application as I drew on my childhood experiences in my essays. I wrote about Christmas, listening to mariachis and visiting Oaxaca.

After a long admissions process, I enrolled in a small boarding school in northern California. At first, the Spanish-to-English transition was difficult. My first year, I remember getting a 60% on a physics exam and feeling completely defeated. But seeing my international friends excel after going through the same transition motivated me to keep trying my best.

It’s crazy to think that I moved away from home at just 15. My parents still live in Mexico while I’m at school thousands of miles away. Of course I was scared to be on my own, but growing up between two cultures has made adapting to a new environment much easier, and California has quickly become my second home.

Throughout the two years that I’ve studied in the U.S., I’ve learned so much. My love for history persists and I have even grown to like math! (sort of). I found that attending Spanish-speaking schools didn’t hold me back, but rather, it is one of the most fascinating parts of who I am.

Now, I am going into my senior year, in which I will be editor-in-chief of the school newspaper and a prefect in the dorms. I continue to challenge myself academically with Advanced Placement (AP) and Honors courses, and can’t wait to have as much fun as possible with my friends.

As the college application process begins, I continue to write about my Mexican upbringing in every essay. I couldn’t be more grateful to have grown up and studied in such a beautiful place. I truly believe that I wouldn’t be as outgoing, determined or academically accomplished had my parents chosen to raise me in Manhattan instead.

Zella Golden grew up in San Miguel de Allende and is a senior in high school in Marin, California. Golden is completing an internship with MND.

World.title: Taylor Farms recalls its Mexico-sourced jalapeños, cuts ties with Sinaloa supplier over salmonella scare
World.content:
Just weeks after Taylor Farms voluntarily recalled iceberg lettuce products sourced from central Mexico, the Salinas, California-based company is voluntarily recalling some products that include jalapeño chiles due to concerns about possible salmonella contamination.

The decision by Taylor Fresh Foods — the parent company — is linked to a recall issued by San Diego-based Coast Citrus Distributors, which announced it was voluntarily recalling fresh jalapeños due to food safety concerns.

Taylor Fresh Foods said in a statement that it is not aware of any reported illnesses linked to its products containing jalapeños.

In its own statement, Coast Citrus said it will “no longer” source peppers from a farmer based in the northwestern Mexican state of Sinaloa, while it “seeks alternative suppliers.”

Taylor Fresh Foods also stated that it no longer purchases products from the Sinaloa farmer and “will fulfill orders with alternative suppliers.”

Besides the chiles themselves, guacamole, pico de gallo, taco salsa, burritos and spicy sandwiches are among the jalapeño-containing prepared foods included in the latest Taylor Farms recall.

Several U.S. states have been notified that all such products that feature a “Best If Used By” date up to and including Aug. 16, 2026, have been recalled. The products were sold at stores such as Kroger, Stop & Shop, Target, Whole Foods, Trader Joe’s and Walmart.

The recall comes as a result of a salmonella outbreak in the U.S. linked to jalapeño peppers imported from Mexico that had sickened 345 people in 27 states and led to 36 hospitalizations as of last Wednesday.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued an alert on Aug. 5, while the Food and Drug Administration is “working to determine if recalled jalapeños went to grocery stores,” so additional recalls could be announced.

As a result of the alert, Coast Citrus immediately agreed to recall the affected products and notify its customers. The Chipotle Mexican Grill and Qdoba restaurant chains also stopped serving the jalapeños in question.

Salmonella infections can cause diarrhea, fever and stomach cramps, and can be especially serious in young children, the elderly and people with weakened immune systems. The illness usually lasts four to seven days, and most people recover without treatment.

The latest recall comes amid heightened scrutiny of food safety in the U.S. restaurant industry, following last month’s outbreak of cyclosporiasis — a parasitic disease — linked to iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell restaurants that was reportedly sourced from central Mexico.

With reports from RTV Noticias, The Associated Press, the BBC and La Jornada

World.title: MND Local: Why is Puerto Vallarta so quiet right now?
World.content:
Walk around Puerto Vallarta right now and something feels different.

It’s not simply quieter in the way Vallarta is meant to feel during low season. There aren’t just shorter waits at restaurants, and there isn’t just a little more room on the beach.

It’s empty.

Restaurants have tables sitting unused. Tour operators are seeing smaller groups. Businesses that depend on visitors are wondering when the crowds will return.

More than just the ‘low season’

Anyone who has lived here for a while knows that summer is slower. That’s nothing new. But this one? This one feels different.

And the question being asked across the city is simple: “Where did everybody go?”

The events of Feb. 22 certainly didn’t help. The violence that followed the military operation against cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as El Mencho, brought roadblocks, burned vehicles, disruptions and international headlines. Several airlines temporarily suspended flights to Puerto Vallarta as the situation unfolded.

For those here at the time, the reality was more complicated than the images broadcast around the world. The immediate crisis passed quickly, and Puerto Vallarta reopened even faster.

But for people watching those images thousands of kilometers away, they may have been all they saw. Fear has a far longer memory than a roadblock.

A viewer in Canada or the United States doesn’t necessarily distinguish between what happened that day and what Puerto Vallarta was like the day after, let alone what it’s like six months later.

If your only knowledge of a place comes from television footage showing burning vehicles and blocked roads, you might think twice about booking a holiday there, too.

However, February isn’t the whole story.

Increased competition for travelers

Travelers have more choices now, and Puerto Vallarta is competing harder for holiday dollars. Airfares and promotions matter, and more destinations are competing for the same travelers than ever before.

People can visit somewhere new, find a cheaper flight, take advantage of a resort promotion elsewhere or simply decide after several trips to Vallarta that they would like a change of scenery.

For a family deciding where to spend a week, a few hundred dollars makes a big difference.

Travelers don’t owe Puerto Vallarta their vacation, which means the city has to keep earning their business. That includes offering solid value.

Some may point out the prices certain restaurants are charging right now.

There are places in Puerto Vallarta where prices have climbed to the point that visitors can legitimately ask whether the experience still represents good value for money, particularly when compared with other destinations.

Yet there is another side to that conversation.

The economics of tourism

Restaurant owners still have employees to pay. They have rent, electricity, ingredients, maintenance, taxes and a list of other costs that don’t disappear because it’s August and the tables are empty.

When fewer people come through the door, every customer matters more. That doesn’t make every price reasonable, nor does it mean visitors should simply pay whatever they are asked. But to encourage lower prices, businesses need both a reason and a way to reduce them.

Volume matters. A restaurant with full tables can afford to make a little less per customer. A tour operator with full boats can offer a better deal. A shop with steady foot traffic can move more product at a smaller margin.

When the customers aren’t there, the math changes. That’s where the impact of a quiet tourism season spreads far beyond the hotel lobby.

Tourism isn’t just hotels. It’s the taxi driver waiting for a fare. It’s the server whose income depends partly on tips. The boat captain. The tour guide. The massage therapist. The shop owner. The market vendor. The person cleaning vacation rentals. It’s an enormous economic ecosystem that most people don’t consider until something goes wrong.

Why locals matter

The question isn’t necessarily whether businesses have any customers. It’s whether they have enough to make the numbers work. That’s where full-time residents come in, because local residents have far more influence than they realize.

Foreign residents often fall into the trap of thinking, “I’m not a tourist. Tourism doesn’t really affect me.”

It does. Local restaurants employ neighbors. Local shops generate community income. Taxis, tours and business recommendations all drive the surrounding economy.

One response to a quiet summer is surprisingly simple: Go out.

Try the restaurant you’ve been meaning to visit. Use the independent shop with the quirky knickknack that caught your eye. Book the local tour you’ve thought about taking. Catch a bus and venture beyond the tourist zone.

Leave a review. Recommend a business. Spend money locally. And when someone back home asks whether Puerto Vallarta is still worth visiting, tell the truth.

A shared investment

Yes, there was violence on Feb. 22. Yes, Vallarta deals with crime, traffic, construction and infrastructure issues. But it also offers extraordinary natural beauty, remarkable food, generous people, neighborhoods full of character and a community that continues to evolve.

Both things can be true.

Don’t sell a fantasy. Tell people why you still live here. Long-term residents offer something tourism campaigns never will: personal credibility.

When a government campaign says Puerto Vallarta is wonderful, people expect it — it’s a sales pitch. But when someone who has lived here for five, 10 or 20 years says, “I know the problems. I know what happened. And I still think you should come,” that carries real weight.

Maybe this unusually quiet summer is a warning. Maybe it’s simply a blip. Either way, it would be foolish not to pay attention.

The question shouldn’t only be “Where did everybody go?” It should also be “What can residents do to make sure they want to come back?” That starts with remembering that tourism isn’t an entitlement; it’s an investment everyone shares.

When those tables sit empty, the impact doesn’t stop with the restaurant owner. It ripples out, eventually reaching everyone who calls Puerto Vallarta home.

And when home is hurting, no one is untouched.

Charlotte Smith is a writer and journalist based in Mexico. Her work focuses on travel, politics and community. You can follow along with her travel stories at www.salsaandserendipity.com.

World.title: Has Mexico reined in its inflation rate? Not yet, says Banxico chief
World.content:
Inflation in Mexico fell to just 0.12 points above the Bank of Mexico’s 3% target in July, but the central bank’s governor says it’s too early to declare victory in the fight against rising prices.

“At the Bank of Mexico, we’re not claiming victory yet,” Victoria Rodríguez Ceja told the newspaper El Financiero in an interview published on Monday.

Her remarks came after the national statistics agency INEGI reported on Friday that Mexico’s annual headline inflation rate was 3.12% in July, down from 3.37% in June.

Rodríguez noted that the headline rate in July was the lowest since May 2020. However, “even though inflation is practically at the [3%] target,” the Bank of Mexico will continue to seek low and stable price rises, the central bank governor told El Financiero.

INEGI’s 3.12% annual inflation reading in July was the product of 3.95% year-over-year core inflation and 0.29% non-core inflation. Annual core inflation remained reasonably high due to factors such as 4.85% year-over-year price rises for processed food, beverages and tobacco and 4.36% year-over-year increases for services.

The low non-core reading was the product of a 3.34% annual drop in prices for agricultural products (fruit, vegetables and meat) and a 3.31% increase in energy prices, including those for electricity and gasoline. Prices for agricultural products also declined on a month-over-month basis in July, falling 1.51%.

Rodríguez: Lower prices for agricultural products won’t last

Rodríguez’s interview with El Financiero came after Mexico’s headline inflation rate fell during four consecutive months from April to July. The headline rate last month was 1.47 percentage points below the 2026 peak of 4.59% in March.

Rodríguez said that the recent decline in inflation is explained, in part, by “changes in relative prices caused by favorable supply shocks.”

That was a reference to increased supply of fresh food, such as fruit and vegetables, and, as a result, lower prices for such products, as reflected in INEGI’s latest inflation data.

Rodríguez said that the Bank of Mexico doesn’t anticipate that lower prices for agricultural products will last due to “the unique characteristics of these prices and their exposure to meteorological phenomena.”

The easing of drought conditions in Mexico is a major reason why fresh food prices have recently come down, but there is no guarantee that weather-related factors won’t cause increases in the future.

Further explaining why the Bank of Mexico isn’t yet declaring victory in the fight against rising prices, Rodríguez noted that core inflation was 3.95% in July, while services were 4.36% more expensive than a year earlier. Inflation for services has recently trended down, but is still higher than the central bank would like. One factor driving the increase in prices for services was a 5.93% year-over-year increase in private school fees in July.

The Bank of Mexico’s inflation outlook

The Bank of Mexico (Banxico) forecasts that Mexico’s average annual headline inflation rate will be 3.5% in both the third and fourth quarters of 2026. In other words, the central bank anticipates that inflation will be higher between August and December than the 3.12% reading in July.

Banxico sees inflation declining in every quarter next year. It anticipates an average rate of 3.4% in Q1 of 2027, 3.3% in Q2, 3.2% in Q3 and 3% in Q4.

Those forecasts are included in a monetary policy statement released by Banxico last Thursday after its governing board voted in favor of maintaining the central bank’s key interest rate at 6.50%. Rodríguez told El Financiero that the bank’s current benchmark rate will contribute to the consolidation of “inflation’s downward path toward the [3%] target.”

However, she noted that the bank’s interest rate is subject to change based on “our assessment of the inflation outlook.”

In its Aug. 6 statement, the Bank of Mexico noted that headline inflation is “expected to converge to the target in the fourth quarter of 2027,” two quarters later than the bank anticipated when announcing its board’s interest rate decision in late June.

It said that its inflation forecasts “are subject to various risks.”

On the upside, they include “persistence of core inflation; disruptions due to foreign trade policies or to an inflationary impact from geopolitical conflicts; climate-related impacts; cost-related pressures, and a trend towards depreciation of the Mexican peso.”

On the downside, the risks include “lower-than-anticipated economic activity in Mexico and/or the United States; lower pass-through from increased costs, and lower pressures stemming from the appreciation that the national currency has been registering since last year.”

In her interview with El Financiero, Rodríguez stressed that the Bank of Mexico’s focus when making monetary policy decisions is the “inflation dynamic,” rather than economic growth, which had been very weak — or non-existent on a quarter-over-quarter basis — until a 1.5% sequential expansion in the second quarter of 2026.

With reports from El Financiero

World.title: Costa Rica Runs Its National Evacuation Drill Wednesday
World.content:
At 10 a.m. Wednesday, offices, schools, hotels, clinics and government buildings across Costa Rica will empty into the street at the same time. Nothing will be wrong.It is the eighth national evacuation drill, and if you are in a building when it starts, someone will ask you to leave it. Follow them, take the stairs, and expect to be back at your desk or in your room within ten or fifteen minutes.

You do not need to have signed up to be swept along by it. If your hotel, your child’s school or your workplace registered, you are taking part whether or not anyone told you in advance.If you want to actually use the exercise rather than just stand outside for it, there are three steps.

Register at simulacro.cr, write or update an emergency plan for your household or business, then evacuate at 10 a.m. Wednesday and report that you did it through the Simulacro CR app. The middle step is the one that matters and the one most people skip. A plan means deciding now who collects the children, where everyone meets if the house is unsafe, which route you take if the usual road is blocked, and what you would grab on the way out.

Standing in a parking lot for ten minutes teaches you nothing if you have never answered those questions. This year’s exercise works differently from previous ones. Rather than everyone rehearsing the same scenario, you practice for the hazard that can actually reach where you are. Eight are on the list — earthquake, flood, landslide, volcanic eruption, tornado, hurricane, fire and tsunami.

The reason for this change is more common sense than anything else. Practicing a tsunami evacuation in Cartago is wasted effort, and practicing an earthquake drill on a beach where the real problem is the water arriving twenty minutes later teaches the wrong reflex. What you rehearse should match what is likely to happen where you live.

Unfortunately, turnout is running behind last year. The emergency commission counted 350,000 people signed up as of August 3, against more than 1.4 million who took part in 2025 — the highest participation on record. Keep in mind that registration and participation are not the same thing and sign-ups tend to surge in the final days, but the gap is wide.

Alejandro Picado, president of the Comisión Nacional de Emergencias, has pointed to emergencies elsewhere as the argument for taking it seriously, noting that Costa Rica deals with emergencies constantly and that knowing how to act is a civic responsibility rather than an optional extra.

Expect some public services to slow. The Tribunal Supremo de Elecciones will run the drill at its main offices, its warehouse in Desamparados, the Civil Registry archive in Los Yoses and all 32 regional offices, with more than a thousand people involved at the main site alone, including members of the public who happen to be mid-transaction. If you have paperwork to do Wednesday morning, do it early or do it Thursday.

The app is worth downloading before Wednesday rather than during it. It carries information about the exercise and is how you log your participation afterward, which is how the commission measures who actually took part. Monday’s magnitude 7.4 earthquake in Colombia, which killed more than a hundred people and closed three airports, is a reminder of why Costa Rica runs this exercise at all. Emergencies do not schedule themselves, and the ten minutes you spend outside on Wednesday are the cheapest preparation available.

World.title: Colombian Camila Osorio Leads Latin American Women at Cincinnati Open
World.content:
Camila Osorio will carry the strongest Latin American hopes in the women’s main draw when the Cincinnati Open begins this week in Mason, Ohio. The 24-year-old Colombian arrives as the region’s only confirmed direct entrant in singles, while four other Latin American women will attempt to reach the tournament through qualifying: Colombia’s Emiliana Arango, Mexico’s Renata Zarazúa and Argentines Nadia Podoroska and Solana Sierra.

Their presence gives Latin American tennis fans several players to follow at one of the final major events before the US Open, but Osorio enters Cincinnati with the clearest opportunity to make an extended run. The former junior world No. 1 has already collected a title this season, winning the WTA 125 tournament in Manila. She defeated Alex Eala in the quarterfinals before overcoming Donna Vekic in the championship match.

That result offered another reminder of the qualities that have made Osorio one of Latin America’s most consistent women on the tour. She does not overpower opponents with her serve, but she moves exceptionally well, absorbs pace and competes with an intensity capable of turning routine matches into long physical battles.

Osorio has enjoyed most of her success on clay, particularly at home in Bogotá, where she has won three WTA singles titles. Her game, however, is increasingly comfortable on hard courts. Cincinnati will provide an important test of that progress against a field expected to include most of the world’s leading players.

The fast conditions in Ohio place a premium on serving and first-strike tennis, two areas that can expose Osorio against the tour’s biggest hitters. Her ability to defend the baseline, vary the height of the ball and force opponents into extra shots will be essential. Cincinnati also represents an important opportunity before the US Open. A favorable draw and several victories would give Osorio ranking points, confidence and valuable match preparation before the final Grand Slam tournament of the season begins in New York on August 30.

Behind her, qualifying may offer an early look at the broader state of Latin American women’s tennis. Arango gives Colombia a second player with a realistic chance of reaching the main draw. She has steadily established herself at tour level after breaking into the Top 100 during the 2025 season and has become an increasingly important part of Colombia’s women’s program.

Zarazúa remains one of the most important figures in Mexican tennis. She became the first Mexican woman in decades to establish herself inside the WTA Top 100 and has built her career around speed, consistency and intelligent point construction. Her counterpunching style can make her a difficult qualifying opponent, particularly when she is able to extend rallies and frustrate more aggressive players.

Argentina will be represented in qualifying by two players at different points in their careers. Podoroska remains best known for her semifinal run at the 2020 French Open, but injuries and fluctuations in form have repeatedly interrupted her progress. Cincinnati gives the 29-year-old another chance to regain momentum at a high-level tournament.

Sierra, meanwhile, represents part of Argentina’s next generation. The 22-year-old has made steady progress through the lower levels of the professional circuit and enters Cincinnati with an opportunity to test herself against players accustomed to WTA competition. The qualifying path will not be easy. The field includes former Grand Slam champion Sofia Kenin, former US Open finalist Leylah Fernandez and a collection of experienced tour players and emerging prospects.

Latin America’s qualifiers may need to defeat established names simply to earn a place in the 96-player main draw. That imbalance illustrates the challenge facing women’s tennis across much of the region. Latin America continues to produce talented competitors, but relatively few have been able to establish themselves near the top of the rankings. Travel costs, limited access to elite training and the small number of major tournaments in the region all make the climb more difficult.

Brazil’s Beatriz Haddad Maia has been the area’s highest-profile women’s player in recent seasons, but she is not currently listed in the Cincinnati field. That leaves Osorio at the front of a smaller contingent seeking to make an impact in Ohio. For Osorio, Cincinnati is more than another stop on the calendar.

It is a chance to show that her success can extend beyond the clay courts of Bogotá and into the demanding hard-court events that shape the second half of the WTA season. For Arango, Zarazúa, Podoroska and Sierra, the first task is more immediate: survive qualifying and give Latin America a larger presence when the main draw begins.

World.title: Two men injured after licensed gun owner fires warning shots during San Pedro altercation
World.content:
Two men injured after licensed gun owner fires warning shots during San Pedro altercation

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating a shooting incident in San Pedro Town after two young men reported sustaining gunshot injuries during an altercation involving several persons early Sunday morning.

Police responded to Lion Street at approximately 1:45 a.m. on August 9, where they spoke with 29-year-old mechanic Francisco Daniel Nah.

According to police, Nah reported that he was at a store when two golf carts arrived and their male occupants became involved in a verbal altercation, during which bottles were thrown.

Nah told investigators that one of the men approached him and reached toward his waist, leading him to believe that the man was retrieving a firearm. Fearing for his life, Nah, who police say is licensed to carry a 9mm pistol, fired three warning shots into the ground.

The occupants of the golf carts subsequently left the area.

However, at approximately 1:30 p.m. later that day, 20-year-old Rennel Aguilar and 19-year-old Edwin Barco reported to police that they had sustained gunshot injuries during the incident. Both men were taken for medical treatment.

Police have not indicated whether investigators have established what caused the men’s injuries or whether they were struck by rounds fired from Nah’s licensed weapon.

The investigation continues.

World.title: Two 19-year-olds hospitalized following Dangriga shooting
World.content:
Two 19-year-olds hospitalized following Dangriga shooting

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating a shooting in Dangriga Town that left two 19-year-old men hospitalized on Saturday night.

Police say that at approximately 8:30 p.m. on August 8, officers visited the Southern Regional Hospital after receiving reports of a shooting and found Kevon Higinio and Jim Mendez, both of Dangriga, suffering from apparent gunshot wounds.

Initial investigations indicate that Higinio had just left an establishment when he was approached by two male persons who opened fire in their direction, injuring both Higinio and Mendez.

Both men were listed in stable condition and remained hospitalized under observation.

Police investigations into the shooting continue. The incident and identities of the two injured men have also been reported by local media.

World.title: Post-mortem confirms Samuel Chi died from drowning; police investigation continues
World.content:
Post-mortem confirms Samuel Chi died from drowning; police investigation continues

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police say a post-mortem examination conducted on fisherman Samuel Chi has determined his cause of death to be asphyxia due to drowning, while toxicology results remain pending.

Chi disappeared at sea along with Albert Vaccaro after the men went on a fishing trip on Sunday, August 2 and failed to return as expected.

A joint search involving the Belize Coast Guard and other authorities was launched, and Vaccaro was found alive the following day floating in waters southwest of Hicks Caye. Authorities said at the time that he was dehydrated and disoriented and was unable to provide a clear account of what had occurred.

Chi remained missing until his body was recovered the following morning in waters west of Hicks Caye.

During Monday’s police press briefing, authorities said the forensic pathologist found the cause of death to be asphyxia due to drowning. Police indicated that the post-mortem did not establish evidence of violence.

However, investigators are still trying to determine the circumstances that led to Chi and Vaccaro ending up in the water.

Police could not confirm during the briefing whether investigators have since obtained a comprehensive statement from Vaccaro, noting that he was initially too disoriented to provide investigators with much information.

Chi’s family has publicly raised questions about the circumstances surrounding his death and expressed suspicions that foul play may have been involved.

Police say the investigation remains ongoing.

World.title: Belize City man charged in connection with Faber’s Road shooting
World.content:
Belize City man charged in connection with Faber’s Road shooting

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have arrested and charged a 26-year-old Belize City man in connection with a shooting incident in the Faber’s Road area over the weekend.

Gregory Williams has been charged with abetment to commit aggravated assault following a police investigation into the incident, which occurred at approximately 7:00 p.m. on Saturday, August 8.

According to police, a man reported that he was at his residence when a motorcycle carrying two men approached him.

One of the men aboard the motorcycle allegedly fired a single shot in his direction.

Police subsequently arrested Williams in connection with the incident.

Authorities say another individual is being sought as part of the ongoing investigation.

World.title: Punta Gorda man charged with drug trafficking after police seize 17.63 grams of crack cocaine
World.content:
Punta Gorda man charged with drug trafficking after police seize 17.63 grams of crack cocaine

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have arrested and charged a 59-year-old Punta Gorda resident following the discovery of two quantities of suspected crack cocaine at his home.

Mark Lopez has been charged with two counts of possession of controlled drugs with intent to supply to another person.

Police say officers executed a search warrant at Lopez’s residence on Friday, August 7, during which they allegedly discovered two separate quantities of suspected crack cocaine.

The drugs reportedly weighed 10.97 grams and 6.66 grams respectively, for a combined weight of 17.63 grams.

Lopez was subsequently detained and formally charged.

World.title: Santa Elena man charged after police allegedly find 5.9 grams of cocaine
World.content:
Santa Elena man charged after police allegedly find 5.9 grams of cocaine

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have arrested and charged a 24-year-old Santa Elena resident after he was allegedly found in possession of suspected cocaine over the weekend.

Christopher Bolon has been charged with possession of controlled drugs with intent to supply.

Police say the arrest followed an operation conducted by Santa Elena police shortly before 1:00 a.m. on Saturday, August 8.

During the operation, officers allegedly found Bolon in possession of 5.9 grams of suspected cocaine.

He was subsequently detained and formally charged.

World.title: Three killed in Mahogany Street motorcycle collision
World.content:
Three killed in Mahogany Street motorcycle collision

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Three men have died following a collision involving two motorcycles on Mahogany Street in Belize City early Sunday morning.

Police say that at approximately 12:26 a.m. on August 9, officers responded to the area near the intersection of Mahogany and Tibruce Streets, where they found two extensively damaged motorcycles.

The victims were identified as Darwin Monroy, Allan Arnold and 22-year-old Theodore Swaso, all of Belize City.

According to police, Arnold was travelling on a motorcycle in one direction while Monroy was travelling in the opposite direction with Swaso as his pillion rider when the two motorcycles collided.

All three men sustained grave injuries. Arnold and Monroy died shortly after the collision, while Swaso was rushed to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where he later succumbed to his injuries.

Police say only one motorcycle helmet was recovered from the scene. Investigators have not yet established who was wearing the helmet at the time of the collision.

The circumstances surrounding the fatal crash remain under investigation.

World.title: Mundialito opening season 2026 kicks off
World.content:
Mundialito opening season 2026 kicks off

By Zoila Palma: The Mundialito Opening Season 2026 officially kicked off on August 8 at Berger Field, bringing together young footballers from across Belize to compete in several youth categories.

The tournament features the U-13 and U-10 male categories as well as the U-15 female category, providing an opportunity for Belize’s young players to showcase their skills and develop their talent.

The competition continues on August 11 at Berger Field, with the next game scheduled for 2:00 p.m. Football fans are encouraged to come out and support the young athletes as they compete for top honors.

World.title: Tougher water fines
World.content:
Water level in the Mona reservoir last week.

SEVEN parishes will face a water prohibition from Monday, August 17 as the Government moves to tighten restrictions amid worsening drought conditions.

At the same time, Minister of Water, Environment and Climate Change Matthew Samuda is set to approach the executive and legislature to punish violators with stiffer fines.

“As we had to do after the first incident that took place with Rio Cobre, where we had to shift the fine, we now have to take the same approach with fines in relation to water prohibition,” Samuda told the Jamaica Observer on Monday.

“Because of the present forecast and warning associated with El Niño, we will have to move with unprecedented speed, and we will have to engage first the Cabinet and then Parliament in the coming weeks to facilitate this,” Samuda added.

On Monday, Samuda’s ministry, through the National Water Commission (NWC), announced that the water prohibition orders will apply to Kingston, St Andrew, St Thomas, St Mary, Portland, St Ann, and St Catherine and will remain in force until further notice.

“Under the orders, no person shall use or cause water supplied by the NWC to be used for non-essential or unusual purposes. Prohibited activities include:

• irrigation or watering of gardens, lawns, grounds, and farms;

• refilling or supplying of ponds or swimming pools and/or for use other than normal domestic services such as drinking, cooking, washing, bathing, and sanitation;

• washing of vehicles by the use of a hose;

• watering or washing of roadways, pavements, paths, garages, or out-rooms;

• any activity requiring excessive or unusual quantities of water,” the ministry release stated.

The ministry said the decision followed a high-level stakeholder meeting earlier Monday with the NWC and the Meteorological Service, which confirmed that rainfall levels remain critically low and temperatures continue to soar.

Underscoring the necessity of the measure, Samuda said, “We understand that there is some disproportionate economic impact on commercial operations, such as car washes, and we have not taken this decision lightly. Ultimately, our priority is to maintain supply to critical services, especially schools, as we prepare for the September reopening.”

He further advised that sanctions will be applied to individuals and entities found in breach of the prohibition order, noting “these penalties are intended to ensure compliance and protect the integrity of Jamaica’s water supply during this critical period”.

The current fine for breaching an NWC prohibition order is $1,000. Failure to pay the court-ordered fine results in imprisonment for up to 30 days.

Samuda’s reference to the Rio Cobre was the action taken by the Government after chemical spills that resulted in fish kills that affected several species and impacted other aquatic organisms four years ago.

In January 2025 he successfully piloted a Bill in the House of Representatives which approved amendments to the Natural Resources Conservation Authority (NRCA) Act and the Wild Life Protection Act to allow for significant increases in fines and related custodial sentences.

Under the Acts, depending on the severity of the offence, as adjudicated by the Supreme Court, corporate bodies may now be subject to a fine of approximately $10 million, individuals in breach of the Acts may face a fine of up to $5 million or serve a term of imprisonment up to five years, subject to the jurisdiction of the parish courts.

On Monday, Samuda told the Observer that the request he will be taking to Cabinet and Parliament is to “move the fines in line with what was done for bodies corporate and individuals under the NRCA Act breaches.

The naturally-occurring El Niño climate pattern, which began in June and is expected to peak later this year, has already amplified unprecedented temperatures across the world.

Some 33 countries recorded their hottest July since records began, according to a detailed analysis of billions of data points from Copernicus’s ERA5 climate model.

The severe drought has triggered food security concerns worldwide.

Last week, the United Nations World Food Programme said that Central America is expected to be the region hardest hit in terms of the relative increase in food insecurity.

Including the Caribbean, the agency estimates that an additional 16 million people could face food insecurity by the end of 2027.

Heat projections for the next three weeks

World.title: Who hurt the child?
World.content:
AN announcement by the Child Protection and Family Services Agency (CPFSA) that it is fast-tracking the installation of security cameras at Glenhope Place of Safety, even as it probes the injuries suffered by a one-year-old boy who had been in its care, has been welcomed by attorney Denise Hinson who is adamant that somebody needs to be held accountable for how the child came to be injured in such a manner.

“The questions still need to be answered. This should not be pushed under the rug. I’m angry, and I think that someone needs to explain why a one-year-old defenceless child, a Jamaican child, looks as if he was in an MMA (mixed martial arts) fight,” Hinson told the Jamaica Observer on Monday.

The attorney is representing the mother of the child who is before the court for immigration issues.

She said the child’s injuries captivated the attention of the St Catherine Parish Court last Friday when the matter was called up before Justice Roneiph Lawrence.

Hinson said the child’s Haitian mother, Fabienne Cherisma, who was recently arrested for overstaying her visa alongside her husband who is said to have used fraudulent documents to obtain Jamaican citizenship, were on Friday brought before the court so it could make a further order for the child to remain in the custody of the State.

However, Hinson said when the child was presented to the court, both parents went into shock.

“The child was taken to court with [healing] black and blue bruises under both eyes; what seemed to be burn marks to the right cheek and chin; swelling of the face, especially to the right cheek; and scratches to the nose. Both eyes were bloodshot in the corners. A medical shown to the court by the CPFSA officer who brought the baby to court, described the injuries as ‘non-accidental’,” Hinson told the Observer.

The attorney said that when the mother saw her child she “screamed and began to cry uncontrollably and the father collapsed. They had to be removed and later returned to the dock”.

Hinson said the court was also “visibly disturbed by the doctor’s findings and the injuries on the baby’s face”.

She said the CPFSA officer, when pressed by the judge about the cause of the child’s injuries, “informed the court that when she asked, on arriving to collect the child, she was told that he had hit his face on the crib”.

The attorney, in making a successful bail application on behalf of the mother, who was released on humanitarian grounds, however countered that, “both eyes were bruised and that could not have occurred if the child simply fell out his crib”.

“I also pointed out that the child is in danger where he is and that he needed his mother. My focus is really to get to the bottom of how the child received those injuries at Glenhope. Also, the bruises were healing and the burn mark almost completely healed. However, the child didn’t see a doctor until the day before court, on August 6, 2026. I need help in finding out when and how the child was injured and why the child wasn’t taken to the doctor until the day before the scheduled court date,” Hinson declared.

The attorney said she is in discussion with the child’s mother to determine the legal options available to her as she presses for answers regarding her son’s health. Hinson told the Observer that her client is adamant that the “child was in perfect health when removed from [their] home”.

The CPFSA issued a statement to the media on Monday saying “the incident is being investigated and is being treated with utmost urgency and importance”.

The agency stated that it “takes a zero-tolerance approach to all forms of child abuse” and said, based on the outcome of the investigation, it stands ready to execute all measures or sanctions regarding child abuse, in keeping with the Child Care and Protection Act (CCPA 2004).

Furthermore, the CPFSA said under its 2025–2027 strategic framework it established an islandwide initiative to equip residential child care facilities with security cameras, ensuring high safety standards are maintained across all locations.

“In light of the recent incident however, deployment has been prioritised to fast-track installation at the facility in which this incident has taken place,” the agency pledged.

World.title: Wellington praises Team Jamaica after World U-20 exploits
World.content:
Shanoya Douglas won three medals for Jamaica — gold in the women’s 4x100m relay and silver in the 100m and 200m. (Photo: Paul Reid)

OREGON, USA — Keith Wellington, team leader for Jamaica at the 21st staging of the World Athletics Under-20 Championships, says the team performed well despite the challenges of a long season.

Jamaica won eight medals — two gold, three silver and three bronze — to finish fourth on the medal table and third in the placing table with 89 points.

Hosts United States topped both tables with 24 medals —12 gold, seven silver and five bronze. Kenya were second with 11 medals — four gold, three silver and four bronze — while Italy finished third with five medals — three gold and two bronze.

Shanoya Douglas was Jamaica’s most successful athlete, winning three medals — gold in the women’s 4x100m relay and silver in the 100m and 200m.

Wellington said the performances were particularly impressive given that most of the athletes had been competing since January.

“I think under any circumstances this would be a really good performance,” Wellington told the Jamaica Observer on Sunday before the final two relays were contested. “Eight medals to date, and third in terms of quality.”

He said the overall standard at the championships had improved significantly.

“We have seen some really world-class standards, not just as juniors but the quality of the performances has been really, really good overall for all the countries. And so, to still be amongst the best, I think, we would be proud of the performances.”

Wellington singled out Michael Andre Edwards’ dramatic victory in the men’s triple jump during which he produced a World Under-20-leading and personal best 17.08m — the fifth-longest winning mark in the history of the event at the championships.

“Yeah, I think the obvious standout would be Team Captain Michael Andre’s performance. Not just the 17.08m but remember, you know, he took the lead with his second-to-last jump. It was taken away from him and he came back and claimed it. So it’s not just the result, but the quality and the performance there.”

He also highlighted the men’s discus throw competition on Sunday involving Jamaicans Joseph Salmon and Kamari Kennedy, when the lead changed several times over the final two rounds.

Jamaica also set two national records in the mixed 4x100m relay, which was contested for the first time at the championships, and the mixed 4x400m relay.

Ten Jamaicans produced personal bests, including Shevaughn Thomas and Sashane Johnson who each recorded two personal best performances.

Wellington said the athletes’ performances should not be judged solely by their results, pointing to the demands of the Jamaican school season.

“I think we don’t want to just look at the results, but look at the performances and you can see quite a few quality performances. And we cannot ignore, again, that our juniors have a really long season; and it is the schools that invest most in these kids, so they have to peak for champs because that is where the investment is,” he said.

“And so, for them to come back five months after their last performance for their schools again is sometimes a challenge that many of them have exams in the middle and all of that. So, I think it’s an incredible performance.”

World.title: STAYING PUT!
World.content:
Sanjay Seymore (left) anchors Jamaica’s men’s 4x100m relay team to victory in the semi-finals of the World Athletics Under-20 Championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon, on Saturday. Jamaica ran 39.51 seconds to advance to the final. At centre is Hong Kong’s Cheuk Fung Jasper Koo, while at right is Australia’s Joshua John. (Photo: Paul A Reid)

OREGON, USA — William Knibb Memorial High School’s Sanjay Seymore has turned down several offers from United States colleges, choosing to remain in Jamaica as he targets places on the country’s teams for the 2027 World Athletics Championships and 2028 Olympic Games.

The ISSA/GraceKennedy Boys’ and Girls’ Athletics Championships and Carifta Games 200m champion is coming off a season of highs and lows, including finishing third in his favourite event at the Jamaica Athletics Administrative Association (JAAA) National Junior Championships and missing out on an individual spot on Jamaica’s team to the 21st World Athletics Under-20 Championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon.

Seymore, who recently signed a professional contract, declined to give details about his plans but confirmed to the Jamaica Observer on Sunday that he would remain in Jamaica for now.

“I can say definitely I’m staying in Jamaica for now. So yes, that’s the only thing I can say right now that I would be staying in Jamaica.”

He said he believes remaining at home gives him the best opportunity to make Jamaica’s teams for the World Championships and Olympics.

“It’s just I think it’s the best for me right now, I don’t really have anything against college,” he said. “I see that when you go college and then come back for the Jamaica trials, athletes are not at their best and then and you know we have World Championship and Olympics coming up.”

At 19, Seymore believes he has time to develop as he prepares to compete against some of the world’s leading sprinters, including Jamaica’s Oblique Seville.

“They already have their reputations, Oblique Seville is a world champion, so you can’t take that from him. So, as the rookie, I would say I’m just going into the big game with the seniors, and I’m just going to give it my best shot always, like I done in junior levels. But I know I have to put the best foot forward if I want to make it big as a Jamaican sprinter. So that’s definitely goal for me.”

Seymore had been expected to qualify for Jamaica’s team in the 200m but suffered an injury shortly before the JAAA Championships. He finished third in the final in 21.01 seconds behind Nathaniel Martin and Kyle Bodden.

He was subsequently added to the men’s 4x100m relay team and ran two strong anchor legs as Jamaica won bronze.

“After Carifta I had some injuries, went to trials and came third as I was coming back from the injury,” he said. “But I got my mind right and told myself I’m going to go on this relay and I’m going to give it my best shot and go into the best possible shape I can for the team.”

Seymore said he was pleased with his contribution to the bronze-medal effort.

“So I just went out there and give my best and we came short of the gold medal, but we still made the podium, so I’m pretty happy for that.”

World.title: BWE organisers respond to viral fight video, reaffirms commitment to patron safety
World.content:
Videograb showing a brawl at a Best Weekend Ever beach event on Sunday, August 10, 2026.

ST ANN, Jamaica – The directors of party series Best Weekend Ever (BWE) has expressed disappointment and regret over a physical altercation involving patrons at its beach event on Sunday.

Videos of the incident have been widely circulated on social media, showing a group of men engaged in a brawl.

In a media release Monday, the party organisers said, “Best Weekend Ever has never condoned, and we abhor the proliferation of violence of any kind at our events.

“We are extremely disappointed and sincerely regret that this unfortunate and isolated situation has occurred,” the release continued. “We have contacted the family of those affected and the individuals involved in the altercation have been clearly identified, and the relevant actions will be pursued by the designated authority.”

According to the directors, over the years, BWE has established a strong track record of providing safe, well-managed entertainment experiences for thousands of patrons.

“The safety and security of our guests remain a priority, and this incident is not reflective of the culture of Best Weekend Ever or the experience we work diligently to provide,” they said.

The directors also sought to clarify that, contrary to some narratives circulating, the MC at the event “brought attention to the incident to allow the appropriate intervention to take place and we have made our team available to the relevant authorities to assist in the process of ensuring this does not reoccur.”

According to the release, throughout the staging of Best Weekend Ever 2026, the events have been enjoyed safely by thousands of patrons with improved traffic management and movement between events.

“We are also grateful for the positive feedback from patrons which is an indication of the high level of satisfaction with the production of the event series,” the organisers said.

“Additional security measures have been put in place for the final event being staged today,” they added. “We thank our patrons, partners, security teams and stakeholders for their support as we continue to remain committed to delivering an environment where everyone can celebrate responsibly and safely.”

World.title: Tropical depression could form in Atlantic by the end of the week
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — The United States National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) is advising that a tropical depression could form in the Atlantic during the latter half of this week.

The NOAA says an area of low pressure located a few hundred miles south of the Cabo Verde Islands is producing disorganised showers and thunderstorms.

As this system moves slowly westward, a tropical wave currently over west Africa is expected to merge with it in a couple of days.

Environmental conditions are forecast to be more conducive for development by midweek, and a tropical depression could form during the latter half of this week while the system moves westward to west-northwestward across the central tropical Atlantic.

Formation chance through 48 hours is low at 20 per cent but formation chance through seven days is medium at 60 per cent.

World.title: Bold Bruce
World.content:
Former Prime Minister Bruce Golding

NEW YORK, USA — Former Jamaican Prime Minister Bruce Golding has earned the backing of many within the Diaspora community here for what is being described as his “bold, factual and truthful position” on the souring relationship between Jamaica and America, two staunch allies.



Speaking in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania last week, Golding expressed hopes that “the United States will soften the tone of its relationship with Jamaica and rekindle the strong, decades-old bond between both nations which Jamaicans cherish.

Saying that current demands by Washington are “at odds with the very essence of true friendship”, he pointed to the many challenges facing the island as established rules are being discarded and “new rules are being handed down, not after discussions and negotiations, but unilaterally by social media postings at 2:30 in the morning when most of us are asleep”.

The former Jamaican leader, who stepped away in 2011 and handed over the reins to now Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness, was addressing the annual Team Jamaica Bickle Independence Gala on Emancipation Day, August 1, 2026.

The gala celebrated Jamaica’s 64th anniversary of Independence and raised funds in support of Jamaican and other Caribbean athletes’ participation in the yearly Penn Relays in the US, a must-stop on the annual sports calendar for speedy Jamaican high school students.

Golding appeared to be voicing sentiments many Jamaicans in his US audience feel but could not express themselves. Some murmured among themselves that he must not fear losing his US visa.

Called to ask his view Sunday, Golding said he did not wish to trivialise the matter and he had said enough on the subject.

But reacting to the former prime minister’s assessment of the bilateral relations, Stafford Grant, founder and president of the US-based Jamaica Ex-Service Men and Women Foundation, said after the speech:

“Golding didn’t just give a speech, he gave Jamaica a masterclass in geopolitical survival. His address laid bare the brutal reality of being a small island nation caught in the cross hairs of superpower diplomacy.

“The former prime minister’s speech should serve as a profound wake-up call for every Jamaican. His vocal defence is more critical than ever, and I trust Jamaicans will understand that international diplomacy is shifting from collaborative negotiations to unilateral madness,” Grant declared.

Raymond Rhoden, a Florida-based retired adjunct professor, described Golding’s stance as “bold, principled, factual and diplomatic”, adding that he believes Jamaica needs to stand up and take a principled position on the current situation.

Irwine Clare Sr, co-founder of Team Jamaica Bickle, said the issues raised by the former head of government were “pungent, timely, and well articulated on behalf of the voiceless and those who have avoided the conversation due to fear of reprisal or just being downright spineless”.

“This speech must also be placed in context, because clearly he [Golding] recognises the agonising situation that Caribbean leaders find themselves in, especially against the backdrop that they do not speak from a united perspective,” said Clare Sr.

In his address, which was punctuated by applause, Golding spoke of the discontinuation of the Cuban medical mission programme, America’s fierce opposition to China’s investments in Jamaica, and the highly controversial third-country nationals arrangements between the US and a number of Caribbean countries, as examples of actions that run counter to harmonious relations.

“True friends don’t abuse your friendship; they don’t make unreasonable demands of you. They should be there to help you. Holding a gun at your head and insisting that you must be reasonable and do things their way is not friendship,” Golding suggested.

“The United States has put us under severe stress, and that’s not what friends are for,” he said, pointing to the damage the Jamaican economy could suffer should Jamaica stand up and try to fight back.

“There are many at home and abroad who are outraged at what is taking place, who are incensed at what is being meted out to us, who are angry that we have not pushed back, that we haven’t stood up like President Lula da Silva of Brazil who declared that, ‘Brazil’s destiny is for Brazilians alone to determine — without foreign interference or otherwise.’ “

Noting that Brazil is large and provides a US$57-billion market for American exports, Golding warned that little Jamaica is not in that league, struggling to find markets for its own goods.

“With the US market accounting for half our total exports, if our exports to the US market were slapped with a 50 per cent tariff our manufacturing sector would fall apart and thousands of persons would lose their jobs,” said Golding.

Agreeing with Golding, Dr Rupert Francis, who heads the Jamaica Diaspora Task Force on Crime Intervention and Prevention, argued that “we need to get back to the more amiable friendship we had with the United States for many years”.

University lecturer Dr Allan Cunningham said Golding’s speech focused on what he describes as the “hypocrisy of the rules-based order”, noting that “the speech acts as a call for regional realism — that without a unified foreign policy Caribbean states remain vulnerable to US cowboy diplomacy”.

World.title: Public funds not enough for climate resilience — Samuda
World.content:
Matthew Samuda, minister of water, environment and climate change, delivers the keynote address at National Commercial Bank Jamaica Limited’s inaugural Corporate Insights Breakfast. Addressing business leaders, Samuda underscored the importance of public-private collaboration in strengthening Jamaica’s climate resilience and preparing businesses, communities and the wider economy for the growing risks associated with climate change..

MINISTER of Water, Environment and Climate Change Matthew Samuda is arguing that Jamaica cannot rely on public funds alone to build the infrastructure and systems needed to withstand the growing effects of climate change.

Samuda said greater participation will be required from private investors, financial institutions, and international partners as the country seeks to strengthen critical infrastructure and improve its ability to recover from climate-related disruptions.

“Public funds are simply not enough to address the challenges posed by climate change. We need financing from all available sources — including public, private, domestic and international partners — if we are to successfully transition to climate resilience,” Samuda said.

He was speaking at the inaugural NCB Corporate Breakfast Series, hosted by National Commercial Bank Jamaica Limited (NCBJ), which brought together policymakers, business leaders and financial sector representatives to discuss climate resilience, infrastructure, and investment.

Samuda said strengthening Jamaica’s resilience will require cooperation across the public and private sectors as the country responds to the increasing threat posed by extreme weather and other climate-related events.

The issue has taken on greater significance as disruptions to electricity, water, telecommunications, transportation and other critical services can have wide-ranging effects on households, communities and businesses.

NCBJ Interim Chief Executive Officer Sheree Martin said the changing environment also requires organisations to rethink how they prepare for and respond to disruptions.

“Strategy sharpens in conversation, not in isolation, and capital works best when it is guided by an honest read on where a business is heading,” Martin said.

She said access to financing, strong partnerships, and informed decision-making will become increasingly important as organisations adjust to economic and structural changes.

“As businesses adapt to changing realities, access to informed perspectives, strong partnerships, and the right financial solutions become increasingly important,” Martin said.

Hugh Graham, director of Paramount Industries, said businesses also have a responsibility to prepare for disruptions and protect their operations and employees.

“For businesses, resilience is about being able to keep operating, protect jobs, and continue serving customers when disruption occurs,” Graham said.
