“That requires investment and preparation at the company level, but it also requires strong infrastructure, sound policy,and access to financing.” Graham said closer coordination among Government, financial institutions, and businesses could improve Jamaica’s ability to withstand shocks and recover more quickly. “The more Government, financial institutions, and businesses can plan together, the better positioned we will be to withstand shocks and recover more quickly,” he said. NCB said the breakfast series is intended to bring together policymakers, business leaders, and other stakeholders to discuss issues affecting Jamaica’s economic development and long-term sustainability.

Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean ruler Kim Jong Un have deepened ties since the Kremlin’s war on Ukraine began. In September last year during a meeting in Beijing, Kim vowed to do “everything we can to assist Russia.”

Zelenskyy also reported attacks on a Kyiv hospital and businesses overnight, with at least one person injured. The capital’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, urged residents late Monday to seek shelter.

Moscow also attacked substations in Kherson and Kharkiv, causing power outages, Zelenskyy said. Further attacks took place in the Donetsk, Dnipro and Mykolaiv regions.

“Every step Russia takes — increasing ballistic missile production, bringing in North Korean equipment, preparing for mobilization — all of this shows that Moscow is preparing not for peace, but for escalation,” Zelenskyy wrote.

Russia has stepped up its missile attacks this summer, with Zelenskyy urging Western allies to help Kyiv strengthen its air defenses and to heap sanctions pressure on companies fueling Moscow’s war. However, Europe is running out of Patriot interceptors to shoot down Russian missiles, according to the continent’s military officials.

Ukraine, meanwhile, has struck back, targeting Russian infrastructure including oil refineries and buildings belonging to e-commerce giant Wildberries.

Russian state media on Tuesday reported that two Wildberries warehouses in the Voronezh region, several hundred kilometers south of Moscow, caught fire following drone strikes, killing one person.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino stands beside U.S. President Donald Trump with the World Cup trophy before presenting it to Spain after the final at New York New Jersey Stadium on July 19, 2026. | Dan Mullan/Getty Images

World.title: Germany’s modern miracle: Churches are losing believers but gaining money
World.content:
Rising salaries have outweighed the cost of hundreds of thousands leaving the church.

German commentators are calling it a modern-day “miracle.”

Hundreds of thousands of worshippers in the country are walking away from their churches each year. The money, however, keeps rolling in.

Some 660,000 people formally quit the country’s Catholic and Protestant churches in 2025, freeing them from a levy automatically charged to registered members as a percentage of their income tax bill.

Despite the exodus, the two institutions collected more than €12.5 billion through the church tax for the 2025 fiscal year, up from around €12.4 billion in 2024.

The apparent miracle has a decidedly earthly explanation: Rising wages and Germany’s progressive tax system mean the shrinking pool of members is paying more.

“At first glance, the development may seem contradictory,” a spokesperson for the Evangelical Church in Germany — the umbrella organization representing Germany’s regional Protestant churches — said. “The reason is that church tax is calculated based on individual income tax.”





Members of Germany’s Catholic and Protestant churches and some Jewish communities pay an additional religious tax equal to 8 or 9 percent of their income tax liability, even if they don’t attend services.

In 2021, the most recent year for which comprehensive data is available, more than 29 million people paid church tax in Germany, amounting to almost half of all income taxpayers in Europe’s largest economy.

The German Finance Ministry’s 2025 payroll tax tables suggests that a single employee without children earning €50,000 gross a year pays approximately €600 in church tax annually on top of income tax, depending on the federal state. Someone earning €70,000 per year pays more than €1,000.

People are registered as part of their religious community at birth or at local government offices. To stop paying the church tax, they must formally leave through a process known as Kirchenaustritt, or “church exit.”

The procedure varies across Germany’s federal states but typically requires appearing in person at a registry office or local court to submit a declaration. Most states also charge an administrative fee.

While those who deregister can still attend services as a visitor and access some church services, they are not allowed to have a church wedding, be a godparent or be guaranteed a church burial.

In 2025, some 310,000 left the Catholic Church, while around 350,000 left one of Germany’s regional Protestant churches.

Church exit

The reasons people give for formally leaving their religious communities range from feeling less connected to the church to simply wanting to save money.

“People are leaving the Church because they feel it no longer plays a role in their lives,” said Matthias Kopp, director of communications for the German Bishops’ Conference.

“Added to this are the scandals of recent years, which have called the Church’s credibility into question,” he added. “There are also people — though this is by no means the primary reason — who leave the Church because of the church tax.”

“These are processes of alienation to which we must respond,” said Kopp.

For Jana Keil, a 33-year-old accountant from Berlin, the decision was both financial and moral. “I no longer wanted to support the system with church tax in light of the [child sex] abuse scandals,” she said.





Lukas Heinich, a 23-year-old working student, said he formally left after completing his apprenticeship because he “didn’t feel like paying the tax or supporting the church.”

That church tax revenues continue to rise despite the exodus is down to the types of taxpayers choosing to remain church members.

Those who are still paying church tax in Germany are “probably the higher earners,” said Zareh Asatryan, professor of empirical economics at the University of Münster. “Those that stay will naturally earn more income because of inflation plus real wage growth, and they will just generate more revenue.”

A miracle with an end date?

But the continued rise in church tax revenue masks significant long-term challenges — and raises questions about how long the trend can last.

While those revenues are going up, they are “relatively sluggish” and “haven’t been increasing by a lot,” said Asatryan.

The increase in revenue from the church tax is considerably lower than the increase in revenue from income tax. State revenue from wage and income taxes rose by 6.65 percent in 2025, said Kopp, whereas church tax revenue increased by 1.93 percent.

“Long-term projections indicate that church tax revenue will decline significantly over the coming decades as church membership continues to decrease,” said the spokesperson for the Evangelical Church in Germany.

Protestant churches are already preparing for their income to decrease “through long-term planning processes,” said the spokesperson. “Without this system, the church’s religious, social and charitable work would not be possible on its current scale.”

That will serve as a point of contact for platforms, fact-checkers and the Commission to quickly flag content so that it can be reviewed and taken down if necessary. The effort comes amid concerns that disinformation is promoting further crossings into the territory on Aug. 15, according to Maldita.es. Maldita.es and the European Fact-Checking Standards Network attended Monday’s meeting.

Another meeting has been set for later this week, one of those people and the third person confirmed.

Meta and TikTok said they were already actively monitoring the situation in line with their policies and had set up dedicated teams to monitor and respond to content in real time.

The crisis has divided EU countries and has reignited Europe’s long-running debate on illegal migration. Italy has since been one of the harshest critics of Spain’s left-wing government and its migration policies, and has implemented border controls for travelers arriving from Spain.

Former EU commissioner Thierry Breton, who was a force behind the EU’s online content rules, on Monday said the bloc should launch a disinformation inquiry into the Ceuta crisis in an interview with Italian newspaper La Stampa.

World.title: Greece’s aging power grid blamed for catastrophic wildfires
World.content:
Two deadly wildfires in late July — one in western Attica and one on the island of Crete —were also linked to the electricity grid in preliminary findings from the Greek fire brigade. The fires destroyed more than 36,000 acres and killed four people.

“Six out of 10 major fires and 55 percent of the area burnt in 2025 were caused by the power grid,” said Elias Tziritis, wildfires actions coordinator at World Wildlife Fund Greece. “Statistically speaking, the majority of fires may not start from the power grid, but these are the ones that cause the most major, devastating fires.”

Loose or sagging power lines, vegetation coming in contact with cables, dust buildup on transmission equipment and other such faults can all generate sparks. The risk rises during strong winds and periods of heavy electricity demand, when aging infrastructure is under greater strain.

Much of Greece’s electricity grid was installed decades ago and runs above ground through fire-prone forests and increasingly depopulated rural areas. In the 1960s, the country opted for an overhead network as a cheaper way to extend electricity across the country, while the prolonged financial crisis that began in 2009 further constrained investment in the system.

Critics say Greece has moved too slowly to bury distribution lines and adapt the network to increasingly severe fire conditions.

“We raised the issue years ago, calling for something to be done with the power grid urgently,” said Christos Kalogeropoulos, a retired lieutenant-general with the Fire Service and former director of the Arson Crimes unit. “We have been calling for urgent underground cabling.”

World.title: Provence, Dordogne and Calabria named the best-value villa destinations in Europe
World.content:
If you’re heading on a multi-generational trip, or are just travelling as a larger group, it might make more sense to book a villa over a traditional hotel stay.

 

Perennial favourites for this kind of holiday include Greece, Spain and Italy – but where do you get the most bang for your buck?

According to a new analysis from Holidu, which looked at 30 of Europe’s most popular villa destinations, the answer can be found in France.

To compile the Villa Value Index, the holiday rental platform looked at the average guest rating scores for every villa in a destination, the median nightly price for the whole villa, and the daytime high temperature across August and September.

Only those with more than 100 villas and 1,000 guest reviews were included, and the ranking was decided by the guest rating relative to the median nightly price.

The best-value villa destinations in Europe

After all that number crunching, Provence region in the southeast of France came out on top, thanks to an average guest rating of 8.9 out of 10, an average high of 30°C, and a median price of €151 per night.

Hot on Provence’s heels is another destination in France, this time in the southwest: The Dordogne.

Here, the average villa rating is 9.0 out of 10, but the median price is higher at €199 per night.

Third place takes us to Calabria, the region in southern Italy, where villas are rated 9.2 out of 10, and will set you back €221 a night.

It’s back to France for number four, which went to the island of Corsica, where you’ll find villas rated 9.1 out of 10 for a price of €234 per night.

Rounding out the top five is Spain’s Costa Blanca, which includes popular tourist spots Alicante and Benidorm, where villas are priced at €224 but have a slightly lower rating of 8.5 out of 10.

The top 10 best-value villa destinations on the continent

Provence, France Dordogne, France Calabria, Italy Corsica, France Costa Blanca, Spain Tenerife, Spain Peloponnese, Greece Lanzarote, Spain Sicily, Italy Madeira, Portugal

According to Holidu, several popular destinations failed to make the top 30, including the Amalfi Coast, where villas cost four times more than similarly-rated spots in Provence with a median price of €655 a night.

World.title: EU compliance, delivered globally: Anthropic to watermark Claude's output worldwide
World.content:
Anthropic will begin embedding invisible watermarks into text generated by its Claude large language model and chatbot in a move designed to satisfy new European Union rules on AI transparency.

 

"Claude models launched on or after August 2, 2026 support marking at launch. We’re also working to add marking support to Claude models released before that date," the San Francisco based AI giant said in a statement.

The new marking policy includes all of the services provided by Claude, including its consumer app, the developer-facing Claude Platform (API), Claude Code, Claude Cowork and Claude Tag, as well as versions of Claude accessed through AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft Foundry.

The watermark will either be weaved in as "an imperceptible watermark directly into the text itself" or as metadata, so that when "Claude generates a supported file type, such as a .svg, .png, or .jpg, it will attach signed provenance metadata... [that] signals that a file was processed by Claude and lets you detect whether the file has been tampered with."

Anthropic said the watermark would apply to every region where Claude is offered, not just the EU.

The marking will not be limited to Europe. Anthropic said the watermark would apply everywhere Claude is offered worldwide, another example of how the EU's standard of compliance has ripple effects on the global standards being set for AI.

How the watermark works

Anthropic uses two separate techniques. The first includes inserting an imperceptible pattern directly into generated text, invisible to readers but detectable by machines and able to travel with the text even after it has been copied and pasted elsewhere.

According to the company, it doesn't change the meaning, quality or readability of Claude's response.

The second technique applies to files. It functions more like a digital paper trail, similar to EXIF data on a photograph, and is designed to be checkable rather than concealed.

Seeing it in practice would likely require a C2PA-aware tool or Anthropic's planned detection system, rather than a standard "properties" menu, and it would not necessarily identify Claude by name so much as flag that the file passed through an AI system.

The company has also been explicit that the metadata can be lost.

Anthropic said a file's marking can be stripped through format conversion, re-saving, screenshots, or other similar processes, meaning a document or image that once carried a Claude mark may no longer show any trace of it after being edited or converted.

Why now

The timing traces directly to the EU's AI Act.

The act requires that AI systems creating synthetic content, such as deepfakes, mark their outputs as artificially generated under Article 50.

Regulators expect providers to rely on a multi-layered marking strategy, combining digitally signed metadata, imperceptible watermarking and, in some cases, fingerprinting or logging as a fallback, since the Code of Practice makes clear that no single marking technique is sufficient on its own.

The transparency obligations under Article 50 took effect on 2 August 2026. Non-compliance can trigger fines of up to €15 million or 3% of total global annual turnover, whichever is higher.

Can people still cover their tracks?

Anthropic has been explicit that a detected watermark is a signal, not proof.

A mark showing up in a piece of text confirms only that it may have passed through Claude at some point, not the full history of how that text came to be.

People often use the assistant to proofread, translate or summarise material that originated elsewhere, so a watermark can appear on text Claude did not originally write.

The reverse is also true: heavy editing, translation, very short passages, or use of an older model without marking support can all mean genuine Claude output goes undetected.

Anthropic is not alone in this. Google DeepMind has already developed SynthID for marking AI-generated text, images and audio, while OpenAI has discussed watermarking approaches but has moved more slowly to deploy them broadly.

World.title: Why do our eyes skip and reread words? AI may reveal how we read efficiently
World.content:
Scientists let an artificial intelligence (AI) model work out the best way to read for itself and it ended up behaving strikingly like human readers.

 

Researchers at Aalto University in Finland, the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, City University of Hong Kong and the National University of Singapore used AI to better understand how people read.

“For the first time we’ve used AI methods to understand – not just mimic – how people read,” Antti Oulasvirta, a professor at Aalto University, said in a press release.

The team built the model around the idea that readers have limited time, memory and ability to take in visual information.

They then trained the AI on millions of texts to maximise how much it could understand within those constraints.

Even though no human gaze or comprehension data were used during learning to copy these human reading habits, researchers found that many of the same patterns emerged when they compared the model with real readers.

For instance, it spent less time on common or predictable words and was more likely to skip them, while difficult or ambiguous words and sentences prompted it to go backwards more often.

“Reading feels effortless, but your brain is constantly deciding where to look, what to skip, and when to backtrack, spending attention like a budget to maximise understanding,” said Shengdong Zhao, a professor at City University of Hong Kong.

Researchers call this “resource rationality”, meaning limited time and attention are directed where they are most useful for understanding the text.

The AI model adapted to time pressure in a similar way to 39 adults who participated in an experiment. When time was short, it prioritised covering more of the text. With more time, it spent more attention on difficult passages and reread more.

However, the results do not prove that the human brain performs exactly the same calculations as the AI, researchers caution.

Instead, the researchers say that the model offers a possible explanation for how different reading behaviours could emerge from the goal of understanding as much as possible with limited cognitive resources.

Towards more personalised reading

A better understanding of how memory shapes reading could eventually help create technologies that adapt text to individual readers and situations, such as customisable apps, according to the research team.

“Now we have this new understanding of something that’s so central to our lives, it’s just a matter of exploring all the possibilities,” said Oulasvirta.

One potential use is augmented reality (AR). The approach could be used in smart glasses to adjust the pace or layout of on-screen text according to a user’s needs and what they are doing.

“We could take the same source text, say, a convoluted piece of legal writing and with little effort produce versions that are more comprehensible for different readers,” said Oulasvirta.

The team plans to investigate whether the technology could help people with dyslexia or lower language proficiency. Researchers also envision adapting text in situations where attention is particularly important, such as presenting information to drivers without unnecessarily distracting them.

“We want to help users in real-time situations, for example, by designing text that helps drivers without distracting them,” Oulasvirta said.

World.title: Qatar sees 'positive' signs in Iran-Oman talks on reopening Hormuz
World.content:
Qatar has seen positive signs in talks between Oman and Iran over reopening the Strait of Hormuz, according to its foreign ministry, despite concerns that demands for compensation could delay an agreement.

 

“We have heard positive statements from both capitals in the recent couple of days,” Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Dr Majed Al Ansari told reporters in Doha on Tuesday.

“We look to this quite positively, and we are waiting to see what transpires at the end.”

According to Al Ansari, Oman and Iran have indicated that the talks have reached the technical stage, with Tehran saying it was preparing an official announcement.

Oman and Iran have agreed on the coordinates of proposed shipping routes through the Hormuz and are working to finalise an arrangement for vessels using the waterway.

Under the proposed system, ships entering the Gulf would use a northern route through Iranian waters, while departing vessels would use a southern route through Omani waters, according to media reports.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said over the weekend that an agreement with Oman was “very close," yet Tehran has linked a wider reopening of the strait to demands from Washington.

These include an end to US sanctions and military threats, as well as compensation for damage caused during the war.

Compensation not part of current talks, Qatar says

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that Iran should compensate people killed or injured in attacks he blamed on Tehran.

Asked whether Trump’s demand was being discussed, Al Ansari said Qatar was focused on the wording currently being exchanged by Oman and Iran.

“I am not aware of any discussion of compensation within these talks,” he said. “We are not there yet, as we are talking right now about the opening of the strait, diplomacy, the ceasefire and the correct parameters.”

Trump said compensation from Iran should form part of any peace talks, after Tehran demanded payment from the US and Israel for damage caused during the war that began with strikes across Iran on 28 February.

Al Ansari said Qatar was concerned about any delay in reaching an agreement.

“We would like to see freedom of navigation restored immediately in the Strait of Hormuz in accordance with international law,” he said.

Qatar’s priority was to reopen the waterway, maintain the ceasefire and clear the way for wider talks, he added.

Commercial traffic through Hormuz, meanwhile, remains far below pre-war levels.

Only six vessels passed through the strait on Monday, compared with a 10-day daily average of around 11 and between 130 and 140 ships a day before the war, Reuters reported, citing shipping data.

The waterway handled around one-fifth of global oil supplies before the war, while Qatar depends on it to export liquefied natural gas.

Al Ansari said Qatar would support any regionally agreed arrangement that protected navigation and complied with international law.

World.title: US court rejects Meta, Google and TikTok's 'lawsuit immunity' claims
World.content:
A US appeals court has ruled that lawsuits accusing Meta Platforms, Google and TikTok, along with other social media companies, of designing addictive platforms can proceed, particularly over claims involving younger users.

 

The US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, based in San Francisco, rejected the companies' attempt to overturn a lower court's ruling allowing more than 3,000 lawsuits to move forward in federal court.

The Ninth Circuit found that the companies had appealed too early, since such challenges typically only follow a final ruling or verdict, not while the case is still ongoing.

The suits have been filed by several US school districts, municipalities, states and individuals, who claim the platforms have intentionally hooked younger users, contributing to soaring rates of anxiety, depression and body-image issues.

The companies, including Snapchat, TikTok, Meta and Google, argued that Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996 shields them from lawsuits claiming they failed to adequately warn the public about the potentially addictive nature of their platforms.

The law generally protects digital companies from liability over content that their users choose to post.

While most appeals arrive only after a case has concluded with a verdict, Meta argued that Section 230 granted it wider immunity and should have allowed it to appeal the lower court's decision immediately.

The Ninth Circuit disagreed, ruling that the law offers a defence to liability, not blanket immunity from being sued, meaning the appeal remained premature.

Social media concerns

Social media companies including Instagram, Facebook, Snapchat and TikTok have already faced fierce criticism worldwide for not doing enough to stop the spread of harmful content on their platforms, on top of concerns over addictive designs.

This is especially pressing given the high number of young users on these platforms, which has contributed to a widespread mental health crisis among younger Americans in recent years.

Central to the concerns are dopamine-driven features such as infinite scroll, autoplay, round-the-clock push notifications and daily streaks, which campaigners say drive rising rates of eating disorders, body dysmorphia, teen suicide, anxiety and depression.

Child safety and exploitation are another major factor. Separate lawsuits allege that features such as Snapchat's "Quick Add" friend-recommendation tool have made it easier for adult predators to connect with underage users.

Meta, which owns Instagram and Facebook, already faces close to $942 million (€816m) in combined penalties in New Mexico.

A jury ordered the company to pay $375 million (€325m) in March after finding it violated the state's Unfair Practices Act, and a judge ordered a further $567 million (€491m) into a youth mental health abatement fund in August, after ruling that Meta's platforms constituted a public nuisance.

World.title: Latvia steps up border security amid surge in irregular migration from Belarus
World.content:
Latvia’s Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs announced on Tuesday the launch of a new security operation, dubbed “Vilkatis” — or “Werewolf” — aimed at strengthening border controls and improving coordination between Latvia’s security services, as the Baltic country is facing an influx of irregular migrants from Belarus.

 

On the same day, Latvia’s border guards detected 15 people who illegally crossed the border through an underground tunnel dug from Belarus.

The security operation will increase the involvement of Latvia’s armed forces in supporting border guards, including through additional personnel and logistical support.

Authorities will also make greater use of drones, helicopters and aircraft to monitor the border and detect people attempting to cross illegally. To stop further migration, security forces will carry out more frequent vehicle checks on roads in the eastern border region.

Latvia is also seeking to tighten cooperation with its Baltic neighbours and Poland to curb illegal crossings and secondary migration flows, which have risen in recent months.

On Monday border guards in Latvia detected 15 persons who illegally crossed the state border through an underground tunnel dug from Belarus. Latvian Border Guard https://www.rs.gov.lv/lv/jaunums/robezsargi-konstate-15-personas-kuras-nelikumigi-skersojusas-valsts-robezu-caur-izraktu-tuneli

Hybrid threats from Belarus and Russia

The Latvian government says the increase in irregular migration represents a hybrid threat orchestrated by Russia and Belarus, framing the eastern frontier as part of a broader security challenge facing both NATO and the EU.

“It is now the fifth year since hostilities began and Russia has been using Latvia’s border as an element of hybrid warfare,” Kulbergs said at the press briefing on Tuesday.

The migrant routes shifted towards Latvia in July, just months before Latvia's parliamentary elections on 3 October, raising concerns that Minsk is once again seeking to exploit migration to destabilise the region.

The scale of the shift is reflected in border data.

Latvia's Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs talks to journalists as he arrives for the EU summit in Brussels, 19 June, 2026 AP Photo

In mid-July, Latvia, which has a 173-kilometre border with Belarus, recorded 111 attempted illegal crossings from the country in a single day.

Lithuania, which shares a border four times longer at 679 kilometres, recorded two attempted crossings on the same day, while Poland reported none the previous day.

Illegal migration from Belarus first started in 2021 after Belarus' President Aliaksandr Lukashenka threatened to flood neighbouring countries with migrants and drugs. L

atvia, Lithuania and Poland subsequently built border barriers, expanded surveillance and increased patrols.

World.title: Oil prices and US bond yields rise as Trump and Iran trade reparations demands
World.content:
Crude and US Treasury yields rose together as traders judged that the exchange of compensation demands between the US and Iran has pushed any potential deal further out of reach.

 

The US president said on Monday he had told his negotiators to seek payment from Iran for Americans killed and wounded in attacks he attributes to Tehran going back decades, including the bombing of the USS Cole in the year 2000 and for Iranians killed in protest crackdowns.

In a follow-up post on Truth Social he expanded on the demand, saying Iran should also pay for "the damages and death caused to the people of Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and Gaza".

Tehran, whose representatives had sought compensation for five months of US and Israeli bombardment, says the Strait of Hormuz will stay shut until Washington lifts its naval blockade, ends sanctions and releases frozen Iranian assets.

The front month contract on Brent traded at around $89.8 a barrel on Tuesday and West Texas Intermediate at about $84.2, both up roughly 2.5%.

The US bond market read it the same way, with yields rising across the US curve in a modest global sell-off, the two-year over 4.25%, the ten-year above 4.7% and the thirty-year higher than 5.27%. The yields for all durations are trading at the highs of this year.

Since yields move inversely to prices, the rise means investors are selling government debt as they expect that costlier oil will feed into inflation and strengthen the case for higher interest rates.

Money markets now put roughly even odds on a Federal Reserve rate hike in September, with July inflation data due on Wednesday.

Control claimed, traffic missing

The current stalling of US-Iran negotiations is deliberate as US President Donald Trump appears to have been favouring a slower approach as of late.

The US president told Axios in an interview published on Sunday that the US is "low-keying it," meaning Washington was only semi-negotiating and content to watch Iran's inflation and empty coffers do the work, a signal he is prepared to let economic pressure mount rather than order a fresh military campaign.

In the Oval Office on Monday, he struck a triumphant note, claiming the US controls "100%" of the Strait of Hormuz, that only the US Navy holds sway in the region, that American forces have swept it clear of Iranian mines and that the blockade of Iranian ports is impenetrable.

However, shipping data tells another story.

Confirmed crossings have run at 6 to 11 vessels a day recently, against the 130 to 140 daily before the war, according to Kpler data, leaving traffic at a fraction of normal levels throughout the five-month conflict.

World.title: Afghanistan five years of Taliban rule: Has Germany kept its promises?
World.content:
After the Taliban retook power in Afghanistan on August 15, 2021, Berlin promised to bring all the Afghan local staff members to Germany. But people are still waiting to leave in Pakistan and Afghanistan.

It is hard to know which promise from German politicians the "local staff" — Afghans who assisted German efforts in the country — relied on most. Perhaps that from then-Foreign Minister Heiko Maas, who on August 26, 2021, 11 days after the Taliban took power, said: "Our work continues until all those for whom we carry responsibility in Afghanistan are safe."

By June this year, more than 37,000 Afghan nationals had arrived in Germany since the Taliban retook power. These are people who worked alongside Germany's Bundeswehr armed forces or German aid programs, plus their relatives. It also includes people who are especially at risk, such as activists and journalists who advocated for human rights and against the Taliban.

For Ahmad Samid, who worked for the Bundeswehr as an audio engineer, Germany kept its promise. For Javad Niazi, who worked for the Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ), it did not. He remains stuck in the city of Peshawar in Pakistan. Both are using false names because they still fear the Taliban and possible repercussions for themselves and their families.

Hundreds of Afghans still waiting

Samid works as a receptionist at a hotel in a large German city and told DW in very good German: "I am very grateful to Germany. But if someone says, 'I will help you,' then it must remain that way. One must keep a promise."

In August 2026, 5 years after the Taliban quickly seized back power in Afghanistan, it seems that Germany no longer wants to know about the big promises it made.

In the case of Javad Niazi, Germany has, one must say, broken its promise. He is in the same position as 600 other Afghans who are desperately holding out in Peshawar and in Kabul, continuing to hope that they can leave for Germany. He and his family say they feel trapped in a small cage, he told DW. Their savings have been used up, he has no residence permit for Pakistan and he cannot leave his temporary accommodation for fear of Pakistani security forces, who arrest and deport Afghan nationals daily.

"My 14-year-old son goes shopping when it gets dark here. We cannot go to any bazaar, park, or hospital; my children cannot go to school. It is an enormous strain on us. We never would have thought that a country like Germany would take back its decision, it's unbelievable."

Afghan refugees at risk as deportations surge in Pakistan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

New government does not want to take in any more local staff

Taking back its decision, as Javad Niazi put it, is what the new German government, comprising the conservative bloc of Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) under Chancellor Friedrich Merz did in May 2025 with its coalition agreement to scrap the resettlement programs.

Half a year later, those who had been left behind appealed to the chancellor directly for help in a two-page letter calling for help: "We wanted and needed to escape Taliban rule to survive. We cannot go back to Afghanistan. It would end brutally and violently for many of us," they wrote.

But the German government remains firm and, in the meantime, is cooperating with the Taliban "on a technical level" via the Afghan diplomatic mission in Germany to send Afghan nationals who have committed crimes in Germany back to Afghanistan — and recently also the first person from Afghanistan with no criminal record.

German Foreign Minister Alexander Dobrindt offered the waiting Afghans money in exchange for forgoing their departure to Germany. A one-time payment of up to €2500 ($2887) before departure, up to €10,000 for a return to Afghanistan or a third country, plus medical care, board and lodging for several months. So far, 300 people have accepted this offer and in doing so given up on a future in Germany.

Afghan migrants stuck in Pakistan reject German cash offer To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Fate of local staff also depends on German courts

Since then, the issue of the future of the 600 waiting Afghans has been primarily dealt with via the court system. In July 2026, Germany's Federal Constitutional Courtruled: The German government's blanket decision revoking the admission programme for at-risk Afghan citizens is in breach of the constitutional prohibition of arbitrariness. Each person's specific case and individual interests must be considered.

In response to questions from DW, the German Interior Ministry maintains it is in the right: "The Federal Constitutional Court largely aligns with the Federal Government's argument that declarations around admissions can be revoked if political interests change. However, the Federal Constitutional Court also instructs the Interior Ministry to consider affected people's individual circumstances when making such decisions."

According to the Interior Ministry, the Federal Constitutional Court allows broad leeway for political decision-making when deciding on the admission of foreign nationals.

German aid organization continues support

For Javad Niazi, the trepidation about his and his family's future continues. He would probably have given up long ago if not for the support of Kabul-Luftbrücke (Kabul Air Bridge). In response to the chaos at Kabul airport 5 years ago, the German non-governmental organization arranged a charter plane to fly 18 people out of Afghanistan. Since then, it has rescued 4,424 people from the Taliban, mostly overland to Pakistan.

Eva Beyer, who had worked as a filmmaker in Afghanistan, recalled the organization's 2021 beginning to DW: "We chartered this plane, flew to Kabul and could haul out a few people. And then we realized, actually the work is just beginning. From early 2022 — I was then in Pakistan — there I organized the land transport on the Pakistani side, took in the people at the border and looked after them in Islamabad. What was originally planned to be 4 weeks has now become 5 years."

Recently, Kabul-Luftbrücke has mainly focused on providing legal advice and support to Afghans. With success: They have won more than 200 lawsuits, and as a result, 1,018 people have been able to travel to Germany since September 1, 2025.

"About 75% of the people who are now still waiting are women and children. That means for all these women and children, who are not attending school, who can no longer build an independent life or pursue a career, the way to a secure future has been blocked," Beyer said.

She advocates for people who have already passed all security checks to quickly receive a visa. "There are also people who already had a visa in their passport and those whose visa had already been issued, but at the last minute they could not take the flight because it was cancelled."

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Bulgaria drone crash a wake-up call for country's defenses
World.content:
The explosion of a Ukrainian decoy drone in Bulgaria near the Romanian border reveals gaps in Bulgaria's defenses, raises questions and shines a light on the country's policy shift on the war in Ukraine.

When a drone entered Bulgaria's airspace on Saturday and exploded in a sunflower field near the northeastern village of Kardam — about 100 meters (328 feet) from a border checkpoint with Romania — the immediate question was where the aircraft had come from.

Following an on-site check, the Bulgarian Defense Ministry said the drone was a Ukrainian-manufactured Maya decoy aircraft used to activate and deceive enemy drone systems.

And while both Bulgarian and Ukrainian officials confirmed that the first drone explosion on Bulgarian territory since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 was in no way deliberate, the case quickly became politically charged.

The Kardam border crossing (pictured here) is close to a Bulgarian compressor station on the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline route, which connects Turkey and Ukraine Image: Mihail Ivanov/AFP

The Bulgarian Foreign Ministry summoned Ukraine's ambassador on Monday and stressed that "any unauthorized entry into Bulgarian airspace is unacceptable."

Kyiv promised to cooperate fully in clarifying the circumstances of the incident.

What is known about the incident?

At 8:10 a.m. local time on Saturday, a blast was heard by a police patrol near the Kardam checkpoint on the border between Bulgaria and Romania.

Police and military units cordoned off the area once the exact location of the fallen drone was established in a field.

In his first statement on the matter, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said there had been neither casualties nor damage to infrastructure but claimed that the drone had been carrying a "significant amount of explosives."

Officials on the ground painted a less dramatic picture, saying the explosion did not even create a crater and that only a few sunflowers had been damaged.

Drone came down near gas pipeline

The drone crashed about a kilometer (0.6 miles) from Bulgaria's compressor station on the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline route, which connects Turkey and Ukraine, and in close proximity to a Romanian station.

Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov (left, pictured here with Prime Minister Radev) has said Bulgaria needs 'new (anti-drone) systems that need to be bought fast' Image: BGNES

This initially raised questions about whether this key infrastructure could have been a potential target.

Prime Minister Radev said that neither Romanian, Bulgarian nor other NATO radars had detected the drone, pointing to the country's lack of advanced equipment capable of detecting traces of such small aircraft, which usually fly very low.

Wake-up call for Bulgaria

Saturday's drone incident was a wake-up call for Bulgaria in terms of its defense capability.

"Yes, we need new [anti-drone] systems that need to be bought fast," Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Monday in an interview with public broadcaster BNT.

While Bulgaria recently reinforced its aerial defense capacity in the northeastern part of the country following an increase in the number of drone incursions in neighboring Romania, these defenses did not prevent the airspace breach.

Stoyanov said Bulgaria wants to acquire up to 10 anti-drone and electronic warfare systems through the EU's SAFE mechanism and speed up radar purchases, though he admitted this would still be insufficient to provide "comprehensive coverage" of the country.

"Drone wars have been waged next to us since 2023, and no concrete measures have been adopted," he said, adding that Bulgaria does not currently have an anti-drone strategy but that his ministry will prepare one.

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy last met at the NATO summit in Ankara in July Image: BGNES

With NATO members scaling up their aerial defenses, Bulgaria now joins the list of countries in Europe that have registered drone incursions linked to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Was Russia involved?

As the decoy drone was partially destroyed, officials have yet to establish its exact trajectory before it crossed Romania and entered Bulgaria.

According to Stoyanov, the drone's GPS system was not protected, which could have allowed its movement to be manipulated.

Although he did not actually name Russia as potentially being behind the incident, he said the crash could have been caused by what is known as a spoofing campaign, an electronic attack that manipulates a drone's GPS signals.

He also pointed to a possible technical failure, as the aircraft's chip was found to be defective.

The Defense Ministry declined to say whether the hypothesis of Russian spoofing was being actively investigated and referred DW's questions to the Military Prosecutor's Office, which had not replied by the time of publication.

Russia praises Bulgaria's 'restrained' response

Former Defense Minister Todor Tagarev, however, feels that it is most likely that Russia played a role in the drone crash.

"The most probable hypothesis is that electronic warfare led to the loss of control over this drone as a result of Russia's actions," Tagarev told DW, adding that Bulgarian authorities have the necessary information to rule out this possibility if it is not the case.

As the investigation continues, the government has not publicly mentioned Russia and is instead seeking answers from Ukraine.

Bulgaria has declined an invitation from French President Emmanuel Macron (center left) to join the Coalition of the Willing, which last met with Ukrainian representatives in Paris in July (seen here) Image: Tom Nicholson/AFP

The handling of the case was even welcomed in Moscow, with Yuri Pilipson, a senior representative of the Russian Foreign Ministry, praising Radev's government for its "more restrained" and "more rational" rhetoric toward the war in Ukraine.

Crash highlights Bulgaria's 'more pragmatic' foreign policy shift

The Bulgarian Foreign Ministry used the incident to reiterate that security in the region can only be achieved through diplomacy after it summoned the Ukrainian ambassador.

"This war will not be decided on the battlefield, but through diplomatic steps," said Defense Minister Stoyanov, echoing the prime minister's longstanding position.

A former president and fighter jet pilot, Radev won an absolute majority in parliament in April with his Progressive Bulgaria party.

While the country had until then steadfastly supported Ukraine, the new government brought a change in the country's foreign policy, promising a "more pragmatic" approach, including toward the war in Ukraine.

Over the past three months, Bulgaria has halted state arms supplies to Ukraine, blocked the EU's efforts to include the head of the Russian Orthodox Church in its sanctions package and declined an invitation by French President Emmanuel Macron to join the Coalition of the Willing, which brings together more than 30 countries supporting Ukraine.

"I think the Bulgarian foreign minister was too quick to summon the Ukrainian ambassador rather than the Russian one," Tagarev told DW. "It doesn't matter whose drone it is, but rather whose actions caused it to end up here."

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

World.title: Germany news: Some shipping stops as Rhine hits new lows
World.content:
Skip next section What you need to know about low river water levels

08/11/2026 August 11, 2026 What you need to know about low river water levels

The level of 19 cm reached last week in Kaub was already a record — but worse is to come Image: 5VISION.NEWS/IMAGO

Water levels in several rivers in Germany, including the Rhine, have hit record lows that are well below normal for this time of year, causing severe disruptions to river traffic, with ships cutting their loads by about 80%.

The water shortage comes during a prolonged dry period in Germany, accompanied by frequent heat waves, both of which are attributed by scientists partly to the effects of human-induced climate change.

But why is the situation so serious for Germany, and what are the key terms in connection with low water levels?

The Rhine: A vital transport waterway

The Rhine has been used as a transport corridor for much of western Europe since Roman times.

It is the most important waterway in Europe, connecting industrial regions in Germany, Switzerland and other countries with big North Sea ports, including Rotterdam in the Netherlands.

Although only one in 10 tons of freight in Germany is transported via rivers such as the Rhine, they are much used for certain goods, including ore, oil, chemical products and coal.

As a result, industries that depend on these for their production are likely to be forced to cut their output, as not only is supply reduced in the current situation, but transport prices have also gone up massively.

What are river gauge measurements?

The depth of water in German rivers is measured by gauges (Pegel) situated at strategic points on their course.

These gauges, which are mostly located near the banks of a river, measure the depth of the river over an arbitrarily selected baseline.

This means the measurements are only an indication of the actual navigable depth, which can be much more.

For instance, although the gauge at the town of Kaub currently measures 16 cm (6.3 inches), the depth of the river in the channel used by shipping there is around 129 cm.

Why is the gauge at Kaub so important?

Kaub is situated on the Middle Rhine between St. Goar and Budenheim.

This section of river is seen as a chokepoint for shipping on the Rhine, as the navigable channel is not as well developed as in other places.

It has also long been used since 1856 as a key location to measure low water levels in the Rhine.

The previous lowest measurement in Kaub was 25 cm (9.8 inches) on October 22, 2018.

The present measurement of 16 cm is thus already a historic low — and it is expected to sink to single figures in the next few days.

World.title: Vietnam's VinSpace taps SpaceX for first satellite launches
World.content:
Vietnam's first private space company is turning to Elon Musk's SpaceX to get its first satellites into orbit. The deal comes as Vietnam steps up efforts to build its own space industry and become a regional space power.

Vietnam's only private space company on Tuesday signed a deal with SpaceX to launch its first satellites into orbit next year.

The satellites will fly aboard a 2027 mission under SpaceX's Transporter rideshare program, which allows multiple customers to share the same rocket and split satellite launch costs.

What do we know about VinSpace and SpaceX?

The company, VinSpace, said it would develop and operate the satellites itself, using the missions to test technology in orbit and pave the way for future commercial services.

"Reliable access to space is fundamental to turning satellite innovation into operational missions," VinSpace CEO Thu Vu said.

The company did not disclose how many satellites it plans to launch, their specifications or the value of the contract with Elon Musk's SpaceX.

What is VinSpace?

VinSpace was established in November 2025 by Vingroup, Vietnam's largest privately-owned conglomerate.

The group was founded by Pham Nhat Vuong, Vietnam's richest man. It has interests ranging from real estate, retail and tourism to healthcare and education.

China's new rocket heats up space race, challenging SpaceX To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In recent years, Vingroup has increasingly expanded into technology, including electric vehicles, artificial intelligence, robotics and aerospace.

VinSpace says it ultimately wants to become a full-service aerospace company, with capabilities spanning satellite design and manufacturing, launch management, satellite operations and space-based data services.

What are Vietnam's ambitions in space?

Vietnam has been building its space capabilities for decades but remains a relatively small player in the global industry.

It launched its first telecommunications satellite in 2008 and a second in 2012.

The government has set a goal of becoming a mid-level space power in Southeast Asia by 2030, with satellite technology seen as part of a wider drive to develop high-tech industries.

In March, Vietnam opened a major space science and technology center at Hanoi's Hoa Lac High-Tech Park, aimed at expanding domestic satellite development and the use of space-based data.

In April, Vietnam licensed SpaceX's Starlink for its first large-scale trial of satellite internet, which uses thousands of low-Earth-orbit satellites to provide high-speed connectivity.

World.title: Syria sentences Bashar Assad to death in absentia
World.content:
A Syrian court has sentenced ousted President Bashar Assad to death in absentia. The ruling comes over a year and a half after the dictator was overthrown and fled to Russia.

A Syrian court on Tuesday sentenced former President Bashar Assad to death in absentia.

Assad was ousted in December 2024 after rebel forces swept into Damascus, ending more than five decades of rule by the Assad family.

He and his family fled to Russia, where he was granted asylum, as Syria's new authorities began pursuing former officials over alleged crimes committed during the country's civil war.

What did the court say about Assad?

Assad was convicted of the crimes of "premeditated and intentional murder of more than one person and of children, torture, arbitrary arrest and crimes against humanity."

"The contribution of the criminal Bashar Assad to the crimes was that of the person ultimately responsible for decision-making, mobilizing state institutions to commit them," the judge said.

The verdict was handed down by Damascus' Fourth Criminal Court and read out live on Syrian state television.

Assad, born in 1965, became president in 2000 after the death of his father, Hafez Assad.

He continued his family's decadeslong rule, maintaining the dominance of the Alawite minority in Sunni-majority Syria and the country's close alliance with Iran as well as hostility toward Israel and the US.

Assad tried in absentia as Syria charges ex-regime members To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Syrian government has been demanding that Moscow extradite Assad.

Assad's brother Maher and several other figures from the ousted government were also sentenced to death in absentia.

They were convicted of premeditated murder and torture resulting in death.

Assad's cousin sentenced in person

In the same case, the court also handed the death penalty to Atef Najib, a senior security official under Assad's rule and a cousin of the former dictator. He was arrested while trying to flee the country in January 2025 and became one of the highest-ranking officials to be put on trial.

Najib, a former Syrian army brigadier general, headed the Political Security Branch in the southern province of Daraa when the uprising against Assad's government began in 2011.

He appeared in court under tight security, standing inside a cage in a prison uniform as the judge read out the sentence.

The court convicted Najib of crimes including murder, the intentional killing of children under 15 and torture resulting in death, describing the acts as crimes against humanity.
