World.title: Coalition demands AFP probe of diplomatic cables over PM’s melon gaffe
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Coalition demands AFP probe of diplomatic cables over PM’s melon gaffe James Massola August 11, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The federal opposition is demanding a police investigation into the apparent leaking of a diplomatic note sent by the Japanese government to its counterparts in Canberra, after details of the note were published in media outlets. The diplomatic note, dated July 13 and sent by the government in Tokyo, addressed Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s appearance on the Bush Deep podcast with Nikki Osborne on July 3, during which the comedian made a joke to the prime minister about Japanese prime minister Sanae Takaichi smuggling in crown melons under her shirt “like Pamela Anderson” to present as a gift to Albanese. Loading The prime minister gestured with both hands in front of his chest as he told Osborne his Japanese counterpart had given him a couple of melons as a gift. While the comment mostly escaped scrutiny when the podcast was first published, a piece in the English-language Japanese Times in late July lamented the comment. This week, former Japanese ambassador to Australia Shingo Yamagami wrote a critical opinion piece in The Australian that labelled Albanese’s gesture “insulting” and ignorant.



Several media outlets have since published extracts of the diplomatic note sent to Canberra from Tokyo, which noted “sensationalised reporting in the Australian media” about the podcast interview and which undertook that “no action” would be taken over the incident. The note also stressed that the melons were not smuggled but bought locally. The sharing of this letter prompted the opposition’s defence spokesman James Paterson and foreign affairs spokesman Ted O’Brien to write to Australian Federal Police commissioner Krissy Barrett and ask for an investigation into the leak. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese arrives for question time on Tuesday. Alex Ellinghausen “We write to refer the possibly unlawful disclosure of confidential and sensitive correspondence from the Government of Japan to the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet,” the pair wrote.



“We are concerned that a diplomatic note with a critical bilateral partner has potentially been provided to the media without authorisation. Given that communications between governments can be classified, it is possible that this disclosure is a criminal offence under Division 122 of the Commonwealth Criminal Code. “It is critically important that Australia’s bilateral partners believe that their confidential correspondence will be handled appropriately by the Australian government. It would be gravely damaging to our national interest if they formed the view the Australian government does not take unauthorised disclosure seriously by promptly investigating it.” The Coalition pursued Albanese over the matter in question time on Tuesday, with backbench MP Mary Aldred twice asking the prime minister if he would apologise to Takaichi to repair relations between the two countries. Related Article Analysis

Political leadership Albanese’s attempts to talk to everyone bear bitter fruit when he goes off script Albanese did not accept the premise of the question and talked up both his friendship with Takaichi, and the growing strength of the strategic relationship between the two countries - before sitting down and cutting his answer short.



In the Senate, Paterson pressed Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong over the matter, suggesting the decision to share Japan’s letter was a “desperate attempt to clean up the prime minister’s self-inflicted melon mess” that risked a critical bilateral relationship. Wong accused the opposition of “confecting a diplomatic issue”. Senior government ministers including Tanya Plibersek, Katy Gallagher and Murray Watt have all defended the prime minister on Monday and Tuesday this week. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Scratching the stats
World.content:
“I completed the census (C8) but don’t understand why there wasn’t a question about ‘fur babies’,” writes Natasha Lee of Alexandria. “Many of us consider our pets to be an important part of the family. The presence of pets paints a more detailed picture of our households, so why are they excluded?”

Here’s hoping Alan Phillips of Mosman doesn’t commit a capital offence: “My wife and I had planned to be in Canberra this week for some walking, cycling and galleries. Checking the weather predictions — freezing temperatures and rain — made us decide to postpone. But shock horror! We’d already filled in our census online which said we would be there. We were now stuck with it or risk possible arrest and imprisonment for lying to the Commonwealth.”

Sticking with the statistics, George Manojlovic of Mangerton says, “Obviously Jack Dikian finds crunching the numbers enlightening. He must have woken Tuesday morning and thought, ‘At last! I’ve finally come to my census!’”

“I believe the Wests Tigers approached the Pope (C8) to play five-eighth next year,” reports Peter Miniutti of Ashbury. “He respectfully declined the offer giving the excuse that not even God could save them.”

Regarding Nola Tucker’s opera (C8) commentary, John Boddington of Dalton reckons “there is really only one plot in opera. According to the comedian Ed Gardner: ‘Opera is when a guy gets stabbed in the back and, instead of bleeding, he sings’.”

World.title: Educators on the line in proposed Zoos Victoria job cuts
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaAnimals Educators on the line in proposed Zoos Victoria job cuts Kieran Rooney August 11, 2026 — 7:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than a third of educator positions could be cut from Zoos Victoria under proposed redundancies, prompting fears the visits by 150,000 students each year will be cut and the standard of teaching affected. The Age revealed in June that Zoos Victoria was preparing a restructure that would cut up to 70 full-time roles from its 950-strong workforce – a figure the organisation has pushed back on as it consults staff about the changes. Among the most contentious proposals is a 38 per cent reduction in education staff at Melbourne Zoo – from roughly 6.2 full-time staff to 3.8 – who assist in teaching students and other groups about wildlife and conservation. A baby giraffe at Melbourne Zoo. Jo Howell The Community and Public Sector Union and United Workers Union said on Monday that about 600 staff – almost two-thirds of the organisation’s workforce – had responded to the proposed changes, which would be finalised later this month.



CPSU state secretary Jiselle Hanna said any cuts to education staff would devastate the 150,000 students who visited Melbourne Zoo, Werribee Zoo, Healesville Sanctuary and Kyabram Fauna Park every year. Related Article Animals Bailout backing was offered to Zoos Victoria a year before job cuts “Staff are telling us that they will not be able to maintain the volume of visits or the standard of education for young learners if these cuts go ahead,” Hanna said. “If this restructure is genuinely being driven by financial pressures, then why would cuts be made to an entity that brings in millions of dollars annually through school visits? “The impacted staff are highly skilled workers with decades of experience. They keep visitors educated, entertained and, most importantly, safe.”



The CPSU and the United Workers Union have urgently demanded Zoos Victoria wind back the scale of the cuts, arguing it will have flow-on effects across all parts of the organisation as staff are asked to handle new responsibilities. “This restructure process has demonstrated how out of touch the executive team is with the realities of the zoo and the work that zoo staff undertake,” Hanna said. A Zoos Victoria spokesperson said frontline services would not be impacted, as official consultation continued before a final decision was announced on August 25. “Our employees have provided valuable feedback through this consultation process, and we are considering this feedback carefully,” the spokesperson said. “Zoos Victoria will remain a world-class wildlife destination, and our commitment to fighting wildlife extinction remains.”



The Age has previously reported staff concerns that the restructure could also affect wildlife and conservation roles across the organisation, however, Zoos Victoria says frontline and animal care roles will not be directly affected. Related Article Animals Zoos Victoria to cut up to 70 jobs, including in conservation and wildlife Animal Justice Party MP Georgie Purcell said Zoos Victoria should be upfront about what the cuts would mean for conservation programs. “With bird flu ravaging our state and our volunteer wildlife carers under enormous strain, we simply can’t afford to lose any of the dedicated Zoos Victoria teams whose job it is to respond to injured wildlife and protect threatened species,” she said. “It’s simply not good enough to say there won’t be cuts to frontline services without being clear about what happens to the conservation and wildlife rescue work that sits behind them.”

World.title: Labor blasted for restricting prisoner rights after gangland boss’s court victory
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaPrisons Labor blasted for restricting prisoner rights after gangland boss’s court victory Lachlan Abbott and Erin Pearson August 11, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wrongfully imprisoned academic Kylie Moore-Gilbert, the ombudsman and a chorus of human rights advocates have voiced serious unease about the Carroll government’s plan to curtail the right of Victorian prisoners to access fresh air daily. Labor is poised to pass legislation with opposition support in the upper house this week to make the right to open air for at least an hour each day “subject to operational considerations” in prisons, despite conceding this breaches Victoria’s human rights charter. Kylie Moore-Gilbert spent years imprisoned in Iran on trumped-up espionage charges. Scott McNaughton The Victorian Ombudsman wrote to the leaders of both major parties this month to express concern about the bill, which opponents say does not adhere to the international minimum standards for prisoners, a set of rules named after Nelson Mandela. The government argues the change is necessary to prevent lawsuits such as that brought by murderer and crime boss George Marrogi, who won a Supreme Court judgment in January that found some of his maximum-security units did not provide adequate open-air access.



Amendments to the Corrections Act would allow the state to limit a prisoner’s open-air rights “on an ongoing basis or for extended periods of time”, according to the bill’s explanatory memorandum. The legislation also stops the state from paying damages for any previous breaches of a prisoner’s open-air rights, despite corrections being plagued with prolonged lockdowns in recent years. Moore-Gilbert, who spent 804 days detained in Iran, said even the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps provided her access to fresh air while she was imprisoned. “This terror organisation gave me a minimum of 30 minutes a day outside, even when I was held in solitary confinement,” she said.



“Why on earth is the Victorian government proposing to lower its human rights standards beneath those of even the despotic regime in Iran?” Related Article Crime Underworld kingpin wins court battle over ‘inhumane’ prison conditions Then-corrections minister Paul Hamer told parliament in June there “may not be any suitable infrastructure solutions available” to provide high-risk prisoners like Marrogi with open air, as the recent Supreme Court decision required. The murderer and drug trafficker is one of the most challenging prisoners in Victoria, having run a $55 million drug empire from behind bars and once spraying prison guards with faeces. Marrogi’s lawsuit revealed corrections officials believed he had previously plotted to break out from Barwon Prison via helicopter.



Prison managers argued different types of roof mesh were necessary for Marrogi’s rear yards to prevent escape, self-harm, weather damage, and contraband being thrown in. Justice Claire Harris, however, ruled certain partially covered cells in the Exford unit at the Metropolitan Remand Centre, plus the Olearia, Melaleuca and Acacia units at Barwon Prison, did not provide adequate open-air access. Harris said there was no “clear bright line” for what constituted being “in open air” but noted the current right relied on experiencing weather, suggesting exposure to the elements such as rain, wind and sun outside was required. Her decision has been appealed.



Opposition police spokesman Brad Battin told parliament the Coalition would support proposed changes to open-air rights as it recognised they were not always practical. “I think it is important that the management of the prison can make a decision in the best interests of staff – not in the best interests of prisoners – to protect the staff who are within that prison,” he said. Jailed crime boss George Marrogi claims he’s being treated cruelly in prison. However, ombudsman Marlo Baragwanath told this masthead: “If these changes are passed into law, they’ll have wide-ranging and significant human rights implications for anyone in custody.” Marrogi’s lawyer, Zyg Zayler, said changing the law after Harris’ decision reflected poorly on Victoria.



“The quality of our society is determined by how we treat our most difficult people,” he said. “Maybe their prospects would be better if we didn’t treat them inhumanely.” Former prisoner Kelly Flanagan said her mental health suffered enormously when she was stuck inside at the Dame Phyllis Frost Centre, where an 18-year-old died last month. Wiradjuri woman Kelly Flanagan outside the Dame Phyllis Frost Centre last year. Luis Enrique Ascui “You’re stripping them of everything that makes them human by taking away their fresh air,” Flanagan said. A state government spokesperson said the open-air right for Victorian prisoners remained, and the changes were “operational decisions” to ensure access could be managed safely.



“This brings us into line with other jurisdictions like NSW, and makes a longstanding practice clear in law,” they said. NSW prisoners confined to their cell are allowed an hour each day for exercise in the open air subject to “practical limitations” but only those “that may from time to time arise”. Normal prisoners are allowed at least two hours outside. The Victorian Aboriginal Legal Service said making open-air rights subject to “operational considerations” was a “vague and open-ended excuse” to deny prisoners fresh air. Australian Lawyers Alliance spokesman Greg Barns, SC, also took issue with retrospective legislation removing compensation rights and called for it to be withdrawn.



Liberty Victoria president Gemma Cafarella said the bill marked just the fifth time a declaration to override Victoria’s human rights charter had been used since it was enacted in 2006. Liberal MP Chris Crewther said last month the government had “not adequately explained why an indefinite exclusion is necessary” compared with a normal five-year exemption. A protest against the bill is planned outside Victorian parliament on Wednesday before a vote in the Legislative Council is expected on Thursday. World.title: ‘Training objects for violence’: Cops, experts fear perverse motive behind ‘sex doll murder scene’
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWCrime ‘Training objects for violence’: Cops, experts fear perverse motive behind ‘sex doll murder scene’ Perry Duffin and Riley Walter August 11, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: Graphic content A sex doll found in a suitcase on a remote stretch of NSW road was dressed like a sex worker with mock bruises and injuries, sparking fears among police and experts that whoever dumped it was acting out a violent fantasy against women. Discovery of the doll on Sunday triggered a short-lived murder investigation when it was located by two men during a bathroom break on a road south of Goulburn. The suitcase containing the doll was discovered metres from the roadside close to the pine tree. Kate Geraghty So disturbing were the doll’s features – a head of rain-matted hair, a nose piercing and markings that resembled bruising and grazes – the men thought they had uncovered an awful tragedy.



Police close to the investigation but not authorised to speak publicly are now concerned the person who dumped the doll might have been acting out a violent fetish. Caitlin Roper, campaigns manager for anti-sexploitation movement Collective Shout, told this masthead the dumping of sex dolls was not uncommon. A sex doll in a packing crate at a sex culture festival in China in 2013. Newer models are much more life-like and can be customised to meet buyers’ desires. NYT “People discover what they initially believe is a woman’s body – often mutilated, ripped apart or decapitated – but is actually a doll,” she said. “These dolls become training objects for violence against women and children.”



Roper has spent hours on sex-doll forums, monitoring owners’ who say they are buying dolls to practise extreme sexual abuse. In 2022, she published a book Sex Dolls, Robots and Woman Hating: The Case for Resistance, documenting her findings. “They shared realistic scenarios of predation that they acted out on their dolls. One user posted photographs of a doll bound with rope, explaining that he was practising how to tie women up and render them helpless,” she said. Superintendent Linda Bradbury revealed that the suitcase did not contain human remains - but instead a sex doll. KATE GERAGHTY “Other men described being so rough that they broke their dolls and had to send them away for repairs. One lamented that his doll would not fight back, saying, ‘If Tonya fought back, I’d be in heaven’.” As with the find on the weekend, many on the forum adorned their doll with fake bruises, cuts, blood and injuries.



Roper said there are multiple cases involving the owners of adult and child sex dolls – the latter are illegal in Australia – going on to carry out violence against women and girls. She pointed to the recent case of Perth man Jason William Forbes, a doll owner, who plotted to kidnap a young girl and keep her as a sex slave in his attic. “[Forbes] allegedly developed an elaborate plot to abduct a child. He had soundproofed an attic, researched chloroform, looked up schools and childcare centres, and marked locations on a map,” Roper said. “He was intercepted after purchasing a second doll.” Doll owner Jason William Forbes plotted to kidnap a girl and hold her captive in the attic of his Perth home. Roper said sex dolls, even childlike ones, are often dismissed as fantasies or mere objects. But many of the men she witnessed online have treated their dolls as partners.



“These are not simply sex toys; they are replicas of human beings that some owners regard as partners.” Criminologist and former NSW Police detective Vince Hurley said using child-like sex dolls could desensitise offenders and normalise abuse of children. It could also evolve into in-person offending. ‘The issue of consent doesn’t even come into it because they just use these sex dolls as they see fit, whenever they see fit.’ Vince Hurley, criminologist “It could reinforce any sexual attraction to children over time that might traverse into the real world,” Hurley said. “There would be nothing to say that it stops in their fake or false reality and then doesn’t transition into a real child.”



Men using sex dolls, similar to those using artificial intelligence chatbots, avoid rejection. Doing so warps their perception of relationships and consent, he said. “They will always have this perception that women will always be accepting of their behaviour and their attitudes because the chatbots never contradict them,” he said. “The issue of consent doesn’t even come into it because they just use these sex dolls as they see fit, whenever they see fit.” The Australian market for sex dolls Life-like sex dolls similar to the one found on Sunday are readily available online and can be customised to meet buyers’ desires.



Related Article Updated

Crime Police said a body was found in a suitcase. It turned out to be a sex doll High-end dolls retail for thousands of dollars. The growing market represents what police say is a worrying trend. In June, Australian Federal Police arrested a 31-year-old Quakers Hill man for trying to import a child sex doll, and allegedly found a second at his home. AFP Commander Jo Cameron said child-like sex dolls may desensitise users from the physical, emotional and psychological harm inflicted on real children. “Child-like sex dolls are not harmless objects – they are illegal to possess and can contribute to the exploitation of victims in the community,” Cameron said. World.title: Kids’ mental health unit shut as staff investigated for use of force
World.content:
A children’s mental health unit has been closed and five of its staff stood down amid allegations of bullying and the use of force against vulnerable young patients. The unit at a major Melbourne hospital has halted admissions to its inpatient unit – which treats children under 13 for severe mental health conditions – and has been referring families to another facility since the allegations emerged last Wednesday. Sources familiar with the investigation, but who are not authorised to speak publicly, said allegations of bullying surfaced a week ago following an outside-of-work gathering between multiple staff. Claims that some staff members used force against young patients also emerged. Related Article Opinion

Mental health I’m a psychiatrist of 40 years. It’s mass gaslighting to claim we’ve made progress Patrick McGorry Psychiatrist and mental health advocate Although five staff members connected with the unit have been stood down pending an investigation, not all are alleged to have used force on patients.



A hospital spokesperson confirmed investigations were under way, but said it would not be appropriate to comment on the specific allegations or individuals involved. The Department of Health and Safer Care Victoria have been advised of the allegations, and mandatory notifications have been made to the Commission for Children and Young People. “We take these allegations seriously and acted quickly when these concerns were raised,” the hospital spokesperson said. “Our priority is to ensure children and their families continue to have access to the mental health care they need while admissions to the unit are paused.” A state government spokesperson said the allegations were “disturbing and completely unacceptable”.



“Everyone deserves to feel safe whether they’re at work or seeking care in our health services,” the spokesperson said. The hospital’s specialist unit is an acute mental health service which caters for children up to 12 years old with severe or complex mental health conditions, who typically stay for two to four weeks, and are accompanied in the unit by a parent or caregiver throughout their treatment. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health Rewritten mental health report scrubs critical findings, doubles progress Because the unit is staffed by a small team and all require specialist skills, the standing down of five of its members means that it cannot continue to operate with its current staffing levels. Children requiring urgent mental health care who present to the hospital will continue to be assessed by its clinicians, and will be supported to appropriate care pathways while admissions are paused.



The allegations come as pressure also mounts on the Parkville Youth Mental Health and Wellbeing Service (PYMHWS), following revelations in The Age on Tuesday that its fly-in, fly-out CEO Dr Leanne Geppert lives in Queensland as concerns of violence, drug use and patient deaths are being raised by its mental health workforce. It also follows revelations in The Age this week that a landmark report into Victoria’s progress following the mental health royal commission had been significantly altered to remove remarks critical of the state government’s progress. Writing in The Age, internationally renowned youth mental health pioneer Professor Pat McGorry accused the state government of gaslighting families and clinicians over its failed implementation of Victoria’s mental health reforms. “The risks to patients, to staff through both moral and physical injury, and to the wider community have continued to worsen as the workforce wilts and demand surges,” the former Australian of the Year writes. “This is the worst-kept secret in Victoria and a once-in-a-generation opportunity has so far been squandered. It is a classic case of implementation failure, which no amount of spin can conceal.”



Mental Health Minister Ingrid Stitt told parliament on Tuesday she had appointed a new chair to PYMHWS and had spoken to her about Geppert. Dr Leanne Geppert has been reappointed as the Parkville Youth Mental Health and Wellbeing Service’s CEO despite living in Queensland. “I have made my expectations very clear to her about the way in which the CEO’s work arrangements ought to occur,” Stitt said. “I am confident that the new chair has a very strong focus on the leadership requirements of the service and also of the clinical governance arrangements that are in place.” Stitt said her department had been following up concerns raised by McGorry about the service.



But she rejected allegations the government had tampered with the independent report into how Victoria was progressing on mental health reforms. Stitt said the initial version was an “early draft”, and between December 2025 and June 2026 the department had “provided factual and technical feedback” before its public release. This characterisation has been rejected by three senior mental health figures familiar with the report’s delay but who refused to discuss the circumstances of its rewriting on the record, fearing reprisals from the government and further financial cuts to vital services. Opposition mental health spokeswoman Emma Kealy said this masthead’s reports showed the government did not want scrutiny on a system taxpayers funded directly. “Victorians pay a dedicated Mental Health and Wellbeing Levy because Labor told them every dollar was needed to rebuild a broken system. They have every right to expect complete transparency about whether that reform is actually happening,” she said. World.title: Coalition demands AFP probe of diplomatic cables over PM’s melon gaffe
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Coalition demands AFP probe of diplomatic cables over PM’s melon gaffe James Massola August 11, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The federal opposition is demanding a police investigation into the apparent leaking of a diplomatic note sent by the Japanese government to its counterparts in Canberra, after details of the note were published in media outlets. The diplomatic note, dated July 13 and sent by the government in Tokyo, addressed Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s appearance on the Bush Deep podcast with Nikki Osborne on July 3, during which the comedian made a joke to the prime minister about Japanese prime minister Sanae Takaichi smuggling in crown melons under her shirt “like Pamela Anderson” to present as a gift to Albanese. Loading The prime minister gestured with both hands in front of his chest as he told Osborne his Japanese counterpart had given him a couple of melons as a gift. While the comment mostly escaped scrutiny when the podcast was first published, a piece in the English-language Japanese Times in late July lamented the comment. This week, former Japanese ambassador to Australia Shingo Yamagami wrote a critical opinion piece in The Australian that labelled Albanese’s gesture “insulting” and ignorant.



Several media outlets have since published extracts of the diplomatic note sent to Canberra from Tokyo, which noted “sensationalised reporting in the Australian media” about the podcast interview and which undertook that “no action” would be taken over the incident. The note also stressed that the melons were not smuggled but bought locally. The sharing of this letter prompted the opposition’s defence spokesman James Paterson and foreign affairs spokesman Ted O’Brien to write to Australian Federal Police commissioner Krissy Barrett and ask for an investigation into the leak. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese arrives for question time on Tuesday. Alex Ellinghausen “We write to refer the possibly unlawful disclosure of confidential and sensitive correspondence from the Government of Japan to the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet,” the pair wrote.



“We are concerned that a diplomatic note with a critical bilateral partner has potentially been provided to the media without authorisation. Given that communications between governments can be classified, it is possible that this disclosure is a criminal offence under Division 122 of the Commonwealth Criminal Code. “It is critically important that Australia’s bilateral partners believe that their confidential correspondence will be handled appropriately by the Australian government. It would be gravely damaging to our national interest if they formed the view the Australian government does not take unauthorised disclosure seriously by promptly investigating it.” The Coalition pursued Albanese over the matter in question time on Tuesday, with backbench MP Mary Aldred twice asking the prime minister if he would apologise to Takaichi to repair relations between the two countries. Related Article Analysis

Political leadership Albanese’s attempts to talk to everyone bear bitter fruit when he goes off script Albanese did not accept the premise of the question and talked up both his friendship with Takaichi, and the growing strength of the strategic relationship between the two countries - before sitting down and cutting his answer short.



In the Senate, Paterson pressed Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong over the matter, suggesting the decision to share Japan’s letter was a “desperate attempt to clean up the prime minister’s self-inflicted melon mess” that risked a critical bilateral relationship. Wong accused the opposition of “confecting a diplomatic issue”. Senior government ministers including Tanya Plibersek, Katy Gallagher and Murray Watt have all defended the prime minister on Monday and Tuesday this week. World.title: Scratching the stats
World.content:
“I completed the census (C8) but don’t understand why there wasn’t a question about ‘fur babies’,” writes Natasha Lee of Alexandria. “Many of us consider our pets to be an important part of the family. The presence of pets paints a more detailed picture of our households, so why are they excluded?”

Here’s hoping Alan Phillips of Mosman doesn’t commit a capital offence: “My wife and I had planned to be in Canberra this week for some walking, cycling and galleries. Checking the weather predictions — freezing temperatures and rain — made us decide to postpone. But shock horror! We’d already filled in our census online which said we would be there. We were now stuck with it or risk possible arrest and imprisonment for lying to the Commonwealth.”

Sticking with the statistics, George Manojlovic of Mangerton says, “Obviously Jack Dikian finds crunching the numbers enlightening. He must have woken Tuesday morning and thought, ‘At last! I’ve finally come to my census!’”

“I believe the Wests Tigers approached the Pope (C8) to play five-eighth next year,” reports Peter Miniutti of Ashbury. “He respectfully declined the offer giving the excuse that not even God could save them.”

Regarding Nola Tucker’s opera (C8) commentary, John Boddington of Dalton reckons “there is really only one plot in opera. According to the comedian Ed Gardner: ‘Opera is when a guy gets stabbed in the back and, instead of bleeding, he sings’.”

World.title: Victoria - you’ve let yourself go
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Victoria - you’ve let yourself go August 11, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. INFRASTRUCTURE It would be overkill to list the grievances or problems Victorians have had to deal with during the last decade or so of Labor government. It hurts to say this, but Victorians have had to put up with a government that is increasingly revealed to have been a closed shop of factional power.

While COVID was difficult to manage, Daniel Andrews got the state through it but had to give up the Commonwealth Games at great cost. Under Jacinta Allan, it appeared only those who wore high vis garments to work were sure of work while criminal factions allegedly took their cut of taxpayers’ money aided by one thuggish union in particular.

Meanwhile, state coffers were plundered of funds that should have gone to state schools, hospitals, teachers and nurses, and roads throughout the state crumbled.

The pothole state, or the state of potholes, is the final straw (″⁣Drivers stranded as potholes wreak carnage in wild weather″⁣, 11/8).

Unless these holes are fixed properly for the long term, road traffic throughout Victoria will slow to a crawl and the economy, dependent on trucking, will suffer as a result. And so will we.

John Whelen, Box Hill Sth When vital services fail, who is accountable?

Yet another day of significant delays and non-arrivals for passengers on V-line services. Passengers were delayed by up to three hours. This is not a minor inconvenience. The loss in productivity and the emotional turmoil is significant and to hear more hapless apologies is wearing thin.

There are two questions.

Firstly, is the government doing anything about the apparent lack of technical expertise that leads to these catastrophic maintenance failures?

The Telstra outage and the debacle of August 10 when a vital piece of infrastructure failed are maintenance failures. Is anyone held to account? Both the minister for transport and the minister for transport infrastructure remain silent, and for all we know so far, indifferent to these disruptions. What actions are being taken?

Secondly, given the inevitability of major disruptions on V-line services, there is no management plan to mitigate disruptions. In the latest maintenance failure, the fault happened at 6.30am of a working day.

Passengers should have been alerted and given the choice to either work from home or find alternative transport.

The government needs to address these problems urgently and explain to the public why these disruptions keep occurring and what they are doing about it.

Anne Bourke, Ocean Grove



Excessive bureaucracy before best-practice services

I totally agree with Professor Pat McGorry’s major concerns about the standards of care and safety for both patients and staff working in Victoria’s public mental health services (″⁣FIFO boss leads Victoria’s flagship youth mental health service amid reports of patient deaths and violence″⁣, 11/8).

I have not worked in the system for several years but have a partner and a number of close friends who recently worked or continue to work in this system.

These are experienced clinicians who have the skills, commitment and fortitude to provide the best care and humanity to people (at all stages of life) who are experiencing extremely distressing and debilitating mental health conditions.

Yet, so many of these clinicians are being hounded out of the services by management that appears more focused on maintaining an image of excellence through corporate awards, arbitrary KPIs, and excessive bureaucracy than on delivering genuine best-practice services.

Another royal commission bites the dust.

Jenny Hutchens, Greensborough Sustainable goals

For many years now, we have been seeing increasing pressure on our systems. Existing infrastructure is being run down, suburban and rural roads are increasingly potholed and damaging vehicles, governments face workforce and funding constraints, schools and hospitals all seem on the never-never road to funding, while proposed developments such as data centres will create enormous additional demands for electricity, water and other infrastructure and cost.

At the same time, our natural environment is being depleted at an ever-increasing rate. Climate change adds another layer to the problem. More extreme heat, flooding, storms, bushfires and pressure on water supplies will require additional investment simply to maintain the resilience of existing communities and infrastructure.

This needs to be factored into decisions about what new development we can realistically afford and sustain. Simply adding more projects to the pipeline does not make us sustainable.

If we do not have the workers, money, energy, water or infrastructure capacity to maintain what we already have, we need to ask whether continually expanding development is economically or socially sustainable, let alone environmentally sustainable.

Paul Caine, Glen Huntly From zoom to doom

I have a friend who claims he’s an expert on potholes. I call him the Roads Scholar (RS for short). He says our number plates should say “Victoria - The Holey State” or “Victoria - State of Holeiness”.

RS says that repairs are too superficial and don’t go deep enough. He says that one day, a distant car ahead suddenly disappeared. When he got there, he said he looked into a gigantic pothole to see the car, which would have been more severely damaged if it hadn’t landed on a B-double!

RS does tend to exaggerate. He says the Hume Highway has gone from zoom to doom. Thank God, RS doesn’t write to The Age, or it could be a very tedious run-up to the November election.

Kevan Porter, Alphington Pothole detector

Cars nowadays are fitted with all sorts of safety technology, such as autonomous emergency braking, lane-keeping assist and adaptive radar cruise control. The car company that develops a system that detects and warns the driver of any upcoming potholes will be an absolute winner in Victoria.

Graeme Daniels, Balwyn North Cars must adapt

The recent wild weather (″⁣Tyres completely shredded: Motorists stranded for hours after falling victim to massive potholes″⁣, 10/8) is only part of the equation in the ″⁣carnage″⁣ reported on country roads across the past few days and makes meaningless any claims of technological progress represented by the cars being sold nowadays.

It’s time consumers stood up against vehicles that aren’t even equipped with spare tyres, instead boasting expensive oversized wheels and fragile low-profile tyres, for little purpose beyond fashion. In addition, the hefty weight of electric cars in particular means that when they encounter potholes, they hit hard. As with extreme climatic conditions, these are predictable variables that need to be addressed by savvy consumers seeing through superficial showroom sheen.

Marish Mackowiak, Ormond



Spending our money

Whose bright idea was it to spend an enormous amount of money on bringing an NFL team to Melbourne, estimated to cost

$10.7 to $15 million? Surely, this event would appeal to a very niche market at most.

New South Wales was smart enough to reject the proposal as too expensive. Victoria could spend that money on far more essential things such as addressing the appalling state of the mental health system.

Or even, dare I say it, the truly horrendous condition of Victoria’s roads. Victoria was once ″⁣the Garden State″⁣; it is now ″⁣the Pothole State″⁣. What happened to common sense?

Oriana Collins, Hawthorn THE FORUM SRL will benefit us

Your correspondent (Letters, 11/8) comments on the two Suburban Rail Loop tunnels, saying they will require energy, and create pollution and transport disruption during construction.

If these are not constructed, just think of all the additional energy, diesel and petrol needed along with the pollution and transport chaos caused by the transport of the growing population.

I think the savings in terms of energy, fuel, pollution and disruption from the use of the SRL will outweigh its construction.

Laurens Meyer, Richmond Densified already

The Age reports (5/8) that urban planning expert Carlos Moreno says Melbourne needs to become a more densely settled city. If we do, he says, this will promote liveability.

The problem with his claim is that census data shows that between 2006 and 2021, Melbourne did “densify” (especially in the inner municipalities – “Tram Track Melbourne”). Yet, at the same time, according to Mercer and The Economist Intelligence Unit, liveability fell.

A further significant problem with densification is that such construction is relatively complex and has shown to be subject to rorting.

The future of housing Australians is actually in the regions, and in DIY construction such as what Robin Boyd facilitated with the Small Homes Service, and Tasmanian architect Jiri Lev is promoting now.

Alun Breward, Malvern East Deaf political class

Ehsan Noroozinejad’s article, “Why Australia’s megaproject boom may deepen the housing crisis” (11/8), is well written and to the point about infrastructure and planning in Australia, but the political elite doesn’t listen to common sense.

Gaye Bryant Burwood



Albanese’s punt

The deal is done. The major parties have sorted out their gambling problem. Aussies can still “have a punt” as the prime minister likes to say. That is a big red herring: gambling is legal and no one was calling for a ban.

So now, against the advice of the Murphy report that the major parties led, gambling ads stay and regulation remains weak.

The gambling lobby will be happy, they can still have confidence to send complaints to the regulator as it remains under-resourced and out of sight in the Northern Territory.

The major parties have bet that gambling reform is not the top issue for ordinary people as we manage cost of living. Sadly, for too many people, the cost of living with gambling is just too high.

When the major parties fail us, do we need more courage and clear thinking of independents like David Pocock to hold the powerful lobby groups and big donors to account?

Jenny Kashyap, Bentleigh Twiggy’s data centre

Andrew Forrest, sometime champion of salmon farmers and giant green energy projects, is planning a super-sized data centre in Australia’s arid Pilbara region.

He may have the clean energy to run his behemoth, but so far, has failed to say which water source will nurture his data centre. The daily water usage of a large data centre is equivalent to that used by a town of up to 50,000 people.

The health of rivers is reliant on ground-water. Maltreating and misusing the waters above or below the earth affects the lot.

Nature is reality. We must protect it. Without water, we living things die.

Yvonne Parker, Portarlington Awash with stupidity

Having seen the awkward snippet of our prime minister with some influencer referring to those melons, it wasn’t Albanese who was making offensive comments or gestures. The real issue here is politicians lowering their standards of communication efforts to engage with influencers on social media.

Looks like we’ll either have to raise the voting age to 40, or ban social media altogether.

Enough with this unaccountable drivel as entertainment for young people who’ve never been taught how to think for themselves.

No wonder we are awash with so much stupidity these days.

Bernadette George, Mildura Netanyahu’s agenda

Of course, Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected the latest US-brokered plan for Gaza (″⁣Netanyahu rejects plan for Hamas″⁣, 11/8). It involves Israel gradually withdrawing from Palestinian land. That is not on the agenda for Netanyahu nor his right-wing allies.

The demands for complete disarmament of Hamas are not genuine negotiating tactics; they are simply a way to prolong Israeli occupation of large swaths of Gaza. The “yellow line″⁣ is moving inexorably forward, squeezing Gazans into a smaller and smaller portion of their own country. The “yellow line’ is moving inexorably forward, squeezing Gazans into a smaller and smaller portion of their own country.

Lorel Thomas, Blackburn South Smart phone problems

Smart phones are radically different to pinball machines, colour television or video games (“″⁣Not snowflakes’: Severe mental disorders surge among young people,” 11/8). Smart phones are carried 24 hours a day, potentially exposing their users to parasocial media and preventing or reducing rsocial contact with friends and family .

The young are particularly susceptible having grown up with smart phones while their brains are developing.

There’s nothing intrinsically wrong with smart phones; they’re great for making phone calls, receiving texts - it’s many of the parasocial apps and games that cause the harm.

Wayne Robinson, Kingsley, WA



AND ANOTHER THING Matt Golding Anthony Albanese

Anthony Albanese needs to stop going on podcasts. He has neither the wit nor dexterity required. In his attempts to appeal to increase his reach and popularity, he only reveals his limitations.

Russell Kidd, Carnegie Anthony Albanese can dismiss his tasteless comments about Japanese melons as much as he likes but his body language was explicit.

Robyn Williams, Sale When it comes to real gambling reform, Anthony Albanese is a complete melon.

Geoff Allen, Parkdale



A great cartoon from Cathy Wilcox (10/8) on the PM and gambling! He prefers to see it as a harmless punt and ignores its potential to destroy lives and families,

Phil Lipshut, Elsternwick John Howard served his time years ago. If I were Albanese or Taylor (or should I say if I were in the shoes of either of them), I’d ignore him too.

Brandon Mack, Deepdene Furthermore

Barnaby Joyce says why can’t Australians pick strawberries and not migrants? Off you go then Barnaby.

Ross Hosking, Blackwood, SA The government can no longer be in any doubt. The state of potholes in our roads is a big issue in the upcoming election.

Matthew Hamilton, Kew Gridiron comes to Melbourne – do the helmets protect their heads one wonders? At what cost?

Greg Curtin, Nunawading



Could I remind your correspondent (Letters ″⁣Global and local″⁣, 11/8) the reason for expending all the energy on building the Suburban Rail Loop tunnels is ultimately to remove vehicles from the road, thus reducing greenhouse gases.

Suzanne Palmer-Holton, Seaford Is Trump trying to avenge the humiliating hostage crisis of 1979, when Iran imprisoned 52 Americans in the American embassy in Tehran for 444 days? I think he’s just opened the door to more humiliation.

Tim Durbridge, Brunswick The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Educators on the line in proposed Zoos Victoria job cuts
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaAnimals Educators on the line in proposed Zoos Victoria job cuts Kieran Rooney August 11, 2026 — 7:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than a third of educator positions could be cut from Zoos Victoria under proposed redundancies, prompting fears the visits by 150,000 students each year will be cut and the standard of teaching affected. The Age revealed in June that Zoos Victoria was preparing a restructure that would cut up to 70 full-time roles from its 950-strong workforce – a figure the organisation has pushed back on as it consults staff about the changes. Among the most contentious proposals is a 38 per cent reduction in education staff at Melbourne Zoo – from roughly 6.2 full-time staff to 3.8 – who assist in teaching students and other groups about wildlife and conservation. A baby giraffe at Melbourne Zoo. Jo Howell The Community and Public Sector Union and United Workers Union said on Monday that about 600 staff – almost two-thirds of the organisation’s workforce – had responded to the proposed changes, which would be finalised later this month.



CPSU state secretary Jiselle Hanna said any cuts to education staff would devastate the 150,000 students who visited Melbourne Zoo, Werribee Zoo, Healesville Sanctuary and Kyabram Fauna Park every year. Related Article Animals Bailout backing was offered to Zoos Victoria a year before job cuts “Staff are telling us that they will not be able to maintain the volume of visits or the standard of education for young learners if these cuts go ahead,” Hanna said. “If this restructure is genuinely being driven by financial pressures, then why would cuts be made to an entity that brings in millions of dollars annually through school visits? “The impacted staff are highly skilled workers with decades of experience. They keep visitors educated, entertained and, most importantly, safe.”



The CPSU and the United Workers Union have urgently demanded Zoos Victoria wind back the scale of the cuts, arguing it will have flow-on effects across all parts of the organisation as staff are asked to handle new responsibilities. “This restructure process has demonstrated how out of touch the executive team is with the realities of the zoo and the work that zoo staff undertake,” Hanna said. A Zoos Victoria spokesperson said frontline services would not be impacted, as official consultation continued before a final decision was announced on August 25. “Our employees have provided valuable feedback through this consultation process, and we are considering this feedback carefully,” the spokesperson said. “Zoos Victoria will remain a world-class wildlife destination, and our commitment to fighting wildlife extinction remains.”



The Age has previously reported staff concerns that the restructure could also affect wildlife and conservation roles across the organisation, however, Zoos Victoria says frontline and animal care roles will not be directly affected. Related Article Animals Zoos Victoria to cut up to 70 jobs, including in conservation and wildlife Animal Justice Party MP Georgie Purcell said Zoos Victoria should be upfront about what the cuts would mean for conservation programs. “With bird flu ravaging our state and our volunteer wildlife carers under enormous strain, we simply can’t afford to lose any of the dedicated Zoos Victoria teams whose job it is to respond to injured wildlife and protect threatened species,” she said. “It’s simply not good enough to say there won’t be cuts to frontline services without being clear about what happens to the conservation and wildlife rescue work that sits behind them.”

World.title: Domestic violence charges against Bondi hero Ahmed Al Ahmed to be dropped
World.content:
Domestic violence charges against Bondi hero Ahmed Al Ahmed to be dropped

Al Ahmed was charged following an alleged incident at a Bankstown property in March, where police accused him of common assault and stalking.

World.title: Labor blasted for restricting prisoner rights after gangland boss’s court victory
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaPrisons Labor blasted for restricting prisoner rights after gangland boss’s court victory Lachlan Abbott and Erin Pearson August 11, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wrongfully imprisoned academic Kylie Moore-Gilbert, the ombudsman and a chorus of human rights advocates have voiced serious unease about the Carroll government’s plan to curtail the right of Victorian prisoners to access fresh air daily. Labor is poised to pass legislation with opposition support in the upper house this week to make the right to open air for at least an hour each day “subject to operational considerations” in prisons, despite conceding this breaches Victoria’s human rights charter. Kylie Moore-Gilbert spent years imprisoned in Iran on trumped-up espionage charges. Scott McNaughton The Victorian Ombudsman wrote to the leaders of both major parties this month to express concern about the bill, which opponents say does not adhere to the international minimum standards for prisoners, a set of rules named after Nelson Mandela. The government argues the change is necessary to prevent lawsuits such as that brought by murderer and crime boss George Marrogi, who won a Supreme Court judgment in January that found some of his maximum-security units did not provide adequate open-air access.



Amendments to the Corrections Act would allow the state to limit a prisoner’s open-air rights “on an ongoing basis or for extended periods of time”, according to the bill’s explanatory memorandum. The legislation also stops the state from paying damages for any previous breaches of a prisoner’s open-air rights, despite corrections being plagued with prolonged lockdowns in recent years. Moore-Gilbert, who spent 804 days detained in Iran, said even the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps provided her access to fresh air while she was imprisoned. “This terror organisation gave me a minimum of 30 minutes a day outside, even when I was held in solitary confinement,” she said.



“Why on earth is the Victorian government proposing to lower its human rights standards beneath those of even the despotic regime in Iran?” Related Article Crime Underworld kingpin wins court battle over ‘inhumane’ prison conditions Then-corrections minister Paul Hamer told parliament in June there “may not be any suitable infrastructure solutions available” to provide high-risk prisoners like Marrogi with open air, as the recent Supreme Court decision required. The murderer and drug trafficker is one of the most challenging prisoners in Victoria, having run a $55 million drug empire from behind bars and once spraying prison guards with faeces. Marrogi’s lawsuit revealed corrections officials believed he had previously plotted to break out from Barwon Prison via helicopter.



Prison managers argued different types of roof mesh were necessary for Marrogi’s rear yards to prevent escape, self-harm, weather damage, and contraband being thrown in. Justice Claire Harris, however, ruled certain partially covered cells in the Exford unit at the Metropolitan Remand Centre, plus the Olearia, Melaleuca and Acacia units at Barwon Prison, did not provide adequate open-air access. Harris said there was no “clear bright line” for what constituted being “in open air” but noted the current right relied on experiencing weather, suggesting exposure to the elements such as rain, wind and sun outside was required. Her decision has been appealed.



Opposition police spokesman Brad Battin told parliament the Coalition would support proposed changes to open-air rights as it recognised they were not always practical. “I think it is important that the management of the prison can make a decision in the best interests of staff – not in the best interests of prisoners – to protect the staff who are within that prison,” he said. Jailed crime boss George Marrogi claims he’s being treated cruelly in prison. However, ombudsman Marlo Baragwanath told this masthead: “If these changes are passed into law, they’ll have wide-ranging and significant human rights implications for anyone in custody.” Marrogi’s lawyer, Zyg Zayler, said changing the law after Harris’ decision reflected poorly on Victoria.



“The quality of our society is determined by how we treat our most difficult people,” he said. “Maybe their prospects would be better if we didn’t treat them inhumanely.” Former prisoner Kelly Flanagan said her mental health suffered enormously when she was stuck inside at the Dame Phyllis Frost Centre, where an 18-year-old died last month. Wiradjuri woman Kelly Flanagan outside the Dame Phyllis Frost Centre last year. Luis Enrique Ascui “You’re stripping them of everything that makes them human by taking away their fresh air,” Flanagan said. A state government spokesperson said the open-air right for Victorian prisoners remained, and the changes were “operational decisions” to ensure access could be managed safely.



“This brings us into line with other jurisdictions like NSW, and makes a longstanding practice clear in law,” they said. NSW prisoners confined to their cell are allowed an hour each day for exercise in the open air subject to “practical limitations” but only those “that may from time to time arise”. Normal prisoners are allowed at least two hours outside. The Victorian Aboriginal Legal Service said making open-air rights subject to “operational considerations” was a “vague and open-ended excuse” to deny prisoners fresh air. Australian Lawyers Alliance spokesman Greg Barns, SC, also took issue with retrospective legislation removing compensation rights and called for it to be withdrawn.



Liberty Victoria president Gemma Cafarella said the bill marked just the fifth time a declaration to override Victoria’s human rights charter had been used since it was enacted in 2006. Liberal MP Chris Crewther said last month the government had “not adequately explained why an indefinite exclusion is necessary” compared with a normal five-year exemption. A protest against the bill is planned outside Victorian parliament on Wednesday before a vote in the Legislative Council is expected on Thursday. World.title: ‘Training objects for violence’: Cops, experts fear perverse motive behind ‘sex doll murder scene’
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWCrime ‘Training objects for violence’: Cops, experts fear perverse motive behind ‘sex doll murder scene’ Perry Duffin and Riley Walter August 11, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: Graphic content A sex doll found in a suitcase on a remote stretch of NSW road was dressed like a sex worker with mock bruises and injuries, sparking fears among police and experts that whoever dumped it was acting out a violent fantasy against women. Discovery of the doll on Sunday triggered a short-lived murder investigation when it was located by two men during a bathroom break on a road south of Goulburn. The suitcase containing the doll was discovered metres from the roadside close to the pine tree. Kate Geraghty So disturbing were the doll’s features – a head of rain-matted hair, a nose piercing and markings that resembled bruising and grazes – the men thought they had uncovered an awful tragedy.



Police close to the investigation but not authorised to speak publicly are now concerned the person who dumped the doll might have been acting out a violent fetish. Caitlin Roper, campaigns manager for anti-sexploitation movement Collective Shout, told this masthead the dumping of sex dolls was not uncommon. A sex doll in a packing crate at a sex culture festival in China in 2013. Newer models are much more life-like and can be customised to meet buyers’ desires. NYT “People discover what they initially believe is a woman’s body – often mutilated, ripped apart or decapitated – but is actually a doll,” she said. “These dolls become training objects for violence against women and children.”



Roper has spent hours on sex-doll forums, monitoring owners’ who say they are buying dolls to practise extreme sexual abuse. In 2022, she published a book Sex Dolls, Robots and Woman Hating: The Case for Resistance, documenting her findings. “They shared realistic scenarios of predation that they acted out on their dolls. One user posted photographs of a doll bound with rope, explaining that he was practising how to tie women up and render them helpless,” she said. Superintendent Linda Bradbury revealed that the suitcase did not contain human remains - but instead a sex doll. KATE GERAGHTY “Other men described being so rough that they broke their dolls and had to send them away for repairs. One lamented that his doll would not fight back, saying, ‘If Tonya fought back, I’d be in heaven’.” As with the find on the weekend, many on the forum adorned their doll with fake bruises, cuts, blood and injuries.



Roper said there are multiple cases involving the owners of adult and child sex dolls – the latter are illegal in Australia – going on to carry out violence against women and girls. She pointed to the recent case of Perth man Jason William Forbes, a doll owner, who plotted to kidnap a young girl and keep her as a sex slave in his attic. “[Forbes] allegedly developed an elaborate plot to abduct a child. He had soundproofed an attic, researched chloroform, looked up schools and childcare centres, and marked locations on a map,” Roper said. “He was intercepted after purchasing a second doll.” Doll owner Jason William Forbes plotted to kidnap a girl and hold her captive in the attic of his Perth home. Roper said sex dolls, even childlike ones, are often dismissed as fantasies or mere objects. But many of the men she witnessed online have treated their dolls as partners.



“These are not simply sex toys; they are replicas of human beings that some owners regard as partners.” Criminologist and former NSW Police detective Vince Hurley said using child-like sex dolls could desensitise offenders and normalise abuse of children. It could also evolve into in-person offending. ‘The issue of consent doesn’t even come into it because they just use these sex dolls as they see fit, whenever they see fit.’ Vince Hurley, criminologist “It could reinforce any sexual attraction to children over time that might traverse into the real world,” Hurley said. “There would be nothing to say that it stops in their fake or false reality and then doesn’t transition into a real child.”



Men using sex dolls, similar to those using artificial intelligence chatbots, avoid rejection. Doing so warps their perception of relationships and consent, he said. “They will always have this perception that women will always be accepting of their behaviour and their attitudes because the chatbots never contradict them,” he said. “The issue of consent doesn’t even come into it because they just use these sex dolls as they see fit, whenever they see fit.” The Australian market for sex dolls Life-like sex dolls similar to the one found on Sunday are readily available online and can be customised to meet buyers’ desires.



Related Article Updated

Crime Police said a body was found in a suitcase. It turned out to be a sex doll High-end dolls retail for thousands of dollars. The growing market represents what police say is a worrying trend. In June, Australian Federal Police arrested a 31-year-old Quakers Hill man for trying to import a child sex doll, and allegedly found a second at his home. AFP Commander Jo Cameron said child-like sex dolls may desensitise users from the physical, emotional and psychological harm inflicted on real children. “Child-like sex dolls are not harmless objects – they are illegal to possess and can contribute to the exploitation of victims in the community,” Cameron said.
